      Key Findings

      • Library volunteers contribute an estimated 50+ million hours annually, valued at over $1.6 billion - roughly equivalent to 25,000 full-time positions.
      • Over 6,000 Friends of Libraries groups operate nationwide, generating $100+ million annually through book sales and membership drives.
      • 90%+ of US public libraries use volunteers in some capacity, ranging from Friends book sales to program assistance to tutoring.
      • The Independent Sector values volunteer time at $33.49/hour (2024), a figure used by libraries for grant reporting and impact statements.
      • VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) programs in libraries return millions in tax refunds to low-income communities each filing season.
      • Volunteer management requires dedicated staff time, background checks, liability insurance, and training - costs that smaller libraries struggle to absorb.
      • Teen volunteers often satisfy high school community service requirements while developing job skills and library advocacy habits.
      • Corporate volunteer partnerships bring both labor and sponsorship dollars, but require coordination and staff supervision.

      This document surveys the landscape of organized library advocacy in the United States -- the coordinated, sustained effort by which libraries, their professional associations, their trustees and Friends, and dedicated political-action organizations secure public funding, defend the freedom to read, and shape the laws and budgets that determine what libraries can do.       Overview

      Library advocacy is the organized, sustained effort to influence public policy, public budgets, and public opinion in favor of libraries. It encompasses direct lobbying of legislators and officials, grassroots mobilization of patrons and community members, public-awareness campaigns, ballot-measure campaigns, media engagement, and coalition-building with allied education, civil-liberties, and broadband organizations.       Lobbying Rules

      Library advocacy in the United States is shaped by federal tax law that distinguishes what different kinds of organizations may do. Most libraries and their support organizations are 501(c)(3) public charities, which may lobby but may not engage in partisan electoral activity. A smaller number of organizations -- notably EveryLibrary -- are 501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations, which may engage in partisan electoral activity and direct ballot campaigning so long as it is not their primary purpose. Understanding this distinction is essential to lawful library advocacy. {'lobbying_permitt

      Grassroots advocacy mobilizes ordinary library users and community members -- not just professional lobbyists -- to contact their officials, show up at hearings, and vote.       Key Findings

      • Library advocacy is structurally essential because roughly 85 percent of US public library revenue comes from local government -- overwhelmingly property taxes -- making libraries unusually dependent on continuous public and political support at the municipal, county, and ballot-box level.
      • Advocacy operates on three reinforcing tiers -- federal (IMLS, E-Rate, copyright, privacy), state (state-aid formulas, anti-censorship, state E-Rate and broadband), and local (appropriations, bonds, levies, and library districts) -- each with its own decision-makers, tactics, and legal rules.
      • The ALA Office for Library Advocacy and Public Policy and Advocacy Office are the national hub for federal library lobbying, providing the toolkits, training, and action tools (District Dispatch, the ALA action center, #FundLibraries, National Library Legislative Day, Letter to Congress) that mobilize the field.
      • EveryLibrary is the only national 501(c)(4) dedicated exclusively to library ballot-measure and pro-library electoral advocacy; paired with the EveryLibrary Institute (c3) for research and education, it fills the direct-campaigning role that ALA, state associations, and Friends groups cannot lawfully perform as charities.
      • Library ballot measures pass at a notably high rate of roughly 70 to 80 percent over the long run, reflecting strong baseline public support for libraries and the effectiveness of organized library vote campaigns supported by EveryLibrary and local committees.
      • The tax-law split between 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4) is the backbone of compliant library advocacy: c3s (ALA, state associations, Friends, United for Libraries) may do limited lobbying and nonpartisan voter education but no partisan electoral activity, while c4s (EveryLibrary) may run direct ballot campaigns -- and public libraries themselves, as units of government, face anti-hijacking limits on using public resources to urge a vote.
      • United for Libraries -- the ALA division uniting trustees, advocates, Friends, and foundations, and successor to ALTA and Friends of Libraries USA -- trains the citizen-advocate backbone of local library advocacy through the Trustee Academy, Advocate Academy, and National Friends of Libraries Week.
      • Thousands of local Friends of the Library groups form one of the largest volunteer-driven advocacy networks in the country, speaking at council and board meetings, funding supplemental services, and organizing grassroots support for library budgets and ballot measures.
      • State library associations run annual advocacy days at every state capitol -- the state-level analogue of National Library Legislative Day -- that bring librarians, trustees, and Friends to meet their state legislators on the state-aid, anti-censorship, and broadband agendas that determine state-level library support.
      • Digital advocacy tools compress the time between a policy threat and mass constituent contact: ALA's District Dispatch and action center, the #FundLibraries hashtag, the I Love Libraries website, and EveryLibrary's digital toolkit let a small staff mobilize thousands of patrons within hours.

      Social Media Deep Dive

      This document surveys how United States libraries use social media platforms to reach patrons, promote collections and programs, deliver reference and customer service, and advance their public-service missions in a fragmented digital attention economy. It is organized around the major platforms in order of library adoption - Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, TikTok, and YouTube - and then by the cross-cutting themes that shape library social practice: content strategy, viral campaigns, the rise o

      Platform Overview

      Social media adoption among US public library systems is effectively universal. Surveys of public library communications consistently find that more than 90 percent of systems maintain an active Facebook page, making Facebook the baseline transactional channel for hours, closures, events, and announcements. Adoption of Instagram and TikTok is lower in absolute terms but growing fastest, and is increasingly concentrated among systems serving younger demographic cores. {'facebook': 'Estimated 90 to 95 percent of US public library systems maintain a Facebook presence; it remains th

      Facebook is the workhorse platform for US libraries: the channel where operational, transactional information is published and where the broadest adult audience can be reached without specialized production effort.       Instagram Presence

      Instagram is the dominant visual and brand channel for US libraries, used to present the library as a welcoming, aesthetic, and culturally current institution. It is the platform where library identity is most actively constructed. Physical book displays - themed monthly displays (Black History Month, Pride, Banned Books Week, summer reading, seasonal cozy reads) - are photographed and posted as carousels and Reels. A distinctive library use of Twitter/X is real-time customer service: patrons ask about hours, holds, interlibrary loan status, database access problems, and event details, and libraries respond publicly or move the conversation to direct message.       YouTube Presence

      YouTube is the library platform for durable, long-form, and instructional video. Unlike the ephemeral feeds of TikTok and Instagram Stories, YouTube content is searchable, evergreen, and accrues views over years, making it the natural home for content patrons will return to repeatedly.       Leading library systems approach social media as digital marketing rather than as ad hoc posting: they define audience segments and goals (card sign-ups, program attendance, database use, summer-reading enrollment), maintain a content calendar, and measure outcomes against those goals rather than vanity metrics alone.       Key Findings

      • Social media adoption by US public libraries is near-universal: more than 90 percent of systems maintain a Facebook presence, making Facebook the baseline operational channel, while Instagram and TikTok show the fastest growth and the greatest reach to younger patrons libraries most want to serve.
      • The New York Public Library's Instagram (~500,000 followers) is the largest-followed library Instagram account in the United States, while the Library of Congress is the most-followed US library account overall across platforms; Boston Public Library and other flagship municipal systems anchor the next tier.
      • #LibraryTok is the single largest source of viral reach in library social media, with individual videos routinely accumulating millions of views and producing measurable, same-week spikes in card registrations, holds, and visits that no other library channel reliably generates.
      • BookTok, though not library-created, is one of the most consequential external forces on library circulation: titles that trend on BookTok repeatedly generate holds queues in the hundreds or thousands and have revived backlist titles years after publication, forcing libraries to track social trends and accelerate copy purchasing.
      • Instagram is the dominant channel for library visual identity, where themed book displays and the 'shelfie' genre construct the library as a welcoming, aesthetically current institution; consistent visual branding at leading systems sets a template smaller systems imitate.
      • Twitter/X remains valuable for real-time customer service and library advocacy networks, but engagement and link reach have declined since the 2022 rebrand, prompting many systems to shift effort to Instagram, TikTok, Threads, and Bluesky while retaining X for service-status updates.
      • YouTube is the library platform for durable, instructional, and evergreen content - recorded storytimes, author talks, and database tutorials - and accrues value over years, justifying its higher production cost where long-term reuse is the goal.
      • Recorded storytime on YouTube, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, raises copyright questions that libraries manage through public-domain works, publisher read-aloud permissions, and documented fair-use reasoning, illustrating how library social practice intersects with intellectual-property law.
      • Effective library social media operates as digital marketing rather than ad hoc posting: defined goals, a content calendar, platform-native assets, and measurement of conversion to cards, registration, and database use - not vanity metrics - separate high-performing systems from merely active ones.
      • ALA and state-library social media policies converge on common elements - authorized posters, separation of personal and institutional voice, patron privacy, viewpoint-neutral moderation, accessibility, and copyright awareness - that allow libraries to speak informally online without abandoning their public-service and intellectual-freedom commitments.

      Cataloging Deep Dive

      Comprehensive overview of cataloging standards, classification systems, subject access, authority control, and the transition from MARC to BIBFRAME linked data in US libraries.

      Overview

      Cataloging is the process of creating bibliographic records that describe library materials, enabling discovery, identification, selection, and access. From card catalogs to MARC (1960s) to RDA (2010) to BIBFRAME (2012-present), cataloging evolved from physical cards to linked data. IFLA LRM provides the conceptual model: work, expression, manifestation, item entities with relationships and attributes.

      MARC Standards

      MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) was developed by Library of Congress in the 1960s. MARC 21 remains dominant in US libraries. MARC records consist of leader, directory, and variable fields with indicators and subfields. 245 (title), 100/700 (author), 260/264 (publication), 300 (description), 650 (subject), 050 (LC call number), 082 (Dewey), 856 (electronic location). International standard defining MARC record structure for interchange. MARC being gradually replaced by BIBFRAME but remains deeply embedded in ILS systems.

      RDA Transition

      RDA (Resource Description and Access) replaced AACR2 in 2013, adopted by Library of Congress and PCC. Based on IFLA LRM, focuses on user tasks (find, identify, select, obtain), uses vocabulary instead of abbreviations. Online subscription resource maintained by RDA Steering Committee. 2021 restructured RDA aligned with IFLA LRM. LC, PCC, and most major US libraries adopted RDA by 2013-2015.

      Classification Systems

      Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC) created by Melvil Dewey 1876, used by 200K+ libraries worldwide, 10 main classes (000-999). Library of Congress Classification (LCC) developed 1897-1900s, used by most academic and research libraries, 21 classes A-Z. National Library of Medicine Classification, SuDocs for government documents, BISAC for retail.

      Subject Headings

      Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) - most widely used subject vocabulary, 400,000+ headings. FAST (Faceted Application of Subject Terminology) - simplified LCSH for digital applications. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) - NLM controlled vocabulary for life sciences. Sears List of Subject Headings - simpler alternative for school and small public libraries. Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms - separate vocabulary for genre/form terms.

      OCLC WorldCat

      WorldCat is the worlds largest bibliographic database maintained by OCLC, containing 500+ million records from libraries worldwide. Libraries contribute original cataloging and copy catalog from WorldCat, reducing duplicate effort. OCLC WorldShare Management Services is a cloud-based library management platform. OCLC Connexion is the primary cataloging interface for WorldCat. 16,000+ member libraries; 500M+ records; 2B+ holdings.

      Authority Control

      Authority control ensures consistent forms of names, titles, and subjects across the catalog. Name Authority Cooperative (NACO) - PCC program contributing authority records to LCNAF. Subject Authority Cooperative (SACO) - PCC program for proposing new LCSH terms. LC/NACO Authority File contains 10+ million authority records.

      Linked Data & BIBFRAME

      BIBFRAME is the Library of Congress initiative to replace MARC with a linked data model for the Semantic Web. 2012 (BIBFRAME 2.0 released 2016) BIBFRAME uses Work, Instance, and Item entities with linked relationships as URIs. LC transitioning cataloging workflows to BIBFRAME using Sinopia linked data editor. Transition requires new tools, staff training, and vendor support. Many libraries use hybrid workflows. BIBFRAME records serialized in RDF (Turtle, JSON-LD) rather than ISO 2709.

      • Authority control through NACO ensures consistent name headings across 10+ million authority records.
      • FAST simplifies LCSH for digital discovery with faceted subject terms for next-generation catalogs.

      This deep summary maps the technology vendor landscape that powers modern U.S. libraries.       The integrated library system (ILS) is the operational backbone of a library, unifying cataloging, circulation, acquisitions, serials control, and the public-access catalog in a single software suite. Since the 2010s the market has bifurcated between traditional ILS products -- mature, often locally hosted, organized around a bibliographic record store -- and next-generation library services platforms (LSP) such as Ex Libris Alma and OCLC WorldShare, which are cloud-native, metadata-driven, and built to unify print and electronic resource management.       Discovery Layers

      A discovery layer is the modern search interface that sits in front of a library's ILS, institutional repository, database subscriptions, and digital collections, presenting patrons with a single Google-like search box across otherwise siloed content. Discovery layers index article metadata, full-text where licensed, and local catalog records, then rank results with relevance algorithms tuned for library content. The four dominant platforms -- Primo, Summon, EBSCO Discovery Service, and WorldCat Discovery -- are typically bundled with or closely tied to a vendor's ILS/LSP, and the ch

      eBook Platforms

      Ebook and audiobook lending platforms license publisher content and deliver it to patrons through library-branded apps. Two commercial models dominate: the one-copy-one-user model (titles licensed like physical books, with holds queues), exemplified by OverDrive/Libby and Axis 360, and the simultaneous-use / pay-per-checkout model, exemplified by Hoopla. cloudLibrary blends both approaches. These platforms mediate publisher licensing terms -- including expiring licenses and per-checkout fees -- that drive much of the complexity in library digital collections budgets. {'vendor': '

      Database Vendors

      Database aggregators license scholarly journals, reference works, ebooks, newspapers, and primary-source collections and resell access to libraries, usually via annual subscriptions negotiated directly or through consortia. Four providers dominate the academic and large-public-library market: EBSCO, Gale, ProQuest, and JSTOR. Their offerings overlap substantially but differ in index depth, full-text coverage, subject strength, and the discovery interfaces they feed. {'vendor': 'EBSCO Information Services', 'flagship_products': ['EBSCOhost (aggregated database

      Makerspace Technology

      Library makerspaces stock equipment spanning additive and subtractive fabrication, textile and craft tools, electronics, and audio/video production. Three hardware vendors are especially common in library makerspaces: MakerBot (3D printing), Cricut (computer-controlled cutting), and Glowforge (desktop laser cutting). These consumer/prosumer-grade machines balance capability, safety, and ease of use -- critical considerations for staff-supervised public environments. {'category': '3D printing (Fused Deposition Modeling)', 'vendor': 'MakerBot (a Stratasys compa

      Digital preservation addresses the long-term stewardship of born-digital and digitized content -- institutional records, digitized special collections, research data, and web archives -- against format obsolescence, media degradation, and bit rot. Two platforms dominate library adoption: Preservica, a commercial preservation and access system, and Archive-It, the Internet Archive's web-archiving service.       Key Findings

      • The library technology market is highly consolidated: Clarivate's 2021 acquisition of ProQuest placed Alma, Primo, Sierra, and Polaris under one corporate parent, leaving libraries with fewer but larger vendors spanning ILS, discovery, and eresource management.
      • A clear split has emerged between traditional integrated library systems (Polaris, Sierra, Symphony, Carlo, Atriuum), dominant in public libraries, and next-generation library services platforms (Alma, WorldShare), dominant in academic and research libraries.
      • Open-source ILS products have captured meaningful share in the public-library sector: Koha (supported by ByWater Solutions) is the most widely deployed open-source ILS worldwide, and Evergreen (supported by Equinox Software) leads in statewide and large public-library consortia such as Georgia PINES and the Indiana Evergreen consortium.
      • Discovery-layer choice typically tracks ILS/LSP choice: Primo is paired with Alma, WorldCat Discovery with WorldShare Management Services, and EBSCO Discovery Service is frequently paired with the open-source FOLIO platform.
      • OverDrive and its Libby app are near-ubiquitous in U.S. public libraries (over 90% of systems), and the 2023 retirement of the legacy OverDrive app consolidated patrons on Libby, the dominant gateway to digital borrowing.
      • Two competing digital-lending business models persist: one-copy-one-user licensing with holds (OverDrive/Libby, Axis 360) and simultaneous-use pay-per-checkout (Hoopla), with cloudLibrary blending both; the pay-per-checkout model trades budget predictability for instant patron gratification.
      • Publisher licensing economics constrain digital collections far more than print: libraries routinely pay several times retail for ebook licenses that expire after 26 or 52 checkouts, and the briefly-imposed 2019-2020 Macmillan embargo demonstrated how quickly publisher terms can disrupt library service.
      • EBSCO, Gale, ProQuest, and JSTOR dominate database aggregation, with overlapping but differentiated portfolios: EBSCO and ProQuest lead aggregated journal coverage, ProQuest owns dissertations and historical newspapers, Gale leads in school and public-library reference, and JSTOR is the near-universal scholarly journal archive.
      • Most database subscriptions are negotiated through consortia, which pool demand to secure better pricing and broader title access than individual libraries could obtain alone.
      • Library makerspace purchasing favors prosumer-grade equipment that balances capability, safety, and ease of staff supervision; MakerBot 3D printers, Cricut cutters, and Glowforge laser cutters are the most common brands, chosen for vendor support and curriculum materials as much as for the hardware itself.

      Streaming Deep Dive

      This document brings together, in one place, the streaming-video and streaming-music platforms that American public, academic, and school libraries offer their patrons, the licensing economics that govern them, the usage and budget patterns they produce, and the in-library programming -- film clubs, documentary discussion series, and community cinema events -- that libraries build on top of them. It centers on Kanopy (the documentary and Criterion-focused film service with roughly 4,000+ partner

      Overview

      Over the last decade U.S. libraries have shifted a meaningful share of their collections from physical media -- DVDs, CDs, and audiobook discs -- into licensed streaming. The shift is driven by two forces: the collapse of consumer demand for physical discs, which has shrunk circulating DVD and CD collections, and patron expectations shaped by commercial streaming services (Netflix, Spotify, Apple Music, Disney+). Libraries cannot license those commercial services for re-distribution, so they have built their streaming presence through specialist library-licensed vendors: Kanopy and Hoopla for

      Music Streaming

      Library music streaming is a smaller, specialized segment distinct from commercial music services. The principal platforms are Freegal Music (DRM-free downloads and streaming from the Sony Music Entertainment catalog, with an estimated 18 million+ songs), Naxos Music Library (classical and world-music streaming for libraries and academic institutions), and Qello Concerts (concert films and music documentaries, often reached via Hoopla BingePass). Hoopla itself includes music as roughly 19% of its 2016 content mix within its multi-format app. Commercial services such as Spotify and Apple Music

      Licensing Models

      Licensing models are the single most important factor shaping library streaming. Because libraries do not own streaming content the way they own a DVD or CD, every title is governed by a license that determines how many patrons can use it at once, how much the library pays, and for how long. The two poles of the market are pay-per-use (the library pays each time a patron watches or listens, giving instant access but unpredictable costs) and simultaneous use (unlimited concurrent patrons for a flat fee or per-circ charge, eliminating holds). Between them sit one-copy/one-user and metered-access

      Key Findings

      • Library streaming is built on licensed specialist vendors, not commercial services: Netflix, Disney+, Spotify, Apple Music, and the Criterion Channel cannot be licensed to libraries for re-distribution, so Kanopy, Hoopla, OverDrive video, IndieFlix, Freegal, Naxos, and Qello fill a distinct niche rather than competing head-to-head with consumer streaming.
      • Kanopy is the leading library film-streaming service, with roughly 4,000+ partner libraries and universities, and its Criterion Collection, documentary, PBS, A24, and Great Courses depth makes it the backbone of library film clubs and cinephile programming; its pay-per-view (30-second-trigger) model is both its differentiator and its cost-control problem.
      • The 2019 discontinuation of Kanopy by the three largest U.S. public libraries (NYPL, Brooklyn PL, Queens PL) over unpredictable pay-per-view costs became the defining episode of library streaming budgeting, pushing the field toward monthly per-patron play-credit caps as standard cost control.
      • Hoopla differentiates on instant, simultaneous, no-holds borrowing across six formats -- movies, TV, music, audiobooks, e-books, and comics/manga -- and its pay-per-circ model is the principal budget-volatility drawback, leading systems such as Sacramento Public to question the model's sustainability.
      • Licensing models, not catalog size, are the central tension of library streaming: the choice between pay-per-use (Kanopy pay-per-view, Hoopla pay-per-circ), simultaneous use, one-copy/one-user, metered access, and flat-fee subscription determines both patron experience and budget predictability, and most libraries run a portfolio of models to balance the two.
      • Video is a small but growing slice of library digital circulation -- roughly 4% of OverDrive checkouts -- as physical DVD collections decline, and OverDrive's 2020-2021 absorption of the RBdigital/Access Video on Demand catalog plus its 2021 acquisition of Kanopy consolidated library streaming video under one corporate parent.
      • Library music streaming occupies a budget-limited niche separate from commercial services: Freegal Music offers permanent DRM-free MP3 downloads from the Sony catalog (an estimated 18 million+ songs), Naxos dominates classical and academic streaming with liner notes and libretti, and Qello concert films reach patrons via Hoopla BingePass.
      • COVID-19 produced a structural step-change in library digital circulation -- OverDrive checkouts jumped from 350M (2019) to 430M (2020) and kept climbing to roughly 600M (2023) -- making streaming and digital borrowing a permanent, not cyclical, share of library circulation and permanently expanding audiovisual streaming budgets.
      • The vendor market has consolidated sharply: OverDrive (Rakuten 2015, KKR 2020, B Corporation 2023) absorbed RBdigital (2020-2021) and Kanopy (2021), Bibliotheca sold cloudLibrary to OCLC (April 2024), and Baker & Taylor's Axis 360 declined under Follett, leaving a single dominant player, a strong #2 in Hoopla, and a tail of specialized niche vendors.
      • Content moderation has become a vendor challenge for streaming platforms: Hoopla faced a 2022 backlash over fascist and Holocaust-denial titles and a 2025 exposé over AI-generated 'slop' books with fictional authors, both of which directly cost libraries money on checkouts of dubious-quality material.

      Assessment Deep Dive

      This document provides a comprehensive overview of the frameworks, tools, and studies that U.S. public and networked libraries use to measure performance, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate impact. It traces the field's evolution from counting inputs and outputs (circulation, visits, holdings) toward measuring outcomes, the tangible changes in patrons' knowledge, skills, behavior, and circumstances that result from library service. It covers the Public Library Association's (PLA)

      Overview

      Library assessment is the systematic process of gathering, analyzing, and using evidence about library services, operations, and programs in order to understand their performance and impact, inform decision-making, improve service, and demonstrate accountability to stakeholders and funders. It spans everything from routine operational statistics (how many items circulated, how many people visited) to sophisticated outcome and impact studies that ask whether and how patrons' lives changed as a result of library service. Assessment serves three intertwined purposes. First, accountability: p

      Performance Metrics

      Performance metrics are the quantitative indicators libraries use to track the volume, reach, and efficiency of their services. For decades the dominant metrics were inputs and outputs, which remain essential for operations and comparability but are now supplemented by outcome and impact measures. The Public Library Association has been the leading national force in defining standard performance measures for public libraries and in helping libraries adopt them. The Public Library Association, a division of the American Library Association, has led public-library performance measurement for dec

      Outcome-Based Evaluation

      Outcome-based evaluation (OBE) is a methodology that defines the intended results of a program in terms of observable changes in participants, then measures whether those changes occurred. Rather than asking 'how much did we do?' OBE asks 'what changed for the people we served, and did our service contribute to that change?' It became a federal expectation for federally funded library projects and is central to demonstrating the public value of library service. OBE is typically organized around a logic model that links inputs (resources), activities (what the library does),

      PLA Project Outcome

      The Public Library Association operates several national projects that together form the backbone of outcome and performance measurement for U.S. public libraries. These projects give libraries free or low-cost tools, standardized instruments, training, and peer benchmarks so that even small systems can produce credible assessment evidence. {'overview': "Project Outcome is PLA's flagship outcome-measurement initiative, launched in 2015 with funding from the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS). It provides a free, standardized toolkit of patron surveys and an onl

      Community Surveys

      Community needs assessments and community surveys are the processes by which libraries learn about the people they serve: their demographics, aspirations, barriers, and unmet needs. While outcome measurement asks 'what changed for our program participants?', community assessment asks 'who is in our service area, what do they need, and are we reaching them?' Robust community assessment is the foundation for equitable service planning and for designing programs whose outcomes matter. ['Demographic analysis using U.S. Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data to und

      Library Impact Studies

      Library impact and return-on-investment (ROI) studies attempt to quantify the value libraries return to their communities, often in monetary terms. They translate library service into a ratio of benefit to cost (for example, dollars returned per dollar invested) or into total economic contribution, and are powerful advocacy tools when seeking funding or defending budgets. They also face methodological limits, since many library benefits (such as civic engagement or lifelong learning) resist easy monetization. A typical public-library ROI study estimates the direct and indirect economic benefit

      Data Collection Tools

      Data-collection and reporting tools give libraries the infrastructure to gather statistics consistently, submit them to state and federal authorities, and benchmark against peers. In the United States these range from the federal IMLS Public Libraries Survey to commercial platforms such as LibPAS offered by Counting Opinions. Many state library agencies adopt a single platform so that all public libraries in the state report through one system. {'name': 'IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS)', 'operator': 'The Institute of Museum and Library Services, the federa

      Benchmarking

      Benchmarking is the practice of comparing a library's measures against those of peer libraries or against the library's own past performance, in order to identify relative strengths, weaknesses, and improvement targets. It turns raw statistics into actionable context: a circulation figure means little until compared against libraries of similar size, budget, and service-area characteristics. Effective benchmarking depends on selecting appropriate peers, typically libraries matched on service-area population, operating budget, urbanicity, and governance structure. Comparing a small ru

      Key Findings

      • Library assessment has shifted decisively from counting inputs and outputs to measuring outcomes and impact, driven by PLA's Project Outcome (IMLS-funded, launched 2015), IMLS outcome-based evaluation requirements, and the international ISO 16439:2014 standard for assessing library impact.
      • Project Outcome gives public libraries a free, standardized survey toolkit and online platform across seven program areas, enabling hundreds of libraries to capture patron-reported knowledge, behavior, and circumstance changes and to benchmark outcomes against peers.
      • The IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS), descended from the Federal-State Cooperative System, remains the authoritative national dataset on public libraries, collected through state library agencies and published by IMLS for research, policy, and federal reporting.
      • Many state library agencies use the LibPAS platform from Counting Opinions as the official channel for annual statistical submission, combining data validation, peer benchmarking, and seamless forwarding to the IMLS PLS.
      • Outcome-based evaluation organizes programs around a logic model linking inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and impact, and is required by IMLS for its grantees under the federal accountability framework rooted in the Government Performance and Results Act (GPRA).
      • Return-on-investment and economic-impact studies, such as those conducted for the Free Library of Philadelphia, the State Library of Florida, and the South Carolina State Library, consistently find that public libraries return multiple dollars in value for every dollar of public investment, making them persuasive advocacy tools despite methodological limits.
      • Community needs assessments grounded in Census and American Community Survey data, patron and non-patron surveys, and focus groups are essential for equitable service planning and for designing programs whose outcomes match real community priorities.
      • Effective benchmarking depends on selecting true peer libraries matched by service-area population, budget, and urbanicity and on comparing per-capita and efficiency measures rather than raw outputs, so that comparisons are fair and actionable.
      • ISO 16439:2014 provides an internationally agreed vocabulary and structured set of methods for library impact assessment, helping libraries produce rigorous and comparable evidence rather than anecdote.
      • Attribution, survey fatigue, comparability, and limited staff capacity remain the chief challenges of library assessment, especially for small and rural libraries, and the field increasingly emphasizes equity in measurement to avoid under-representing marginalized populations.

      Law Deep Dive

      United States libraries operate inside a layered legal structure that draws on constitutional doctrine, federal statute, state enabling law, local charters, and the self-governance norms of the profession. This summary surveys that structure in one place. It begins with the constitutional foundations -- the First Amendment's protection of speech and the correlative right to receive information, the public forum doctrine as applied to the library building, and the Fourteenth Amendment's

      Legal Foundations

      Public, school, and academic libraries in the United States are governmental entities, so their conduct is constrained by the Constitution. The First Amendment -- binding on the states through the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment -- protects freedom of speech and of the press and, as the Supreme Court has recognized in a line of cases beginning with Lamont v. Postmaster General (1965), a correlative right to receive information and ideas. Because a library's central function is to make information available, the right to receive is the constitutional value most directly impl

      State Library Law

      Each of the fifty states and the District of Columbia authorizes the establishment of public libraries by statute. The state also establishes a state library agency (variously a state library, archives, or library development office) that administers federal LSTA funds, sets standards, and often oversees statewide resource sharing. State library law typically addresses: (1) the enabling of municipal and county libraries; (2) the creation of independent library districts; (3) library board structure and powers; (4) the confidentiality of library records; (5) open-meeting and public-records obli

      Local Library Law

      Local library law concerns how libraries are created and governed at the municipal, county, and special-district level. The state enabling statute supplies the menu of permissible structures; the local jurisdiction selects among them, often by ordinance or referendum. The choice of structure determines who controls the library, how it is funded, and how it may grow or combine with neighboring libraries. A municipal library is established by ordinance of a city or town council under state enabling authority. The library is a department of the municipality; its budget is typically a line item in

      Federal Laws

      Federal law affects libraries principally through spending conditions, generally applicable criminal and intelligence law, and copyright. There is no comprehensive federal library statute; instead a handful of statutes shape funding, internet access, patron privacy, and the legal uses of collection materials. {'citation': '20 U.S.C. ch. 72; administered by IMLS', 'year': 1996, 'description': 'The Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA), enacted as part of the Museum and Library Services Act, is the primary federal grant program for libraries. LST

      Board Governance

      A library board is the body to which state law entrusts governance of the library. Boards vary along several dimensions: whether members are appointed or elected; whether the board is governing (holds the budget and employs the director) or advisory (recommends to a city or county governing body); the size of the board and length of terms; and whether the library serves a single jurisdiction or a multi-county region. These structural choices, set by state law and local charter, determine the library's independence from political pressure and its capacity to plan over the long term. {'

      Policies

      Although not law in the enforceable sense, the policy statements of the American Library Association function as the professional constitution of U.S. librarianship and are frequently incorporated by reference into library board policy manuals, accreditation standards, and even state funding conditions. Two instruments are foundational: the Library Bill of Rights and the ALA Code of Ethics. {'adopted': '1939 (ALA Council)', 'amended': '1948, 1961, 1967, 1980, 1996', 'description': "The Library Bill of Rights is the ALA's foundational

      Intellectual Freedom Law

      Intellectual freedom in libraries is the point at which constitutional doctrine, state confidentiality law, and professional policy converge. The core legal propositions are five: (1) patrons have a First Amendment right to receive information; (2) a public library is a limited public forum subject to reasonable, content-neutral regulation; (3) a school library may not remove books for partisan political reasons (Pico); (4) a public library may exclude disruptive patrons through reasonable behavior rules (Kreimer); and (5) patron reading records are protected by state confidentiality statutes

      Key Findings

      • Libraries are creatures of state law: there is no general federal statute establishing public libraries, and the existence, funding, and governance of every public library trace to a state enabling statute implemented by a local ordinance, charter, or district referendum.
      • Every state and the District of Columbia has a statute protecting the confidentiality of library records, generally excepting registration and circulation records from public-records disclosure and limiting compelled disclosure to a court order or the patron's consent -- a near-universal consensus unusual in American law for its breadth.
      • The First Amendment right to receive information and ideas, recognized in Lamont v. Postmaster General (1965) and Stanley v. Georgia (1969), is the constitutional value most directly implicated in library access and is the doctrinal anchor for patrons' claims against content-based restrictions.
      • Public libraries are limited public forums under Kreimer v. Morristown (1992), which means content-based restrictions attract strict scrutiny while reasonable, viewpoint-neutral behavior rules are permitted -- giving libraries both the duty of access and the right to exclude disruptive patrons.
      • School libraries occupy a distinct doctrinal space: under the plurality in Board of Education v. Pico (1982), school boards may not remove books for partisan or political reasons, though later cases (Virgil) show that educational-suitability justifications can survive Pico scrutiny.
      • Internet filtering is legally settled at the federal-funding level: CIPA (2000) was upheld in United States v. American Library Association (2003) as a spending condition, and courts have since required that adults have a practical path to unblocking (Bradburn, 9th Cir. 2010).
      • Federal surveillance authority overlaps with library privacy: PATRIOT Act Section 215 and national security letters can compel production of library records notwithstanding state confidentiality law, although the USA FREEDOM Act (2015) and Doe v. Gonzales (2006) narrowed the gag provisions and bulk-collection authority.
      • Board structure materially affects independence: appointed boards predominate and offer civic continuity, while elected boards (common in library-district states such as Illinois, Michigan, and Oregon) provide democratic accountability but can expose collection and policy decisions to electoral politics.
      • Sunshine (open-meetings) laws apply to library boards as public bodies, requiring advance notice, public access, minutes, and limited executive sessions -- meaning that strategic board deliberation about, for example, a challenge or a personnel matter must occur within carefully circumscribed closed sessions.
      • Professional policy statements have acquired legal force through incorporation: Illinois (2023) and Maryland (2024) conditioned state library aid on adherence to the Library Bill of Rights, effectively treating the ALA's policy as a funding-eligibility standard.

      Friends & Foundations Deep Dive

      This dataset synthesizes the two parallel ecosystems of private support for public libraries in the United States: the nationwide grassroots network of Friends of the Library groups (an estimated 10,000+ organizations) and the professionally staffed Library Foundations (501(c)(3) organizations separate from Friends) that pursue major gifts, endowments, and capital campaigns. Friends groups are volunteer-driven and concentrate on used-book sales (estimated at $100 million+ annually nationwide), m

      Friends Overview

      Friends of the Library (often styled 'Friends of the [Name] Public Library') are grassroots, largely volunteer-driven nonprofit organizations that support their local public libraries through fundraising, advocacy, volunteer service, and community engagement. An estimated 10,000 or more Friends groups operate across the United States, attached to public library systems of every size -- from one-room rural branches to the largest urban systems. Friends groups are the most widespread form of private support for American public libraries, and for many small and rural libraries a Friends

      Foundation Overview

      Library Foundations are 501(c)(3) charitable organizations that are legally and operationally SEPARATE from Friends groups and from the library they support. Where Friends groups are volunteer-driven and grassroots (book sales, memberships, small-dollar fundraising), Library Foundations are typically professionally staffed and focus on major gifts, endowments, capital campaigns, planned giving, and corporate and institutional partnerships. The largest urban library foundations -- the NYPL Foundation, the Chicago Public Library Foundation, Friends of the San Francisco Public Library, The Seattl

      Organizational Models

      Private support for a public library is organized through several overlapping but distinct structures. The most common are the Friends group (volunteer, grassroots), the Library Foundation (professional, major-gift), and the library board of trustees (governance). Many large systems run a Friends group AND a Foundation side by side; some communities combine them; and all are linked nationally through United for Libraries, the ALA division that serves Trustees, Advocates, Friends, and Foundations.       Fundraising Activities

      Friends groups and Library Foundations together deploy a broad fundraising toolkit that ranges from $5 used-book purchases to eight-figure capital-campaign pledges. The activities fall into several tiers: grassroots revenue (book sales, memberships, events), annual giving (annual fund campaigns, corporate sponsorships), and transformational giving (capital campaigns, endowments, planned giving). Most libraries draw on multiple tiers simultaneously, with Friends groups concentrating on the grassroots tier and Foundations concentrating on the transformational tier. [{'activity': '

      Book Sales

      Used-book sales are the single most iconic and widespread fundraising activity of Friends of the Library groups. Friends collect donated books year-round and resell them through ongoing in-library bookstores, seasonal mega-sales, and increasingly online channels. Aggregated across the estimated 10,000+ Friends groups nationwide, book-sale revenue is estimated at well over $100 million annually -- a figure that makes used-book sales collectively one of the largest private revenue streams supporting American public libraries, and one that operates almost entirely outside the public budget. 100,0

      Membership Programs

      Membership programs are the other pillar of grassroots Friends fundraising alongside book sales. Members pay annual dues in exchange for benefits (newsletters, event discounts, bookstore discounts, early-sale access), creating a renewable revenue base and -- just as importantly -- a roster of citizens who can be mobilized for advocacy when library budgets are threatened. Membership is thus a dual-purpose tool: a fundraising stream and an advocacy army. [{'tier': 'Individual / Student / Senior', 'typical_dues_usd': '10 - 25', 'benefits': 'N

      Grant Writing

      Grant writing is the institutional fundraising engine of Library Foundations (and, to a lesser extent, of larger Friends groups and the libraries themselves). Professional grant writers pursue awards from private foundations, corporate giving programs, family foundations, and government agencies -- most prominently the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) and the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH). Library Foundation grants fund programmatic innovation, technology access, capital projects, and capacity-building that public operating budgets cannot sustain. [{'source&#x

      Key Findings

      • Friends of the Library groups are the most widespread form of private support for American public libraries: an estimated 10,000+ operate nationwide, attached to library systems of every size, and for many small and rural libraries a Friends group is the single most important source of supplemental funding, programming dollars, and political defense.
      • Library Foundations are legally and operationally distinct from Friends groups: both are 501(c)(3) charities, but Foundations are professionally staffed and pursue major gifts, endowments, capital campaigns, and planned giving, whereas Friends are volunteer-led and concentrate on grassroots revenue (book sales, memberships) and advocacy. Large urban systems often run BOTH, with each optimizing a different donor tier.
      • United for Libraries -- the ALA division formed in 2009 by the merger of Friends of Libraries U.S.A. (FOLUSA, founded 1979) and the American Library Trustees Association (ALTA) -- is the national umbrella uniting Trustees, Advocates, Friends, and Foundations, providing shared resources, training, awards, and a national network for citizen library support.
      • Used-book sales are the signature Friends fundraiser and, aggregated across the 10,000+ groups nationwide, generate an estimated $100 million+ annually -- collectively one of the largest private revenue streams supporting US public libraries, operating almost entirely outside the public budget through ongoing bookstores, seasonal mega-sales, and online resale.
      • The largest urban library foundations operate at a scale that rivals major cultural institutions: the NYPL Foundation holds estimated total assets on the order of hundreds of millions of dollars, and foundations supporting Los Angeles, Seattle, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Brooklyn each hold tens of millions, underwriting transformative projects that public appropriations alone cannot sustain.
      • The fundraising toolkit of Friends and Foundations spans tiers from $5 used-book purchases and $20 memberships to eight-figure capital-campaign pledges and estate bequests; mature Library Foundations run annual giving, capital campaigns, endowment cultivation, planned giving, corporate sponsorships, and an active grant portfolio simultaneously, with each stream funding a different layer of the library's aspirations.
      • Because US public library funding is overwhelmingly local (~85% of income from local government), private support from Friends and Foundations is structurally important in two ways: it funds programming, collections, and capital investment beyond the operating budget, AND it organizes the citizen advocacy that protects the public appropriations on which baseline operations depend -- especially during ballot-measure and budget-hearing seasons.
      • Capital campaigns led by Library Foundations frequently provide the private match that unlocks or enhances publicly funded building projects; the Seattle Central Library (opened 2004) and many branch systems nationwide were built through combined public bond and private capital-campaign funding, illustrating how private philanthropy and public investment are deliberately paired.
      • Endowments and planned giving are the principal routes to long-term financial stability for library foundations: permanently restricted endowment funds generate spendable income in perpetuity and insulate programs from annual budget cycles, while bequests and charitable trusts build that endowment over time through legacy societies cultivated by major foundations.
      • Grant writing is a core function of Library Foundations, which often both WRITE grants (to IMLS, NEH, private and corporate funders) and RECEIVE and REDEPLOY restricted grant funds on behalf of the library; this dedicated grant-management infrastructure is a capacity that public libraries, constrained by procurement and staffing rules, often cannot maintain internally.

      Self-Publishing Deep Dive

      Across the United States, public and academic libraries have moved well beyond collecting and lending books to actively supporting, hosting, and producing books authored by the communities they serve. This deep summary maps that landscape in seven dimensions. (1) The self-publishing overview: the scale of the self-publishing market, the ISBN counts tracked by R.R. Bowker, and the historic access problem that kept self-published works out of library collections. (2) Indie author services: the SEL

      Overview

      Self-publishing is now the largest source of new book titles in the United States. R.R. Bowker, the U.S. ISBN agency, reports roughly 2.7 million self-published ISBNs issued in 2023 against about 1 million traditional new titles (and approximately 4.3 million total ISBNs), a more-than-tenfold increase from the 133,036 self-published ISBNs recorded in 2010. This explosive growth -- driven by Amazon KDP, IngramSpark, and other digital platforms -- created a structural problem for libraries: an enormous body of new titles that had no practical path into public-library collections. {'self_pub

      Indie Author Services

      Indie author services are the curated programs by which libraries open a vetted distribution channel to self-published (indie) authors who lack a trade publisher. The two flagship national programs -- SELF-e and its successor the Indie Author Project -- were built specifically to solve the library access problem, giving indie authors a librarian-reviewed path into library collections. {'name': 'SELF-e (Self-published E-books)', 'launched': '2014-2015', 'partners': 'Library Journal + Biblioboard (BiblioLabs, Charleston, SC)', 'mec

      Pressbooks Platform

      Pressbooks is an open-source book-authoring platform built on WordPress that lets users write, format, and export professionally structured e-books (EPUB) and print-ready PDF files from a single source. Its education-focused product, PressbooksEDU, is used by more than 50 libraries and educational institutions to give patrons and faculty a free authoring environment for OER, monographs, community histories, and personal memoirs. {'base': 'WordPress-based, open-source publishing platform', 'outputs': ['EPUB (reflowable e-book for Kindle, Apple Books, Kobo)

      Library as Publisher

      The Library as Publisher movement reframes the library as a producer and disseminator of texts, not merely a custodian. It began most visibly in higher education, where university presses merged organizationally into the library (Michigan, Purdue, Penn State, Pittsburgh), and has spread to public libraries that publish local history, community memory, and patron work that commercial publishers would not undertake. {'name': 'Library Publishing Coalition (LPC)', 'parent': 'Program of the Educopia Foundation (since 2014)', 'founded': 2013, 'r

Together they position the library as the front-line support system for authors who are not (and may never be) trade-published. {'overview': 'Community author programs provide local writers with structured support -- workshops, manuscript feedback, authoring tools, and sometimes publication -- through the library.       E-book distribution is the channel by which self-published titles reach library readers.       Key Findings

      • Self-publishing is now the largest source of new U.S. book titles. R.R. Bowker reports roughly 2.7 million self-published ISBNs in 2023 versus about 1 million traditional new titles (and 4.3 million total), a more-than-tenfold increase from the 133,036 self-published ISBNs recorded in 2010.
      • Until the mid-2010s, self-published authors had essentially no path into public-library collections because they lacked the reviews, MARC records, and distribution that selectors require; library self-publishing programs were built specifically to open this channel.
      • SELF-e (launched 2014-2015 by Library Journal and Biblioboard/BiblioLabs) was the first national-scale program giving self-published authors a library-distribution channel, using a librarian-staffed juried review process.
      • The Indie Author Project is the successor to SELF-e, running statewide indie-author programs (California, Georgia, Virginia, Arizona, Connecticut, Minnesota, and others) that vet self-published submissions with library editorial teams and feed Library Journal's annual 'Best Indie' selections.
      • The SELF-e / Indie Author submission process lets an indie author upload an e-book that librarians then read and evaluate; accepted titles enter a statewide Biblioboard collection at no cost to the library or author, with top selections forwarded for national review while authors retain their rights.
      • Pressbooks, an open-source WordPress-based authoring platform, is used by more than 50 libraries (via PressbooksEDU) to let patrons write, format, and export e-books and print-ready PDFs, democratizing professional book production.
      • The Library as Publisher movement reframes the library as a producer of texts, not merely a custodian; the Library Publishing Coalition (an Educopia program, founded 2013) documents 150+ member library publishing programs in its annual Directory.
      • Public libraries act as publishers too: Topeka & Shawnee County Public Library's LibraryPress and Sacramento Public Library's I Street Press demonstrate that public libraries, not just universities, can sustain publishing and print-on-demand programs.
      • The Espresso Book Machine (On Demand Books) lets a library manufacture a finished bound paperback from a digital file in minutes; Sacramento's I Street Press is the most cited public-library use of the EBM, paired with writing workshops.
      • Community author programs -- writer-in-residence programs, memoir workshops, and indie-author showcases -- make the library a site of literary production, with durable examples at Pikes Peak Library District (CO) and Chicago Public Library (IL).

      Genealogy Deep Dive

      This document surveys the infrastructure of family-history research as it is supported by libraries and allied institutions across the United States. It traces the central role of FamilySearch and its global network of more than 5,000 FamilySearch Centers and affiliate libraries, the near-universal deployment of Ancestry Library Edition in over 10,000 libraries, ProQuest's HeritageQuest Online and MyHeritage Library Edition as the standard companion genealogy databases, the newspaper archiv

      Overview

      Genealogy -- the study of family descent and ancestry -- has become one of the most common adult research activities conducted in libraries. The explosive growth of online genealogy since the 1990s, amplified by digitized records, DNA matching, and television programs, has drawn millions of new researchers to libraries seeking primary evidence of birth, marriage, death, immigration, military service, and residence. Libraries occupy a privileged position in this ecosystem: they combine free or low-cost access to the major subscription databases, curated print and microform collections, the loca

      FamilySearch Partnership

      FamilySearch, operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, is the largest genealogical organization in the world and the keystone of library-based family research. Its flagship Family History Library in Salt Lake City holds the world's largest genealogy collection, and its online platform makes billions of records freely searchable. Crucially for libraries, FamilySearch licenses much of its restricted digital image content only to be viewed inside FamilySearch Centers and at designated affiliate libraries, creating a distributed, library-anchored access network of more tha

      Ancestry Library Edition

      Ancestry Library Edition, distributed to libraries by ProQuest under license from Ancestry, is the most widely deployed subscription genealogy database in American libraries. It is available in more than 10,000 libraries -- including the great majority of U.S. public library systems and many academic and school libraries -- and gives library patrons in-building access to the same census, vital, immigration, military, and newspaper record collections that consumer Ancestry subscribers reach from home. {'library_count': 'Available in 10,000+ libraries worldwide.', 'licen

      HeritageQuest

      HeritageQuest Online, a ProQuest product, is the standard companion to Ancestry Library Edition in American public libraries. Unlike Ancestry Library Edition, HeritageQuest is commonly licensed for remote access with a library card, making it the after-hours genealogy database for patrons at home. MyHeritage Library Edition, distributed by EBSCO and by ProQuest in some markets, is a third major subscription genealogy database increasingly bundled into library electronic resource suites. {'provider': 'ProQuest.', 'access_model': 'Frequently offered as remote-a

      Newspaper Databases

      Historic newspapers are among the most valuable sources for genealogy, recording obituaries, marriage and birth notices, anniversaries, legal notices, and the everyday community news that vital records omit. Libraries provide access to the principal newspaper archives -- Newspapers.com, NewspaperArchive, and the free Chronicling America program of the Library of Congress -- alongside their own microfilmed local newspaper holdings and state digital newspaper projects. {'provider': 'Ancestry (operated as a sister product to Ancestry.com).', 'scope': 'One of the

      Local History Rooms

      Local history rooms, maintained by public libraries, preserve the documents, photographs, newspapers, and ephemera of individual cities, counties, and regions. They are typically the only institutions that systematically collect municipal directories, high school yearbooks, local newspaper morgues, church and cemetery records, and the vertical files of clippings and pamphlets assembled by library staff over decades. While national genealogy platforms hold the broad-stroke records, public library local history rooms hold the granular, place-based evidence that resolves questions national databa

      DNA & Genealogy

      Direct-to-consumer DNA testing has transformed genealogy since the 2010s, allowing researchers to confirm documentary lineages, discover unknown relatives, infer ethnic origins, and break through the brick walls that records cannot resolve. Libraries have responded by adding DNA education to their genealogy programming, hosting DNA interest groups, and developing guidance on the ethical and privacy dimensions of genetic genealogy. {'ancestry_dna': 'The largest consumer DNA database, integrated with the Ancestry family-tree platform; offers ethnicity estimates and a large match l

      Key Findings

      • FamilySearch, operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, anchors library genealogy through the Family History Library in Salt Lake City -- the world's largest genealogy collection -- and a global network of more than 5,000 FamilySearch Centers and affiliate libraries that provide local, no-cost access to restricted digital images.
      • Ancestry Library Edition, distributed by ProQuest, is available in more than 10,000 libraries and gives patrons in-building access to the same census, vital, immigration, and military record collections that consumer Ancestry subscribers reach from home, making it the most widely deployed subscription genealogy database in American libraries.
      • ProQuest's HeritageQuest Online is the standard remote-access companion to Ancestry Library Edition, offering library-card access from home to the U.S. census, genealogy and local history books, Revolutionary War pension files, the Freedman's Bank records, and PERSI.
      • PERSI, the Periodical Source Index, was compiled at and is maintained by the Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and is the largest subject index of genealogy and local history periodical articles in the world.
      • The Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center holds the second-largest genealogy collection in the United States, with more than 1.2 million items, and operates as a FamilySearch affiliate library giving on-site access to restricted FamilySearch images.
      • Chronicling America, a partnership of the Library of Congress and the National Endowment for the Humanities, provides free, searchable access to millions of pages of historic American newspapers from 1777 to 1963, with no subscription or login required.
      • Newspapers.com and NewspaperArchive are the principal commercial newspaper archives used in libraries for obituary and notice research, with NewspaperArchive often valued for its coverage of small-town and rural papers that larger services overlook.
      • Local history rooms in public libraries are typically the only institutions that systematically collect municipal directories, yearbooks, church and cemetery records, and local newspaper morgues, making them indispensable for the granular, place-based evidence that national genealogy platforms do not hold.
      • Direct-to-consumer DNA testing has transformed genealogy since the 2010s, and libraries have responded by adding DNA education, interest groups, and privacy-and-ethics programs that help patrons integrate genetic evidence with documentary research.
      • The New England Historic Genealogical Society, founded in 1845, is the oldest and largest genealogical society in the United States and operates the AmericanAncestors.org portal, anchoring colonial and New England family research.

      Youth Services Deep Dive

      This document provides a comprehensive overview of the services, frameworks, and programs that U.S. public libraries offer to children and adolescents from birth through the teenage years.       Early Literacy

      Public libraries are the most widespread and accessible providers of free early-literacy programming in the United States. Their work in the first five years of life is designed to build the vocabulary, print awareness, letter knowledge, and narrative skills that predict later reading success, and to equip parents and caregivers with the practices that sustain that development at home. Because participation is free and does not require enrollment or a diagnosis, library early-literacy services reach children across the income spectrum, though they are especially valuable for families who canno

      Summer Reading

      Summer learning loss -- the regression in reading and math skills that occurs when students are out of school -- disproportionately affects low-income students and contributes to the achievement gap. Public libraries are the most widespread and accessible providers of summer learning programming in the United States; nearly every public library in the country runs a summer reading program, and most rely on a shared collaborative to supply themes, artwork, and programming ideas. {'sponsor': 'Collaborative Summer Library Program (CSLP)', 'description': 'CSLP is

      Storytime is the signature recurring public-library service for young children and one of the most consistently attended free programs in the country.       Teen services -- typically defined as serving patrons ages 12 to 18 -- is a distinct specialty within public librarianship, anchored by the Young Adult Library Services Association (YALSA). Effective teen services combine a dedicated, welcoming physical space; a collection that reflects teen interests and identities; and programming co-designed with teens themselves. The field increasingly frames teens not as a problem to be managed but as a developmentally distinct user group whose autonomy and voice should be centered. {'description': 'Teen advisory boards (TABs), sometimes ca

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries are the most widespread providers of free early-literacy programming in the United States, and frameworks like Every Child Ready to Read have shifted storytimes from entertainment toward deliberate caregiver education in the five early-literacy practices of talking, singing, reading, writing, and playing.
      • Programs such as 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten and Dolly Parton's Imagination Library partnerships build home libraries and reading habits before school entry, addressing kindergarten-readiness gaps that disproportionately affect low-income children.
      • The storytime continuum -- lap-sit for infants, toddler storytime, and preschool storytime -- is calibrated to child development and often functions as a child's first structured group-learning experience, making it an important school-readiness intervention for children who do not attend preschool.
      • Nearly every public library in the country runs a summer reading program, and collaboratives such as the Collaborative Summer Library Program (CSLP) and iREAD supply shared themes, artwork, and manuals that let even the smallest systems present a polished program at low cost.
      • Research links participation in public library summer reading programs to higher reading achievement at the start of the next school year, and pairing summer reading with USDA Summer Food Service Program meals addresses both literacy and nutrition gaps for children who lose access to school meals.
      • Library STEM/STEAM programming -- including makerspaces for kids, LEGO clubs, robotics, and coding for kids -- has established public and school libraries as key venues for informal STEM education, expanding access to technology tools and mentorship for children who lack them at home.
      • Initiatives such as NASA@My Library and Girls Who Code library clubs direct STEM resources specifically to underserved and rural communities and to girls, using library infrastructure to narrow long-standing opportunity gaps in science and computing.
      • Effective teen services combine a dedicated teen space, a reflective young-adult collection, and programming co-designed with teens; teen advisory boards give adolescents authentic leadership roles and ensure library offerings reflect teen interests and identities.
      • YALSA's Teen Read Week and Teen Tech Week are national hooks that libraries use to spotlight young-adult literature and digital literacy respectively, connecting teen reading and technology use to future academic and career pathways.
      • Homework help centers -- exemplified by Columbus Metropolitan Library's model -- and online tutoring platforms such as Brainfuse and Tutor.com give students free academic support during the critical after-school window, particularly benefiting those without quiet study space or home internet.

      Workforce Development Deep Dive

      This document provides a comprehensive overview of how U.S. public libraries serve as frontline workforce-development institutions. It covers the headline finding of the Public Library Funding & Technology Access Study (PLFTAS) that roughly 92% of public libraries provide access to online job resources, resume software, and/or job-skills training; the full range of job-search services libraries offer, including career-center partnerships, job fairs, and one-on-one help completing online job

      Overview

      Public libraries have become core infrastructure for the American workforce, providing free access to the computers, internet, software, training, and one-on-one help that job seekers, career changers, immigrant workers, veterans, and aspiring entrepreneurs need to find work and build skills. {'full_name': 'Public Library Funding & Technology Access Study', 'operator': 'Conducted by the American Library Association (ALA) together with the University of Maryland Information Policy & Access Center (iPAC).', 'period': 'Annual national

      Job Search Services

      Libraries offer a broad suite of job-search services: free internet and computer access, curated job-listing resources, career-center partnerships, on-site job fairs, and staff and volunteer help navigating online job applications. The PLFTAS finding that 92% of libraries provide job resources reflects how central this function has become. Free public-access computers, Wi-Fi, printing, scanning, and faxing give job seekers the basic tools needed to search listings, upload documents, and communicate with employers. For patrons without home broadband or a device, the library is often the only pr

      Resume & Career Help

      Resume and career help is among the most requested workforce services at public libraries. Libraries combine staff expertise, volunteer resume coaches, specialized software, and structured workshops to help patrons present themselves effectively to employers. Libraries offer recurring resume-writing workshops that walk patrons through structure, content, keyword optimization for applicant-tracking systems, formatting, and tailoring a resume to a specific posting. Workshops are often offered in person, hybrid, and online, and many are delivered in languages other than English. Many libraries pr

      Digital Skills Training

      Because most jobs now require at least basic digital skills, libraries have become primary providers of free computer and digital-literacy training, from turning on a device to using spreadsheets and writing code. Training is delivered through staff-led classes, volunteer instructors, online platforms, and standardized curricula. {'description': 'Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment, developed by Literacy Minnesota (formerly the Minnesota Literacy Council), defines the basic skills needed to perform tasks on computers and online and provides assessments in areas such as Basic C

      ESL & Workforce

      Libraries are central to immigrant workforce integration, offering English as a Second Language (ESL) instruction, conversation practice, citizenship preparation, digital literacy in multiple languages, and help navigating U.S. employment and credential systems. For many new Americans the library is the first and most trusted workforce resource. Many libraries offer free beginner, intermediate, and advanced ESL classes, often in partnership with community colleges, adult-education providers, or volunteer organizations. Classes are scheduled around working hours, including evenings and weekends

      Entrepreneurship Support

      Public libraries support entrepreneurs and small businesses at every stage, from idea to launch to growth, through SCORE mentoring, Small Business Development Center (SBDC) partnerships, USPTO Patent and Trademark Resource Centers, business-research databases, makerspace prototyping, and free meeting and coworking space. {'description': 'SCORE is a nonprofit association and resource partner of the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) that provides free, confidential business mentoring and low-cost education through a nationwide network of volunteer, often retired, business e

      Partnerships

      Library workforce impact is amplified through formal and informal partnerships with the public workforce system, small-business ecosystem, federal agencies, adult-education providers, and employers. Under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA), libraries are recognized as accessible access points that complement American Job Centers. {'description': 'Workforce Development Boards (WDBs, also called Workforce Investment Boards) are regional bodies that oversee American Job Centers and set local workforce strategy under WIOA.', 'library_role': 'Libr
