      Key Findings

      • The Public Library Funding & Technology Access Study (PLFTAS) found that approximately 92% of U.S. public libraries provide access to online job resources, resume software, and/or job-skills training, making libraries one of the most universal workforce-access points in the country.
      • Libraries function as neighborhood workforce hubs by combining free internet and computers, curated job resources, and patient one-on-one help, reaching job seekers who are not served by or do not access the formal American Job Center system.
      • A defining library service is hands-on help completing online job applications and e-government forms (such as unemployment-insurance claims), which PLFTAS documented as a widespread and growing function during and after the Great Recession.
      • Resume-writing workshops, one-on-one resume coaching, and subscription resume software (such as Optimal Resume and Brainfuse JobNow) give job seekers free access to tools and expertise that would otherwise carry a cost.
      • Northstar Digital Literacy Assessment, developed by Literacy Minnesota, gives libraries a nationally recognized, standardized way to benchmark and credential basic computer and internet skills, with hundreds of libraries serving as approved testing sites.
      • Free Microsoft Office classes, especially Excel and Word, are among the most consistently offered and attended library classes because spreadsheet and word-processing fluency are explicit requirements in a large share of job postings.
      • A growing number of libraries host coding bootcamps, learn-to-code series, Girls Who Code clubs, and makerspace programming that introduce patrons to HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python as pathways into technology careers.
      • Libraries are central to immigrant workforce integration, offering ESL classes, conversation groups, citizenship preparation, multilingual digital literacy, and help navigating U.S. employment and credential systems in trusted, low-stigma settings.
      • Through SCORE, libraries host free mentoring from volunteer business executives, extending U.S. Small Business Administration expertise to aspiring entrepreneurs who cannot afford private consulting.
      • Small Business Development Center (SBDC) partnerships bring free business consulting and training into library branches, complementing SCORE with deeper market-research and growth support for existing small businesses.

      Technology Infrastructure Deep Dive

      A deep summary of the technology infrastructure that powers U.S. public libraries in the mid-2020s, organized around the systems patrons touch every day. It covers broadband connectivity and the fiber/cable/DSL speed landscape; the near-universal free public Wi-Fi network and the hundreds of millions of annual Wi-Fi sessions it carries; public-access computing, including the widely cited benchmark of roughly twenty public workstations per branch, PC reservation and time-management software (Envi

      Broadband Overview

      Public libraries are among the most important public broadband on-ramps in the United States. Their external internet connections range from multi-gigabit dedicated fiber at large urban central libraries to comparatively slow DSL, cable, or fixed-wireless links at small rural branches -- which are very often the only source of free, public broadband in their community. The library broadband landscape is therefore a microcosm of the national digital divide: the same fiber-to-the-premises buildout that connects a downtown central library at a gigabit or more may never reach the small branch twen

      Wi-Fi Statistics

      Free public Wi-Fi is now effectively universal at U.S. public library outlets: the long-cited 2012 figure of 91% of libraries offering free wireless internet has risen to 99%-plus today, making the library the most ubiquitous free public Wi-Fi network in the country. The IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS) FY2024 records approximately 418.4 million annual Wi-Fi sessions across reporting systems, and Wi-Fi has overtaken wired public computers as the way most patrons get online in a library, since most now bring their own devices. {'pct_offering_wifi_2012': 91, 'pct_offering_wifi_2

      Public Computers

      Public-access computers remain a core library technology service even as patrons increasingly bring their own devices. A widely cited benchmark puts the average public library branch at roughly twenty public-access internet workstations, though the authoritative IMLS Public Libraries Survey (PLS) FY2024 reports about 260,000 public-access computers across roughly 9,100 reporting systems -- an average of about 29 per system, with large central libraries concentrating far more. Public computers are governed by reservation and time-management software, CIPA-mandated filtering, and a replacement c

      Printing Services

      Printing, scanning, and faxing are standard public-library technology services, and the category has expanded well beyond black-and-white document printing to include 3D printing, large-format/poster printing, passport-photo printing, and -- increasingly -- mobile and cloud printing that lets patrons send jobs from home or their phone for release at the branch. {'description': 'Most public libraries offer patron printing (often fee-based per page), scanning to email or USB, and a declining but still significant number offer faxing. Print-management software with coin- or card-op

      Network Infrastructure

      The wired and wireless backbone connecting libraries to the internet and to each other is funded through local operating budgets plus federal E-Rate discounts. E-Rate (the Schools and Libraries Program of the Universal Service Fund) is the single most important federal funding source for library connectivity, subsidizing the external circuit and the internal connections -- switches, cabling, and Wi-Fi access points -- that distribute it within the building. {'name': 'E-Rate (Schools and Libraries Program of the Universal Service Fund)', 'administrator': 'Univ

      Website Platforms

      A public library's web presence is typically assembled from several layers: a public website built on a content management system (commonly WordPress or Drupal); a patron-facing catalog/discovery portal layered over the integrated library system (BiblioCommons, Polaris PowerPAC, Ex Libris Primo, OCLC WorldCat Discovery, or a vendor-native OPAC); and a suite of subject guides, event calendars, and service modules very often built on Springshare's LibApps platform (LibGuides, LibCal, LibAnswers, LibWizard). No central registry tracks which libraries use which platform, so adoption figu

      Digital Equity

      Public libraries are the most widely available free public internet access point in the United States and have become central actors in national digital-equity efforts: providing the broadband, devices, skills help, and one-on-one support (digital navigators) that close gaps commercial broadband buildout leaves behind. Roughly 24 million U.S. households still lack home internet, and libraries -- especially in rural and low-income communities -- are where those households go online. {'households_without_home_internet': '~24 million', 'adults_without_home_broadband_pct_2

      Key Findings

      • Free public Wi-Fi is effectively universal at U.S. public library outlets today (99%+), up from 91% in 2012, making the library the most ubiquitous free public Wi-Fi network in the country; IMLS PLS FY2024 recorded roughly 418.4 million annual Wi-Fi sessions, a conservative lower bound since only 76.2% of systems report Wi-Fi sessions separately.
      • Wi-Fi has overtaken wired public computers as the way most patrons get online in a library: FY2024 Wi-Fi sessions (~418M) dwarf wired public-internet-user sessions (~101M), reflecting the shift to patron-owned devices (BYOD).
      • A widely cited benchmark puts the average public library branch at roughly twenty public-access internet workstations, while the authoritative IMLS PLS FY2024 reports about 260,000 public computers across ~9,100 reporting systems (an average of ~29 per system); the two figures differ because large multi-branch systems concentrate computers at central locations.
      • The FCC's E-Rate program -- discounts of 20-90% on telecommunications, internet access, and internal connections, with a budget raised from $2.25B to $3.9B in 2014 and a $1B/year Wi-Fi target -- is the keystone federal funder of library network infrastructure, without which many small and rural libraries could not afford broadband.
      • CIPA (2000) ties E-Rate eligibility to internet filtering that blocks obscene images, child pornography, and content harmful to minors; filtering is typically enforced at the network edge (firewall or Wi-Fi controller) across both wired public computers and the guest Wi-Fi SSID, with an adult-unblock provision that remains an intellectual-freedom tension.
      • Public computing is governed by PC reservation and time-management software -- chiefly Envisionware and LPT:One -- that enforces daily time limits, manages waitlists, and wipes session data between users, underpinning the Open Access self-service model that is now the default at nearly all U.S. public libraries.
      • Mobile and cloud printing (PrinterOn, Princh) lets patrons send jobs from a phone or home computer and release them at the branch, a service that surged during and after the COVID-19 pandemic and is now standard at many systems, often with integrated mobile payment.
      • 3D printing, introduced to libraries with the 2011 Fayetteville Free Library makerspace, is now offered by an estimated 500-700 public libraries and is typically the first maker service a library adopts, usually an FDM printer from MakerBot, Prusa, or Bambu Lab.
      • Library websites are assembled from layered platforms: a CMS (most often WordPress or Drupal), a Springshare LibApps suite (LibGuides, LibCal, LibAnswers) for guides and events, and a discovery/catalog portal (BiblioCommons, Polaris PowerPAC, Primo, WorldCat Discovery, or a vendor-native OPAC) atop the ILS; LibGuides is so dominant that 'LibGuide' has become a generic term for a research guide.
      • Technology replacement cycles are chronically underfunded: industry guidance recommends replacing public computers every 4-5 years, but E-Rate funds connectivity and internal connections, not the end-user computers themselves, so refreshing the workstations patrons actually use falls entirely on local budgets and grants.

      Youth Programs

      Storytime (lap-sit, toddler, preschool) is the most widespread youth program offered by virtually every public library. Teen advisory boards, makerspaces, anime clubs, gaming tournaments, college prep programs.       Cultural Programs

Heritage month programming - Black History, Hispanic Heritage, AAPI, Native American Heritage, Pride Month.       Educational Programs

      Adult literacy tutoring, family literacy, ESL instruction, GED preparation. Computer basics, internet essentials, email, online safety, social media help, smartphone basics. Lecture series, online learning (Gale Courses, LinkedIn Learning), test prep, citizenship test prep. Every Child Ready to Read workshops, early literacy skill-building, kindergarten readiness.

      Health & Wellness Programs

      Health information literacy, health insurance enrollment (ACA navigators), blood pressure screenings. Mental health first aid, mindfulness sessions, therapy dogs, stress reduction. Yoga, tai chi, Zumba, walking groups, meditation in library spaces. Opioid overdose reversal training and Narcan distribution with public health departments.

      Civic Programs

      Libraries serve as voter registration sites; National Voter Registration Day events. Many libraries are passport acceptance facilities processing thousands of applications. Citizenship preparation classes, naturalization information, immigration legal clinics. Community conversations, deliberative forums, Living Room Conversations. Many libraries offer free or low-cost notary services.

      Collections Development Deep Dive

      This document surveys the collections held by the roughly 9,200 public library administrative entities and more than 17,000 outlets that together constitute the U.S. public library system. It surveys the total scale of those collections -- more than 800 million books, serials, audio, video, and electronic items reported to the Institute of Museum and Library Services Public Libraries Survey -- and the roughly $1.5 billion spent each year on library materials nationwide.       Overview

      Public library collections are the circulating and reference holdings that public libraries build, maintain, and make freely available to the communities they serve. Unlike research library special collections, public library collections are built primarily for use rather than preservation: they are expected to circulate, to reflect current community demand, and to be continuously refreshed through new purchases and systematic weeding.       The materials budget is the portion of a public library's operating budget devoted to building and refreshing the collection: books, periodicals, audiovisual, electronic resources, and the processing supplies and service contracts that support them.       Weeding & Deaccession

      Weeding -- the deliberate removal of items from the collection -- is as essential to collection maintenance as selection. Without weeding, shelves fill with outdated, damaged, and rarely used materials that crowd out current, relevant titles and undermine the library's usefulness. The dominant professional method in U.S. public libraries is CREW: Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding, codified in the Texas State Library and Archives Commission manual CREW: A Weeding Manual for Modern Libraries. {'full_name': 'Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding', 'orig

      Collection Development Policy

      A collection development policy is the written statement that defines what a library collects, how it selects, how it handles challenges, and how it weeds. The American Library Association regards a current, board-approved collection development policy as foundational professional practice: it guides selectors, informs the public, and provides the institutional defense when materials are challenged. ALA's Library Bill of Rights and the Freedom to Read statement anchor the values such policies are expected to uphold. ["A statement of purpose and community served, identifying the libra

      Diversity in Collections

      Diverse-collections initiatives seek to ensure that public library holdings reflect the full diversity of the communities they serve -- across race, ethnicity, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, and economic background. These efforts span conscious selection (the We Need Diverse Books and #OwnVoices movements), systematic assessment (diversity audits), and the deliberate building of world-language and Spanish-language collections. Diversity in collections is treated by ALA not as an add-on but as a core obligation under the Library Bill of Rights. {'summary':

      Community reads and One Book programs invite an entire city or region to read and discuss a single title over a defined period, accompanied by author talks, book discussions, and themed programming.       Key Findings

      • U.S. public libraries collectively hold more than 800 million items and spend roughly $1.5 billion per year on materials, according to the Institute of Museum and Library Services Public Libraries Survey, making the public library collection one of the largest collectively held cultural resources in the nation.
      • Digital collection growth is the dominant trend in twenty-first-century public library collections: OverDrive / Libby digital circulation rose from roughly 50 million checkouts in 2013 to more than 600 million by the mid-2020s, with a sharp pandemic-driven surge in 2020.
      • The shift from ownership to access is reshaping collections: while print books and physical AV are owned outright, most e-books, e-audiobooks, and streaming titles are licensed for limited terms, meaning the digital collection is only partially under library control and raises enduring preservation and equity questions.
      • The CREW method -- Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding -- codified in the Texas State Library and Archives Commission manual, is the standard weeding framework in U.S. public libraries, using the MUSTIE criteria (Misleading, Ugly, Superseded, Trivial, Irrelevant, Elsewhere) plus circulation data to keep collections current.
      • Collection age analysis measures the average copyright date of holdings by Dewey range, with the ALA benchmark of no more than ten years for most nonfiction; aging collections, especially in medicine, science, and technology, signal under-investment in weeding and replacement and can mislead patrons.
      • The #OwnVoices movement, coined by author Corinne Duyvis in 2015, and the We Need Diverse Books campaign have reshaped public library selection toward authentic first-voice representation, guiding selectors to prioritize books about marginalized groups written by authors who share those identities.
      • Diversity audits -- systematic assessments of how well a collection represents diverse identities -- became a standard equity tool in the late 2010s, quantifying representation gaps and informing targeted purchasing to close them.
      • Spanish-language collections are the largest and most widespread world-language holdings in U.S. public libraries, concentrated in Sun Belt and metropolitan systems such as Los Angeles, Phoenix, Houston, and San Antonio, and increasingly include Spanish and bilingual e-content.
      • Large-print collections and partnerships with the National Library Service for the Blind and Print Disabled extend the diversity of formats available to older adults and readers with low vision, making accessibility a recognized dimension of collection diversity.
      • Audiovisual collections followed a boom-and-bust arc: DVD and audiobook holdings grew rapidly in the 2000s and contracted in the 2010s as streaming displaced disc and CD lending, even as digital e-audiobooks became the fastest-growing format.

      Outreach Services Deep Dive

      Comprehensive analysis of U.S. public library outreach services, covering bookmobiles, homebound delivery, pop-up libraries, mobile Wi-Fi hotspot lending, automated kiosks, and community partnerships. It draws on IMLS Public Libraries Survey data, ALA resources, and documented programs at individual library systems to explain how libraries extend services beyond their buildings.

      Overview

      Library outreach encompasses services delivered beyond the physical building to reach patrons who cannot easily visit a branch, including bookmobiles, homebound delivery, pop-up sites, and mobile technology lending. Outreach extends equitable access to rural residents, homebound individuals, children, and digitally excluded communities who would otherwise be unserved by fixed branches. Outreach spans mobile collections, doorstep delivery, pop-up libraries in public spaces, Wi-Fi hotspot lending, automated kiosks, and partnerships with community organizations.

      Bookmobiles

      Bookmobiles are mobile library branches: specially outfitted vehicles carrying collections, Wi-Fi, and staff to scheduled stops in underserved areas. Approximately 800+ bookmobiles operate across U.S. public libraries, according to IMLS Public Libraries Survey data reported by the American Library Association. Large fleets include Mid-Continent Public Library (MO), Pioneer Library System (OK), and Fairfax County Public Library (VA), each operating multiple vehicles on regular routes.

      Homebound Services

      Homebound services deliver library materials directly to patrons who cannot visit due to age, disability, or illness, ensuring continued access to reading and media. Common models include staff-driven delivery routes, volunteer driver networks, and free postal 'Books by Mail' or 'Mail-A-Book' services. Many systems rely on trained volunteers to select and deliver materials, which expands capacity but requires coordination and background screening.

      Pop-Up Libraries

      Pop-up libraries are temporary, mobile service points set up where people already gather, bringing card signup, materials, and programming outside the building. Typical sites include public parks, beaches, farmers markets, laundromats, transit stations, and community festivals. Seattle and Multnomah County librarians use cargo bikes to bring books and Wi-Fi to parks and events, while other systems deploy pop-up tents at summer meal sites.

      Mobile Hotspots

      Mobile hotspot lending lets patrons borrow portable Wi-Fi devices to access the internet at home, bridging the digital divide for those without broadband. Major programs include NYPL's Library HotSpot, Chicago Public Library's Internet to Go, and King County's Tech to Go, many launched with Sprint or Knight Foundation support. Hotspot lending surged during COVID-19 as libraries addressed the homework gap, extending curb Wi-Fi to parking lots and loaning devices to students.

      Kiosks & Stations

      Automated lending kiosks and book dispensers provide self-service access to materials in high-traffic locations without staffed branches. Types include book-vending machines in transit hubs, DVD dispensers, and 'Library of Things' kiosks lending tools, hotspots, or technology.

      Community Partnerships

      Libraries extend outreach through partnerships with schools, food banks, shelters, senior centers, hospitals, and parks departments that share patrons and goals. California's Lunch at the Library pairs free summer meals with reading programs, while many systems partner with schools for mobile STEM and literacy stops.

      • Approximately 800+ bookmobiles operate across U.S. public libraries, according to IMLS Public Libraries Survey data, serving rural, suburban, and urban communities lacking easy access to fixed branches.

      • Wi-Fi hotspot lending expanded rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic as libraries sought to close the homework gap for students and families without home internet.
      • Pop-up libraries extend service to nontraditional locations such as parks, beaches, farmers markets, laundromats, and transit stations, reaching patrons where they already gather.
      • Automated lending kiosks and book dispensers allow libraries to place collection access in transit hubs and community centers without staffing a full branch.
      • The Association of Bookmobile and Outreach Services (ABOS), an ALA affiliate, supports professional development and standards for outreach librarians nationwide.
      • Bookmobiles trace their U.S. history to Mary Titcomb's 1905 book wagon at Washington County Free Library in Maryland, making mobile outreach one of the oldest library service models.
      • Community partnerships with schools, food banks, shelters, and senior centers multiply outreach impact, as seen in programs like California's Lunch at the Library.
      • Many hotspot lending programs depend on grants and corporate partnerships (e.g., Sprint/T-Mobile, Knight Foundation) rather than stable operating budgets, creating sustainability concerns.
      • Outreach services are most effective when combined with traditional library values like reader advisory, programming, and library card signup, rather than treated as mere delivery logistics.

      Social Workers in Libraries Deep Dive

      An in-depth look at the integration of professional social workers into U.S. public libraries, tracing the movement from its San Francisco origins to the widespread adoption seen in urban systems today, including service models, harm-reduction practices, and funding strategies.

      Overview

      A library social worker is a licensed or trained human-services professional embedded within a public library to assist patrons facing homelessness, mental-health crises, substance use, and other complex needs. As libraries became de facto daytime shelters and community safety nets, staff lacked the specialized training to respond to patrons in crisis. Social workers fill that gap while freeing librarians to focus on their core educational mission. What began as a single position at one library has grown into a nationwide movement, with dozens of urban and suburban systems now employing social

      Pioneering Programs

      Two early-adopter systems demonstrated that on-site social work could succeed in a library setting and inspired replication across the country. The San Francisco Public Library became the first U.S. public library to hire a full-time social worker when it brought on Leah Esguerra in 2009, staffing a dedicated social-services team that became a national model. The DC Public Library launched its social-work program to serve patrons experiencing homelessness, pairing licensed social workers with peer specialists across branches including the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library.

      Service Models

      Libraries adopt social-work services through two main organizational approaches, each with distinct advantages and trade-offs for staffing, supervision, and cost. In the embedded model, the library hires a social worker as a direct employee, giving tight integration with library operations but requiring the system to handle licensure, liability, and clinical supervision. In the contracted model, the library partners with a county health department or nonprofit agency that places its own social workers on-site, lowering employment overhead while sharing expertise and casework infrastructure.

      Services Offered

      Library social workers address a broad range of patron needs that fall outside traditional library services, blending direct assistance with warm referrals to community resources. Outreach includes connecting patrons with shelters and housing programs, distributing hygiene kits, assisting with ID and benefits enrollment, and de-escalating incidents that disrupt shared spaces. Social workers provide crisis intervention, brief supportive counseling, and referrals to clinical and behavioral-health providers, often in coordination with mobile crisis teams.

      Harm Reduction

      A growing number of libraries embrace harm-reduction services, treating the library as a low-threshold public-health site where patrons who use drugs can access life-saving resources. Many systems now stock and distribute NARCAN (naloxone), an opioid-overdose reversal nasal spray, and train staff and patrons to administer it, turning libraries into active overdose-response locations. Staff training covers recognizing overdose signs, administering naloxone, and post-overdose support, often delivered in partnership with local public-health departments or harm-reduction organizations.

      Funding Models

      Because library operating budgets rarely include dedicated social-work lines, systems piece together funding from grants, partnerships, and philanthropic support to sustain these roles. Federal sources such as Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) grants, along with state and local funds, help seed and expand social-work positions, though grant cycles can make long-term funding uncertain. Collaborations with county health departments, behavioral-health authorities, and nonprofits allow libraries to share costs and tap external expertise, often making the contracted model more financi

      • Two dominant service models have emerged: embedded social workers employed directly by the library and contracted workers placed by partner agencies.

      • Funding is frequently cobbled together from IMLS and other grants, making some positions vulnerable to grant-cycle disruptions.
      • Partnerships with county health departments and nonprofits lower costs and expand access to clinical supervision and case-management infrastructure.
      • Urban systems led adoption, but suburban and mid-sized libraries increasingly add social workers as community needs grow.
      • Social workers reduce the burden on librarians, who are rarely trained to handle mental-health or behavioral crises.
      • Peer specialists and outreach workers often complement licensed social workers, drawing on lived experience to build patron trust.

      Climate Resilience Centers Deep Dive

      Public libraries have emerged as critical infrastructure for community climate resilience, leveraging their trusted status, extended hours, robust buildings, and free public access to serve as cooling centers, warming centers, emergency shelters, and air-quality refuges during increasingly frequent and severe climate-driven events.

      Overview

      Library climate resilience refers to the role public libraries play in helping communities prepare for, withstand, and recover from climate-driven disruptions by serving as trusted, accessible, climate-controlled community assets before, during, and after emergencies. Libraries are already publicly funded, universally accessible, staffed by trained professionals, located in nearly every community, and widely trusted, making them the most cost-effective and equitable existing infrastructure to repurpose for climate resilience. Adoption has accelerated sharply since the mid-2010s as heat waves,

      Cooling Centers

      Libraries are among the most common municipally designated cooling centers because they offer air conditioning, seating, restrooms, water fountains, free Wi-Fi, and welcoming staff at no cost to visitors. During heat emergencies, libraries typically extend hours, cancel nonessential programs to preserve cooling capacity, distribute water and hydration information, and coordinate with public health and emergency management agencies to direct vulnerable residents indoors. Major systems including Chicago, New York City, and Los Angeles routinely list dozens of library branches among their officia

      Warming Centers

      In cold-climate regions, libraries serve as warming centers during extreme cold, arctic vortex events, and winter power outages, providing heat, seating, power outlets, and a safe daytime refuge for unhoused and energy-insecure residents. Many northern and Midwestern systems extend hours, partner with outreach workers, offer hot beverages, and suspend quiet-use enforcement during cold snaps to maximize shelter capacity for vulnerable populations.

      Emergency Shelters

      Libraries function as emergency shelters and disaster-recovery sites during hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, ice storms, and earthquakes, leveraging durable construction, backup power, and communications infrastructure to keep communities connected when other facilities close. During and after disasters, libraries provide device charging, internet and FEMA-registration assistance, document printing and laminating, unmet-needs referral, and safe meeting space, often remaining open when schools and government offices shut down. FEMA and state emergency management agencies increasingly recognize li

      Air Quality Refuge

      Libraries act as clean-air refuges during hazardous air-quality events by providing filtered, climate-controlled indoor space where residents, especially those with respiratory conditions, can escape outdoor pollution. Following record 2020 and 2023 wildfire-smoke events on the West Coast and across North America, many libraries upgraded HVAC to MERV-13 or better filtration and extended hours so the public could shelter indoors during hazardous Air Quality Index spikes.

      Sustainability Programs

      Libraries advance climate resilience through green building, energy efficiency, renewable energy, waste reduction, and public sustainability education, reducing both their own carbon footprint and community emissions. A growing number of new and renovated libraries pursue LEED certification, with several, including Cedar Rapids and Greensburg, achieving Platinum status and serving as national models for sustainable civic architecture. Common upgrades include rooftop solar arrays, geothermal heating and cooling, LED lighting, high-performance building envelopes, and battery backup that doubles

      Community Resilience Hub

      The resilience hub model reframes libraries as neighborhood-scale assets that support the community every day and pivot to disruption response and recovery without needing new construction, because the facility and trust already exist. The Urban Sustainability Directors Network (USDN) Resilience Hub framework defines four service areas, day-to-day services, disruption response, recovery operations, and communications, and calls for reliable backup power, water, and connectivity so the hub can operate when the grid is down.

      Key Findings

      • Libraries are the most widely distributed, universally accessible, and publicly trusted civic infrastructure in the United States, making them an ideal and low-cost backbone for community climate resilience.
      • A large and growing share of municipal heat-emergency plans in cities such as Chicago, New York, and Los Angeles officially designate library branches as cooling centers.
      • During extreme heat, library branches consistently report sharp visit increases, confirming that residents already intuitively turn to libraries as refuge sites even without formal outreach.
      • Hurricane Sandy in 2012 was a turning point, with Queens and other affected systems proving that libraries could anchor disaster-recovery operations by providing power, internet, and FEMA-registration support.
      • The 2020 and 2023 wildfire-smoke seasons drove rapid HVAC filtration upgrades, with many systems moving to MERV-13 or better filtration to serve as clean-air refuges.
      • The Urban Sustainability Directors Network Resilience Hub framework gives libraries a shared vocabulary and service model, covering day-to-day services, disruption response, recovery, and communications.
      • Backup power is the critical gap; resilience-hub readiness depends on solar-plus-storage or generators so a library can keep cooling, communications, and medical-device charging running during grid outages.
      • Green building leadership at libraries such as Cedar Rapids and Greensburg demonstrates that sustainable design and disaster resilience can be achieved simultaneously through LEED Platinum construction.
      • Federal recognition is growing, with FEMA incorporating libraries in disaster frameworks and IMLS funding disaster-preparedness and continuity grants for library systems.
      • Equity outcomes are central to the library model, because libraries reach heat-vulnerable, unhoused, elderly, and low-income residents who are often missed by other emergency-response channels.

      Gaming in Libraries Deep Dive

      A deep dive into gaming as a library service in the United States, covering video game collections and circulation, tabletop and board game lending, Dungeons & Dragons and RPG programs, esports tournaments, game design and game jams, and the American Library Association's national gaming initiatives. It highlights fifteen notable library gaming programs and ten key findings about gaming as an engagement and literacy tool.

      Overview

      Gaming in libraries refers to video game collections, tabletop and board game lending, role-playing game programs, esports tournaments, and game design activities offered as part of library services and programming. Gaming attracts teens and patrons who do not otherwise use the library, builds problem-solving and collaboration skills, and advances digital and media literacy. The ALA recognizes games as a legitimate format and a powerful engagement and learning tool. Library gaming grew from a handful of pioneering collections in the early 2000s into a mainstream service after ALA launched Nati

      Video Game Collections

      Many U.S. public libraries circulate video games alongside books and DVDs, treating games as a core media format. Video game collections are especially effective at drawing teen and family patrons who are not traditional library users. Video games are among the fastest-circulating media formats in libraries that offer them, often outpacing DVDs on a per-copy basis. Adoption has grown steadily since the mid-2000s, though only a minority of systems currently circulate games. Nintendo Switch dominates library video game collections because of its broad family appeal, followed by PlayStation (PS4/

      Tabletop Gaming

      Tabletop gaming in libraries includes circulating board game collections, hosting board game nights, and running role-playing game programs. It is relatively low-cost to launch and fosters in-person social interaction. Libraries lend board games such as Catan, Ticket to Ride, and Azul and host regular game nights for children, teens, and adults. Board game collections are cheaper to build than video game collections and support face-to-face community building. Dungeons & Dragons and other tabletop RPG programs surged in libraries after D&D's fifth edition (2014) and the popularity

      Esports

      A growing number of libraries host competitive gaming and esports programs for teens, paralleling the rise of scholastic esports. Esports in libraries build teamwork, digital citizenship, and pathways to STEM and technology careers. Super Smash Bros. is the most common library tournament title, alongside Mario Kart, Fortnite, Rocket League, and Splatoon. ALA's International Games Day has long featured national tournament events linked across participating libraries. Esports-capable libraries invest in gaming PCs, current-generation consoles, low-latency monitors, headsets, and streaming g

      Game Design

      Libraries run game design and creation programs that teach coding, systems thinking, and digital literacy while aligning with STEM and STEAM education goals. Game design positions the library as a creation space, not just a consumption space. Common tools include Scratch, Minecraft, Roblox, Gamestar Mechanic, Unity, Godot, and GameMaker, often delivered through workshops and after-school clubs. The Joan Ganz Cooney Center and E-Line Media's National STEM Video Game Challenge (2010-2017) partnered with libraries to promote youth game design. Libraries host game jams -- time-bounded game cr

      ALA Gaming Initiatives

      The American Library Association champions gaming through the Games and Gaming Round Table (GamERT, est. 2011), publications, advocacy recognizing games as a format, and the Games in Libraries initiative, which provides toolkits and best practices. National Gaming Day @ your library was first held on November 15, 2008; it became International Games Day @ your library in 2012 and later expanded to International Games Week. By 2013 more than 1,800 libraries across all 50 states and several countries participated.

      • Gaming is one of the most effective tools libraries have for reaching teens and non-users, with video game and tabletop collections consistently drawing patrons who do not otherwise visit the library.
      • The ALA formally recognizes games as a legitimate library format and a literacy tool, codified through the Games and Gaming Round Table (est. 2011) and years of advocacy and toolkits.
      • National Gaming Day (2008) became International Games Day (2012) and then International Games Week, growing to over 1,800 participating libraries across all 50 states and multiple countries by 2013.
      • Nintendo Switch is the dominant platform in circulating library video game collections owing to its family appeal, followed by PlayStation and Xbox titles.
      • Dungeons & Dragons programming exploded in libraries after D&D fifth edition (2014) and the Stranger Things phenomenon, with many teen campaigns maintaining waiting lists.
      • Tabletop and board game lending is cheaper to launch than video game collections and uniquely supports in-person social interaction and intergenerational programming.
      • Esports in libraries is a fast-growing service area, with the North America Scholastic Esports Federation (NASEF) partnering with libraries to provide curriculum and club models.
      • Super Smash Bros. is the most popular library tournament game, featured in ALA's national International Games Day tournament events linked across participating libraries.
      • Game design and game jam programs connect library gaming to STEM and STEAM education, using tools like Scratch, Minecraft, Unity, and Godot and ties to the National STEM Video Game Challenge.
      • No authoritative national census of library gaming services exists; adoption and circulation figures are best-effort estimates drawn from ALA, IMLS, and Library Journal surveys rather than a single federal dataset.

      Preservation & Conservation Deep Dive

      This document provides a structured overview of how U.S. libraries preserve and conserve their physical and digital collections. It covers the preservation work of the Library of Congress and major research-library conservation laboratories, digital-preservation standards such as OAIS and TRAC, disaster preparedness with the dPlan tool, environmental controls, reformatting through microfilm and digitization, and professional training and certification programs. It is intended as a single referen

      Overview

      Preservation encompasses all activities that prolong the usable life of library and archival materials, including proper housing, environmental control, disaster planning, reformatting, and conservation treatment. It addresses both the original physical item and the intellectual content it carries, applying to collections in every format. Library collections are built largely on organic materials such as paper, leather, adhesives, photographic emulsions, and magnetic and optical media that inevitably decay. Active preservation safeguards the cultural, legal, and scientific record held by libra

      Conservation Labs

      Conservation is the physical treatment of individual items to stabilize, repair, or restore them, performed by trained conservators in specialized laboratories. Large research libraries and nonprofit regional centers operate conservation labs equipped for surface cleaning, paper mending, binding, and complex structural treatment. Leading U.S. conservation operations include the Library of Congress Conservation Division, the New York Public Library's Barbara Goldsmith Conservation Laboratory, the Weissman Preservation Center at Harvard Library, Yale University Library's Conservation &

      Digital Preservation

      Digital preservation safeguards born-digital and digitized content so it remains authentic and accessible despite changing file formats, media decay, and software obsolescence. It is an active, ongoing process rather than a one-time act, requiring managed storage, metadata, format migration, and regular fixity checks. The OAIS reference model (ISO 14721) defines the functions of a trustworthy digital archive, while TRAC and its successor ISO 16363 provide criteria for auditing and certifying repositories. The NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation offer a practical, tiered self-assessment framewo

      Disaster Preparedness

      Disaster preparedness protects collections from water, fire, mold, pests, and other emergencies through written plans, staff training, and stocked supplies. A written disaster plan that assigns roles and lists salvage priorities and emergency contacts is the foundation of an effective response. dPlan is a free, online disaster-planning tool developed by the Northeast Document Conservation Center (NEDCC) and the Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners, with IMLS funding, that guides libraries step by step through writing a customized disaster plan. The companion PReP (Pocket Response Plan)

      Environmental Controls

      Stable temperature and relative humidity, controlled light, clean air, and integrated pest management slow the chemical, biological, and mechanical deterioration of collections. Environmental monitoring with dataloggers and regular review of the readings are core preservation practices. For general collections a target around 65 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit and 30 to 50 percent relative humidity is common, while special collections benefit from cooler, drier conditions and daily swings should stay within about five percent RH. The Image Permanence Institute's Preservation Index (PI) and Time-

      Reformatting

      Reformatting transfers the intellectual content of fragile or deteriorating originals onto more durable or accessible media, preserving access even as the source item degrades. The two principal strategies are preservation microfilming and digitization, often pursued in combination. Polyester-base silver-gelatin microfilm processed to ISO standards has a life expectancy of 500 years (LE-500) and was the backbone of the NEH-funded Brittle Books Program of the 1980s and 1990s, which microfilmed millions of embrittled volumes. Microfilm remains a trusted, low-tech, long-term preservation medium w

      Training Programs

      Professional conservation training is concentrated in a small number of graduate programs and continuing-education providers, supplemented by workshops from regional centers and national organizations. Preservation administrators often combine a library or information science degree with specialized conservation coursework or apprenticeship. The American Institute for Conservation (AIC) offers a tiered professional structure culminating in the Professional Associate and Fellow (FAIC) designations, which require demonstrated experience and peer review rather than a state license. NEDCC, Lyrasis

      Key Findings

      • Preservation and conservation are related but distinct: preservation covers the full range of activities that extend collection life, while conservation is the hands-on physical treatment of individual items by trained conservators in specialized labs.
      • The Library of Congress Preservation Directorate, established in 1967, is among the largest preservation operations in the world, encompassing conservation treatment, research and testing, mass deacidification, and collections care across millions of items.
      • Acidic groundwood paper from the mid-19th through late-20th century is the single greatest cause of brittle-book loss in U.S. research collections, driving decades of microfilming, deacidification, and digitization programs.
      • OAIS (ISO 14721) provides the standard reference model for digital archives, and TRAC and its successor ISO 16363 define the criteria for auditing and certifying trustworthy digital repositories; together they anchor digital-preservation practice.
      • dPlan, a free online tool from NEDCC and the Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners, lets libraries and archives generate a customized disaster plan, while the one-page PReP plan ensures first-response information is always at hand.
      • Stable temperature and humidity are the most cost-effective preservation strategy; the Image Permanence Institute's Preservation Index translates environmental data into a single measure of how storage conditions affect collection longevity.
      • Preservation microfilm produced to ISO standards has an estimated 500-year life expectancy and remains a trusted long-term medium, even as digitization has become the dominant access strategy.
      • Digitization is not the same as digital preservation: high-resolution masters only remain accessible over time if managed through a program of fixity checks, metadata, format migration, and trusted repository storage.
      • Formal conservation training is concentrated in a handful of graduate programs at UT Austin, the Winterthur/University of Delaware Program in Art Conservation, and Buffalo State's Garman Art Conservation Department, while AIC's Professional Associate and Fellow designations recognize practitioner expertise.
      • Federal investment through IMLS, notably the Connecting to Collections and Save America's Treasures grant programs, has been essential to building preservation capacity in smaller libraries and museums that could not fund this work alone.

      Book Clubs & Reading Groups Deep Dive

      A comprehensive overview of book clubs and reading groups hosted by U.S. public libraries, covering community-wide reading programs, virtual clubs, specialty genre and demographic groups, book club kits, and author discussion events.

      Overview

      Library book clubs are facilitated reading discussion groups hosted by public libraries, offering community members free, structured conversations around selected titles. Book clubs rank among the most widely offered recurring adult programs at U.S. public libraries, with thousands of groups convening monthly nationwide. Originating as informal in-person discussion circles, library book clubs have diversified into themed, demographic-specific, hybrid, and fully virtual formats to meet changing community needs.

      One Book One Community

      One Book, One Community programs coordinate entire cities or regions to read and discuss a single title simultaneously through library-organized events, discussions, and author visits. The concept began in 1998 with 'If All of Seattle Read the Same Book,' launched by librarian Nancy Pearl at the Seattle Public Library's Washington Center for the Book, with Russell Banks's 'The Sweet Hereafter' as the inaugural selection. The model spread rapidly; the Library of Congress documented 404 community reading programs by 2007, with programs now active in nearly every U.S

      Virtual Book Clubs

      Virtual book clubs use online platforms to host reading discussions, broadening access for readers regardless of geography, mobility, or schedule. Libraries employ Zoom, Facebook Groups, Goodreads, and dedicated library portals, often pairing live video discussions with asynchronous message-board conversations. The COVID-19 pandemic rapidly accelerated virtual programming adoption, and many libraries retained online options permanently after discovering they reached new and larger audiences.

      Specialty Clubs

      Specialty book clubs center on specific genres, identities, or interests, enabling libraries to serve niche audiences within their broader communities. Genre-focused clubs commonly include mystery, science fiction and fantasy, romance, and literary fiction discussion groups, each drawing devoted readers. Libraries host demographic-targeted groups such as LGBTQ+ reading clubs, Spanish-language 'club de lectura' gatherings, teen and youth clubs, senior groups, and men's or women's book clubs.

      Book Kits

      Book club kits, often called 'bags of books,' are curated sets containing multiple copies of a single title plus discussion materials that libraries lend to private and community book clubs. Typically packaged as 8 to 15 copies in a tote bag with author biographies and discussion questions, these kits allow clubs to borrow enough copies for all members at no cost.

      Author Discussions

      Libraries regularly host author talks and book signings where writers discuss their work directly with readers, frequently tied to book club or community reading selections. Virtual author visits via video conferencing have made it affordable for smaller and rural libraries to host prominent authors, democratizing access to author discussions.

      • Library book clubs are among the most popular and cost-effective adult programming offerings at U.S. public libraries.
      • The One Book, One Community movement originated in Seattle in 1998 and has since expanded to over 400 programs nationwide.

      • The Big Read, an NEA program running since 2006, provides grants that enable libraries of all sizes to mount community reading celebrations.
      • The COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lasting shift toward virtual book clubs, expanding participation beyond traditional in-person audiences.
      • Specialty book clubs targeting genres like mystery and science fiction, and demographics like LGBTQ+ and Spanish-speaking readers, help libraries serve diverse niche audiences.
      • Book club kits or 'bags of books' are a widely adopted service that lets libraries lend multiple copies of a title to community book clubs at no cost.
      • Virtual author visits have lowered the cost barrier for smaller libraries to host well-known authors for reader discussions.
      • State humanities councils, such as those in Maryland, Iowa, and Vermont, partner with public libraries to run statewide one-book programs.
      • The ALA and Library of Congress maintain resource lists and program guides that support libraries in organizing and sustaining book clubs.

      Reentry & Justice-Involved Services Deep Dive

      A deep, narrative summary of how U.S. public libraries serve formerly incarcerated and justice-involved people. Covers the scale of reentry, expungement clinics run with legal-aid partners, job-search and skills assistance, reentry resource guides, library service inside correctional facilities and books-to-prisoners programs, family support including video visitation and services for children of incarcerated parents, notable programs by state, and key findings. Compiled from ALA, IMLS, the Just

      Overview

      Reentry is the process by which a person transitions from incarceration back into the community. Library reentry services are the programs, collections, and referrals public libraries offer to formerly incarcerated and justice-involved people to support that transition. Libraries are free, non-stigmatizing, require no appointment or proof of income, and are located in nearly every community, making them one of the few public institutions justice-involved people can use immediately on release without triggering surveillance or judgment. Roughly 600,000 people are released from U.S. state and fe

      Expungement Clinics

      A growing number of public libraries host expungement and record-sealing clinics where patrons can meet with attorneys to learn whether their criminal record qualifies for sealing or expungement and begin the paperwork. Because a criminal record blocks employment, housing, and licensing, libraries frame these clinics as a direct reentry intervention. Libraries run these clinics through partnerships with legal aid societies, public defender offices, bar association pro bono programs, and law school clinics, supplying the meeting space, computers, and outreach while attorneys provide the legal e

      Job Assistance

      Employment is one of the most stabilizing factors after release, and libraries are a primary free site for job search, applications, and skills building. Many libraries extend their general workforce services with reentry-aware help and partner with American Job Centers and workforce boards. Libraries offer one-on-one and workshop-style help with resumes, cover letters, online applications, and interview practice, and increasingly coach patrons on how to address a criminal record honestly without derailing an application. Libraries provide digital-literacy classes, GED study materials and test

      Reentry Resource Guides

      Many libraries compile and publish reentry resource guides that consolidate the scattered information a returning citizen needs into a single, navigable document, often produced with reentry coalitions and corrections departments. Typical guides list housing and shelter contacts, benefits and ID offices, food pantries, transportation, substance-use and mental-health treatment, legal aid, and employers known to hire justice-involved people, frequently maintained both in print and online.

      Library Inside Programs

      Some public and state libraries extend service into local jails and state prisons through rotating collections, reference-by-mail, and reentry planning, connecting readers to a community library card and resources before release. ALA's 2024 Revised Standards for Library Services for the Incarcerated or Detained encourage this public-library-as-correctional-partner model. Books-to-prisoners programs are volunteer nonprofits that mail donated books directly to incarcerated readers, filling gaps where in-facility collections are minimal or nonexistent. Examples include Books Through Bars (Ph

      Family Support

      Incarceration separates millions of families, and libraries increasingly serve the family members left behind - especially children - with visitation support, books, and programming that maintains the parent-child bond across distance. A few library systems host free video visitation, letting families conduct video calls with incarcerated loved ones from a library branch when home internet or devices are unavailable or when visiting a facility is impractical. The Brooklyn Public Library's Televisit program is a leading example. Libraries serve children of incarcerated parents with book gi

      Key Findings

      • Approximately 70 million Americans have some type of criminal record, and roughly 600,000 people are released from U.S. prisons each year, making reentry support a population-scale need rather than a niche service.
      • Libraries are uniquely positioned for reentry work because they are free, non-stigmatizing, require no appointment or proof of income, and are open in nearly every community, so returning citizens can use them immediately on release.
      • Expungement and record-sealing clinics hosted by libraries in partnership with legal aid societies, public defenders, and bar association pro bono programs are among the most direct reentry interventions a library can offer, because a sealed record unlocks employment, housing, and licensing.
      • ALA's 2024 Revised Standards for Library Services for the Incarcerated or Detained (the first update since 1992) and the ALA/SFPL Justice-Involved Services Toolkit give libraries a national framework for both in-facility and post-release justice-involved service.
      • Books-to-prisoners nonprofits such as Books Through Bars, the Prisoners Literature Project, Inside Books Project, and the Women's Prison Book Project fill critical gaps where in-facility library collections are minimal or nonexistent.
      • Job-search and skills assistance is a core reentry service at many libraries, including resume help, digital-literacy and GED classes, Career Online High School, and partnerships with American Job Centers and workforce boards.
      • Reentry resource guides compiled by libraries consolidate scattered information on housing, benefits, ID, treatment, legal aid, and second-chance employers into a single navigable document, often in partnership with reentry coalitions.
      • Video visitation programs such as the Brooklyn Public Library's Televisit let families conduct free video calls with incarcerated loved ones from a library branch, removing the cost and travel barriers of prison visits.
      • Libraries serve children of incarcerated parents with book giveaways, storytimes, caregiver resources, and curricula like the Sesame Street 'Little Children, Big Challenges: Incarceration' toolkit, often alongside nonprofits such as the Osborne Association.
      • Service depends heavily on partnerships: public libraries with legal aid and workforce boards for post-release services, and state library agencies, nonprofits, ALA, NIC, IMLS, and foundations such as Mellon for in-facility and book-donation work.

      Reference Services Deep Dive

      This document provides a deep summary of reference service in libraries across the United States, tracing its evolution from the staffed reference desk of the twentieth century to today's blended mix of chat, text, email, statewide Ask a Librarian cooperatives, 24/7 cooperative reference, scheduled research consultations, and government-information assistance. It covers the reference interview and RUSA professional guidelines, the rise and sunset of virtual-reference cooperatives such as Qu

      Overview

      Reference service is the personal assistance librarians give patrons in finding information, answering questions, and learning to use library resources. Its defining technique is the reference interview, the structured dialogue that uncovers a patron's true information need behind an initial query. Reference began as an in-person desk service in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, later adding telephone query lines, then email and web forms in the 1990s, and live chat and text in the 2000s. Each new channel was layered onto, rather than fully replacing, the desk, producing the multi-c

      Virtual Reference

      Virtual reference (also called digital or e-reference) delivers reference help through digital channels rather than in person. It includes asynchronous email and form services plus synchronous chat, and is valued for extending service to remote users and off-hours. Live chat is the dominant synchronous virtual-reference format, typically embedded as a widget on the library website or catalog and often backed by platforms such as Springshare LibChat and LibraryH3lp. Chat sessions support co-browsing, transcript archiving, and follow-up by email, and are frequently staffed cooperatively. SMS or

      Ask a Librarian

      'Ask a Librarian' is the common public-facing brand for virtual reference at both individual libraries and statewide cooperatives. Statewide versions pool staffing across many libraries so that one shared service can offer longer hours and broader expertise than any single library could sustain alone. Florida's Ask a Librarian, launched in 2002, became the model for statewide cooperative reference, offering chat, email, and text staffed by participating public, academic, and school libraries and funded by LSTA grants. Similar programs later appeared in Maryland, New Jersey, Ohio

      Research Consultations

      Research consultations are scheduled, in-depth, one-on-one meetings between a patron and a subject librarian. They address complex projects, literature reviews, data help, and methodology that exceed what a quick desk or chat exchange can provide. The appointment model is now standard in academic libraries, where subject specialists offer bookable sessions for undergraduates, graduate students, and faculty. Bookings are made through online scheduling tools, and the format has spread to public libraries serving job seekers, small businesses, and genealogists.

      Government Information

      Reference service for government information helps patrons find laws, regulations, statistics, census data, and agency publications. This expertise is concentrated in depository libraries, whose staff are trained in the specialized catalogs and finding aids of government publishing. The Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP), administered by the Government Publishing Office (GPO), designates libraries to provide free public access to federal information and expert assistance with it. As publications shift to digital-only formats, FDLP reference work has moved from shelving expertise to navi

      Reference Statistics

      The IMLS Public Libraries Survey has long tracked reference transactions, defined as information contacts involving knowledge, use, recommendation, or instruction of resources. The metric gives a national picture of reference demand but has grown harder to measure consistently as service moves online. PLS national totals show reference transactions peaking at about 310 million in 2009, declining to roughly 221 million by 2019, then collapsing to about 108 million in 2021 during the pandemic before partially rebounding to about 145 million in 2024. The long pre-pandemic slide reflects both a re

      AI & Reference

      Generative AI, accelerating after the late-2022 release of ChatGPT, is reshaping reference by offering instant drafts, summaries, and search guidance that overlap with basic reference help. Libraries are weighing how to adopt these tools for efficiency without abandoning the accuracy and human judgment at the heart of reference. AI chatbots are being piloted to triage repetitive questions, extend after-hours coverage, and guide patrons to resources, with complex queries routed to human librarians. Concerns include hallucinated answers, bias, privacy of patron data, transparency about AI use, a

      Key Findings

      • Reference service has evolved from the physical reference desk toward a blended model combining in-person, chat, email, text, and scheduled consultations, with virtual channels now handling a large share of questions once fielded at the desk.
      • The reference interview, the structured dialogue that clarifies a patron's real information need, remains the core professional skill and is codified in RUSA's Guidelines for Behavioral Performance of Reference and Information Service Providers.
      • Statewide cooperative Ask a Librarian services, led by Florida's 2002 program, pooled staffing across public, academic, and school libraries to offer chat reference that no single library could sustain alone.
      • The 24/7 Reference Cooperative within OCLC's QuestionPoint, launched in 2002 with the Library of Congress, extended chat coverage around the clock through cooperative staffing and backup queues before OCLC sunset the service at the end of 2019.
      • Research consultations, scheduled in-depth one-on-one sessions with subject specialists, have grown as a higher-value complement to drop-in reference, especially in academic libraries supporting complex coursework and research.
      • Federal Depository Libraries in the FDLP, administered by the Government Publishing Office (GPO), provide specialized reference assistance for government information that has grown more complex as publications shift to digital-only formats.
      • IMLS Public Libraries Survey data show reference transactions peaking at about 310 million in 2009, falling to roughly 221 million by 2019, dropping to about 108 million in 2021, and partially rebounding to about 145 million in 2024.
      • The pre-pandemic decline in counted reference questions reflects both a real drop in desk traffic and the migration of routine questions to search engines and online self-service, while the COVID-era collapse mirrored the plunge in library visits.
      • Generative AI chatbots, accelerating after 2022, are being piloted to triage repetitive questions and extend after-hours coverage, but raise concerns about hallucination, bias, privacy, transparency, and the loss of the human reference interview.
      • The future of reference is likely a hybrid human-plus-AI model in which librarians focus on complex, evaluative, and culturally responsive help while AI assists with triage and 24/7 availability, guided by emerging ALA and RUSA ethical frameworks.

      Seed Libraries & Library of Things Deep Dive

      A deep dive into U.S. public library seed libraries, tool libraries, and the Library of Things movement: how non-book lending collections work, their origins and growth, the items they circulate, and their impact on sustainability, food security, and community resilience.

      Seed Library Overview

      A seed library is a free, community-based collection of seeds that patrons borrow, plant, grow, and then return saved seed from at the end of the season. Hosted overwhelmingly in public libraries, it treats seeds as a shared, renewable community resource rather than a commercial product. The public-library model is credited to the Richmond Grows Seed Lending Library, opened in May 2010 at the Richmond Public Library (California), which freely shared its how-to toolkit so others could replicate it. Earlier community seed projects, such as the Bay Area Seed Interchange Library (BASIL) in Berkele

      How Seed Libraries Work

      Seed libraries operate on a simple borrow-grow-save-return cycle that is free and usually requires no traditional library-card transaction. Most also pair the collection with gardening workshops and seed-saving education to build grower capacity. Patrons check out a few seed packets per season, typically via a simple sign-out sheet or card, choosing from vegetables, herbs, and flowers suited to the local climate. There is no fee, and overdue fines do not apply because seeds are meant to be planted. At season's end, gardeners let some plants go to seed, harvest and dry the seed, and return

      Tool Libraries

      Tool libraries lend hand and power tools the way libraries lend books, giving patrons free or low-cost access to equipment they would otherwise have to buy. The concept predates the broader Library of Things movement by decades, with some public library tool collections dating to the late 1970s. Tools are checked out for a short loan period (often a few days to a week), sometimes with a small deposit or membership fee to cover maintenance and replacement. Many tool libraries rely on volunteers for staffing, repair, and inventory, and partner with makers or local hardware stores for donations.

      Library of Things

      The Library of Things is the broader movement to lend non-book items -- kitchen equipment, musical instruments, sports and outdoor gear, electronics, games, and more -- recasting the library as a shared community inventory. It gained momentum in the mid-2010s as libraries sought to serve patrons who needed access to things, not just information. Among the more unusual items lent are telescopes, metal detectors, thermal cameras, kill-a-watt electricity monitors, karaoke machines, GoPro cameras, specialty baking pans, and ukuleles. Some libraries also lend knitting machines, button makers, or vi

      Community Impact

      Seed libraries, tool libraries, and Library of Things collections expand the library's role from information provider to shared community infrastructure, reducing the cost of living and building local self-reliance. They also strengthen social ties by connecting patrons around shared resources and skills. By enabling reuse and shared ownership, these programs reduce consumption, waste, and the carbon footprint of goods that are used only occasionally. Seed libraries additionally preserve crop biodiversity and regionally adapted plant varieties that industrial agriculture has displaced. Se

      Key Findings

      • Seed libraries are the fastest-growing nontraditional library movement, expanding from a single public library in 2010 to an estimated 500+ today, returning the means of food production to communities and rebuilding seed-saving knowledge.
      • The borrow-grow-save-return cycle makes seed libraries self-renewing: returned seed restocks the collection and gradually adapts it to local growing conditions, distinguishing them from ordinary lending collections.
      • Tool libraries predate the Library of Things by decades, with the Berkeley Public Library's 1979 tool collection showing that shared non-book lending is a long-established, not merely recent, library function.
      • The Library of Things reframes the library as shared community inventory, lending kitchen equipment, instruments, sports gear, and electronics so patrons can access infrequently used items without buying them.
      • WiFi hotspot lending is one of the most widely adopted Library of Things items, directly addressing the digital divide for patrons without home broadband.
      • The 2014 Pennsylvania seed-law case and the subsequent AASCO resolution clarified that noncommercial community seed sharing should be accommodated, securing the legal footing the seed-library movement needed to grow.
      • These programs reduce consumption and waste by enabling reuse and shared ownership, lowering households' cost of living and cutting the carbon footprint of goods used only occasionally.
      • Seed libraries advance food security at its root by giving people free access to seeds and the knowledge to grow and save food, complementing library gardens and cooking programs.
      • Partnerships with nonprofits, extension services, utility companies, and Friends groups are essential, supplying the tools, telescopes, seeds, expertise, and funding that libraries rarely possess in-house.
      • No single authoritative registry counts seed libraries, tool libraries, or Library of Things collections; figures like the 500+ seed libraries are widely cited community estimates and should be verified against current sources before publication.

      Interlibrary Loan Deep Dive

      A detailed overview of interlibrary loan (ILL) and resource sharing in U.S. libraries, covering the major systems (OCLC WorldShare ILL and Tipasa, RapidILL), reciprocal and consortial borrowing, document delivery, fee structures, and notable programs.

      Overview

      Interlibrary loan (ILL) is a cooperative service that lets a patron of one library borrow materials -- books, articles, or media -- held by another library, extending access far beyond a single institution's collection. It is also known as resource sharing, document delivery, inter-lending, or inter-library services. A patron requests an item at their home (borrowing) library, which locates holding (lending) libraries through a union catalog or network and places a request. The lender ships the physical item or sends a scanned copy electronically; the borrowing library then delivers it to

      OCLC Resource Sharing

      OCLC, founded in 1967 as the Ohio College Library Center and later renamed the Online Computer Library Center, runs the dominant U.S. resource-sharing network, built on WorldCat -- the world's largest online public access catalog. Its ILL platforms let borrowing libraries identify lenders across thousands of institutions and track requests end to end. WorldShare Interlibrary Loan is OCLC's earlier cloud-based resource-sharing application, part of the WorldShare Management Services platform, providing request management, lender discovery, and reporting. It has been superseded for most

      Rapid ILL

      RapidILL was developed at Colorado State University in 1997 after the Spring Creek flood destroyed much of its physical journal holdings, as a fast resource-sharing solution emphasizing near-instant article delivery. It grew to more than 300 member libraries internationally and was acquired by Ex Libris (now part of Clarivate) in 2019. RapidILL's core is an automated routing protocol that matches a request to the best-positioned lender based on holdings and expected turnaround, enabling article requests to be filled in hours rather than days. The 'rapid' design prioritizes speed

      Reciprocal Borrowing

      Reciprocal borrowing lets a patron with a card from one library check out materials in person at other participating libraries, typically at no charge. Most U.S. states operate some form of statewide or regional reciprocal program, often coordinated by state library agencies and supported with federal Library Services and Technology Act (LSTA) funds administered by the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS). Examples include the Colorado Library Card program, the Michigan eLibrary (MeL), Minnesota's MNLINK statewide catalog, and Massachusetts regional reciprocal borrowing. These

      Consortial Borrowing

      Consortial borrowing is resource sharing among libraries that have formal agreements to lend to each other's patrons, usually through a shared union catalog and a shared courier or delivery service. Consortia may be academic, statewide, or regional, and members frequently share electronic-resource licensing and a delivery infrastructure that speeds fulfillment. Major consortia include OhioLINK (Ohio academic libraries), the Orbis Cascade Alliance's Summit (Oregon/Washington), Prospector (Colorado/Wyoming), TexShare (Texas), PALCI (Pennsylvania), ConnectNY (New York), the Big Ten Acad

      Document Delivery

      Document delivery is the electronic supply of scanned journal articles or book chapters -- rather than lending a whole physical item -- often used when only a specific article is needed. It overlaps with ILL but is governed by copyright law and license terms that frequently restrict how articles may be transmitted. Lending libraries scan requested articles and transmit them via secure electronic delivery, adhering to CONTU 'rule of five' guidelines and paying royalties through the Copyright Clearance Center's pay-per-use system. Many e-journal licenses now specify whether and ho

      Cost & Funding

      ILL costs include staff time, shipping, scanning, and copyright royalties; libraries fund these through operating budgets, consortial membership fees, per-transaction charges, and federal LSTA grants. Many academic libraries absorb ILL costs as a free patron service, while others pass all or part of the cost to the requester. Fee models range from free reciprocal lending among consortial partners to per-transaction charges (commonly $5-20 for lending plus shipping), with copyright fees billed separately via the Copyright Clearance Center. OCLC's Interlibrary Loan Fee Management (IFM) syst
