      Key Findings

      • ILL is a foundational cooperative service enabling patrons to access materials beyond their home library's holdings, with roots back to 1876 when Samuel Swett Green proposed interlibrary lending and ALA's 1917 national code formalized it in the United States.
      • OCLC operates the dominant U.S. resource-sharing network, built on WorldCat (the world's largest union catalog), and offers cloud-based ILL management through Tipasa, the successor to WorldShare Interlibrary Loan.
      • RapidILL, created at Colorado State University in 1997 after the Spring Creek flood destroyed journal holdings, pioneered automated request routing for near-instant article delivery and was acquired by Ex Libris in 2019.
      • ISO standards 10160 and 10161 define the international communication protocols that let disparate ILL systems interoperate, underpinning machine-to-machine request and response messaging.
      • Consortial borrowing programs such as OhioLINK, Orbis Cascade Alliance's Summit, and Prospector give patrons unified catalogs and rapid delivery across dozens of member libraries, often within days.
      • Most U.S. states operate some form of reciprocal borrowing that lets a resident with a local card borrow from participating libraries statewide, frequently coordinated by state library agencies and supported with LSTA/IMLS funds.
      • Document delivery -- the electronic supply of scanned articles and chapters -- is governed by CONTU 'rule of five' guidelines and copyright licensing, with secure electronic transmission now the norm.
      • ILL fee structures range from free reciprocal lending among partners to per-transaction charges (commonly $5-20), with OCLC's Interlibrary Loan Fee Management (IFM) system used to net and settle charges monthly.
      • Specialized networks serve particular communities: NNLM and DOCLINE route biomedical materials among health sciences libraries, while the Center for Research Libraries lends rare research items to its member universities.
      • Annual U.S. ILL volume runs into the millions of transactions, with OCLC's network handling a large share alongside RapidILL and regional consortia, making resource sharing a core pillar of equitable library access.

      Copyright & Information Literacy Deep Dive

      A consolidated reference on copyright and information literacy education across U.S. libraries, covering the ACRL Framework, fair use and Creative Commons, media and digital literacy, instructional design models, and assessment instruments.

      Overview

      Information literacy is the set of integrated abilities encompassing the reflective discovery of information, the understanding of how information is produced and valued, and the ethical use of information in creating new knowledge. The concept evolved from bibliographic instruction in the 1970s-80s, to the ACRL Information Literacy Competency Standards (2000), and then to the threshold-concept-based Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education (2016). Major frameworks include the ACRL Framework (2016) for higher education, the AASL Standards for the 21st-Century Learner for K-12, t

      ACRL Framework

      The ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, adopted in 2016, replaced the 2000 competency standards with a flexible, concept-based approach built on threshold concepts and metaliteracy. The six frames are: (1) Authority Is Constructed and Contextual, (2) Information Creation as a Process, (3) Information Has Value, (4) Research as Inquiry, (5) Scholarship as Conversation, and (6) Searching as Strategic Exploration. Threshold concepts are transformative, irreversible, integrative, bounded, and troublesome ideas that, once understood, permanently change how a learner percei

      Copyright Education

      Library copyright education helps patrons and educators understand the rights of creators alongside limitations such as fair use, first sale, and classroom exceptions under U.S. copyright law (Title 17). Fair use (17 U.S.C. Section 107) permits limited use of copyrighted works without permission, judged by four factors: purpose, nature, amount, and market effect; libraries apply the Code of Best Practices in Fair Use to guide decisions. Creative Commons (CC) licenses provide a standardized way for creators to grant use permissions, ranging from CC BY (attribution only) to CC BY-NC-ND; librarie

      Media Literacy

      Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all forms of communication; libraries integrate it with information literacy to help patrons navigate an information-saturated environment. Following the 2016 U.S. election, ALA and member libraries expanded programs to combat misinformation through news literacy, source evaluation, and fact-checking instruction, often using tools such as the CRAAP test. Libraries promote fact-checking skills using PolitiFact, Snopes, FactCheck.org, and the News Literacy Project's Checkology platform, teaching lateral readin

      Digital Literacy

      Digital literacy encompasses the skills to use information and communication technologies to find, evaluate, create, and communicate information, and is a core public library service alongside broadband access. Digital inclusion ensures equitable access to technology, broadband, and digital skills training; library hotspots and federal programs address the digital divide affecting rural and low-income communities. Google's Be Internet Awesome curriculum teaches children digital safety and citizenship; AASL partnered to distribute it through school libraries, while PLA's DigitalLearn.

      Instructional Design

      Instructional design in libraries applies learning theory and pedagogy to information literacy instruction, often using backward design and active learning to align outcomes with assessments. One-shot sessions are single, typically 50-90 minute library instruction sessions embedded in a course; they remain the most common model despite recognized limits in depth and retention. Embedded librarians integrate deeply into a course or program over a term, participating in learning management systems, discussion forums, and assignment design, producing stronger student outcomes.

      Assessment of Literacy

      Assessment of information literacy measures student learning through pre/post tests, rubrics, portfolios, and standardized instruments to demonstrate effectiveness and inform improvement. Project SAILS (Standardized Assessment of Information Literacy Skills), developed at Kent State University, is a standardized multiple-choice test librarians administer to assess skills and benchmark against peer institutions. Standardized tests such as Project SAILS and ETS iSkills offer comparable cross-institutional data but are criticized for measuring decontextualized skills rather than authentic, course

      Key Findings

      • The 2016 ACRL Framework shifted information literacy from skills-based standards to threshold concepts, emphasizing metaliteracy and contextual understanding of authority and value.
      • Fair use is the most powerful but most misunderstood exception for libraries and educators; the Code of Best Practices in Fair Use clarifies professional norms.
      • Creative Commons licensing underpins the open access and open educational resources movements championed by academic libraries.
      • Misinformation and fake news after the 2016 election prompted libraries to expand news literacy programming and source-evaluation instruction.
      • Digital inclusion remains uneven; rural and low-income communities depend on public libraries for broadband access and digital skills training.
      • Google's Be Internet Awesome and PLA DigitalLearn exemplify scalable, free digital literacy curricula distributed through libraries.
      • One-shot instruction remains the dominant model despite evidence that sustained, embedded engagement improves learning outcomes.
      • Embedded librarianship and faculty collaboration produce measurable gains in students' research quality and information literacy.
      • Project SAILS and similar standardized tools enable cross-institutional benchmarking but face criticism for decontextualizing information literacy.
      • Copyright education in libraries is frequently under-resourced, relying on a small number of scholarly communication specialists to serve campus-wide demand.

      Lifelong Learning & Adult Education Deep Dive

      This document examines how U.S. public libraries serve as accessible, trusted hubs for lifelong learning and adult education. It covers adult basic education and high school completion pathways such as GED preparation, Career Online High School, and Excel Adult High School; English as a Second Language conversation groups and citizenship preparation; digital literacy through Northstar Digital Literacy and PLA DigitalLearn; personal enrichment programming; and online learning platforms such as Ga

      Overview

      Lifelong learning is the ongoing, voluntary, and self-motivated pursuit of knowledge for personal or professional reasons, spanning formal and informal learning across all life stages. Libraries are uniquely positioned to support lifelong learning because they are free, non-judgmental, and open to all, reaching adults who are not served by traditional schools or workforce systems. They lower barriers to skills, credentials, and personal growth for underserved populations. Library-based lifelong learning ranges from adult basic education and high school completion to ESL, digital literacy, citi

      Adult Education

      Public libraries provide and host adult basic education (ABE) and high school equivalency services, often in partnership with adult education providers, and supply study materials, practice tests, and quiet space for adult learners. Many libraries offer GED preparation classes, official practice tests (often via GED Testing Service partners), and study collections, and some serve as GED testing or proctoring sites. Libraries frequently partner with local adult education programs and literacy councils to deliver instruction. Libraries increasingly sponsor accredited online high school completio

      ESL Services

      English as a Second Language (ESL) services are among the most common adult programs in U.S. public libraries, supporting immigrants, refugees, and newcomers with language learning, conversation practice, and civic integration. Services range from formal classes to informal drop-in groups. ESL conversation groups are informal, volunteer- or staff-led sessions where adult English learners practice speaking and listening in a supportive environment. They are low-cost to run, highly scalable, and among the most widely offered adult programs in public libraries. Many libraries offer citizenship pr

      Digital Skills

      Digital literacy is a core lifelong-learning service as libraries help adults gain the computer and internet skills needed for jobs, health, government services, and daily life. Libraries offer classes, one-on-one tutoring, and self-paced online curricula to close the digital divide. Northstar Digital Literacy, developed by Literacy Minnesota, defines and assesses foundational digital skills across domains like basic computer use, internet, email, and software. Hundreds of libraries and adult-education providers use its free assessments and standards to benchmark and teach digital literacy. PL

      Personal Enrichment

      Beyond credentials and workforce skills, libraries support informal lifelong learning through personal enrichment programming that engages curiosity and community. These free programs are open to all ages and require no registration or prior experience. Libraries commonly host hands-on hobby classes such as knitting, painting, gardening, cooking, coding, and genealogy workshops, often led by staff, volunteers, or local experts. These classes build skills and social connection without the cost of fee-based providers. Many libraries run author talks, book discussions, lifelong learning lecture s

      Online Learning

      Libraries extend lifelong learning beyond the building by licensing curated online learning platforms that cardholders can access for free. These platforms expand course selection far beyond what a single library could deliver in person. Gale Presents: Udemy offers libraries a subscription to thousands of on-demand video courses on business, technology, and creative skills, taught by industry instructors. Cardholders can stream courses anytime through their library's digital portal. LinkedIn Learning (formerly Lynda.com) provides professional video courses on software, business, and creat

      Partnerships

      Libraries rarely deliver adult education alone; they partner with schools, colleges, literacy organizations, and workforce agencies to share curriculum, instructors, funding, and referrals. These partnerships let libraries offer robust programming without duplicating state adult-education infrastructure. Libraries partner with community colleges to host adult basic education, ESL, and high school equivalency classes taught by college instructors, and to provide study space and resources for college students. These partnerships connect adult learners to credit-bearing pathways. Libraries collab

      • Libraries function as accessible, trusted on-ramps to lifelong learning, reaching adults who are not served by formal schools or workforce systems and lowering barriers of cost, stigma, and transportation.

      • Citizenship preparation programs in libraries are frequently supported by USCIS citizenship and integration grants and help lawful permanent residents prepare for the naturalization test.
      • Northstar Digital Literacy, created by Literacy Minnesota, provides widely used free assessments and standards that libraries adopt to benchmark and teach foundational digital skills.
      • PLA DigitalLearn (DigitalLearn.org) supplies free, self-paced, beginner-friendly tutorials that libraries use to build local digital-skills programming and supplement in-person help.
      • Online learning platforms such as Gale Presents: Udemy and LinkedIn Learning extend library course offerings far beyond what branches could deliver in person, though licensing costs shape availability.
      • Partnerships with community colleges, workforce development boards, and American Job Centers let libraries connect adult learners to credit-bearing education and employment pathways.
      • Funding and staffing are persistent constraints; many lifelong-learning and adult-education programs rely on grants, IMLS support, and partner organizations to sustain services.

      Library Governance & Board Structures Deep Dive

      This document surveys how public libraries in the United States are governed -- the legal structures, boards, state agencies, funding mechanisms, and standards that determine who controls a library, how it is funded, and how it is held accountable. Because US public libraries were founded under differing state laws over two centuries, no single national model exists. Instead libraries fall into four principal governance models: municipal departments of city government, county departments or syst

      Overview

      Library governance is the legal and administrative framework that establishes who owns and controls a public library, how its governing board is constituted, how it is funded, and to whom it is accountable. Governance determines a library's funding stability, operational autonomy, and political accountability, and therefore shapes its ability to plan long-term, defend intellectual freedom, and serve its community consistently. Four principal models coexist across the country -- municipal departments, county systems, independent special districts, and private nonprofit or association libra

      Governance Models

      The four governance models differ in who holds legal control, where funding originates, and how insulated the library is from the budget pressures of its parent government. State enabling law determines which models are permitted in a given state. The library is a department of city government, funded through the municipal general fund and overseen by the city council or mayor, often with an advisory or governing board appointed by the mayor. This model is common in older eastern and midwestern cities such as Boston, Chicago, and Los Angeles. The library is a department or system of county gov

      Library Boards

      Most public libraries are overseen by a board of trustees (or board of directors) that serves as the governing or advisory authority, sets policy, and hires and evaluates the library director. Board powers range from purely advisory in some municipal systems to fully governing in district and association libraries. Trustees are appointed by mayors or city councils in municipal libraries, by county commissioners in county systems, or elected by voters in some district libraries, while association library boards are self-perpetuating. Terms typically run three to five years and are often stagger

      State Library Agencies

      Every state has a state library agency -- variously titled State Library, State Library Commission, or a division within a larger department -- that serves as the principal state-level oversight and support body for libraries. These agencies employ professional staff and are led by a state librarian or director appointed by a board, governor, or department head. State library agencies administer federal LSTA funds passed through from IMLS, distribute state aid to public libraries, set or recommend library standards, provide consulting and continuing education, and coordinate statewide resource

      Funding Authority

      Roughly 85 percent of US public library revenue comes from local sources, predominantly property taxes, with state aid and federal grants making up the remainder. The legal mechanism by which a library secures and renews that local revenue is the core of its funding authority. Libraries frequently place bonds, operating levies, and millages on local ballots to fund construction or operations, and these measures pass at roughly 70 to 80 percent, reflecting strong baseline public support. Operating levies expire and must be renewed, making ballot campaigns a recurring institutional competency. S

      Accreditation

      There is no single national accreditation program for public libraries; standards and accreditation are overwhelmingly state-level and frequently voluntary. Where standards exist, they typically address hours of service, staffing, collection size, and per-capita spending. Many states publish minimum or model standards for public libraries, and a number tie compliance to eligibility for state aid or per-capita grants, creating a practical incentive to meet them. Examples include Illinois per-capita grant requirements and Texas Public Library Standards. Several states operate tiered voluntary ac

      Key Findings

      • The United States has no single national governance model for public libraries; governance is set by state enabling law and local history, producing a patchwork of municipal, county, special district, and nonprofit structures that vary even within a single state.
      • Because roughly 85 percent of public library revenue comes from local sources -- predominantly property taxes -- the local governance structure and ballot-box support are far more decisive for library funding than state or federal policy.
      • Library boards of trustees are the central governance mechanism in nearly every model, hiring the director, setting policy, and approving budgets, but their authority ranges from purely advisory in some municipal systems to fully governing in district and association libraries.
      • Board appointment methods vary widely across the country: mayoral appointment, council appointment, county commission appointment, popular election, and self-perpetuating election in association libraries, each creating different lines of accountability to the public.
      • Special library districts with independent taxing authority are the fastest-growing governance model because they insulate library funding from the competing demands of municipal general funds and provide long-term revenue stability.
      • State library agencies administer federal LSTA funds passed through from IMLS and set standards and distribute state aid, but their placement -- independent, within education, or within cultural affairs -- and their rulemaking authority vary dramatically by state.
      • Nonprofit or association governance, concentrated in New England and New York, grants libraries strong operational autonomy but creates accountability tensions because a private board controls an institution funded largely by public money.
      • Library ballot measures such as bonds, operating levies, and millages pass at roughly 70 to 80 percent, reflecting strong public support, but because operating levies expire they must be renewed, making ballot campaigns a recurring institutional competency rather than a one-time event.
      • Accreditation and standards for public libraries are overwhelmingly state-level and frequently voluntary; there is no national public library accreditation, though many states tie compliance with minimum standards to eligibility for state aid or per-capita grants.
      • Governance choices have measurable consequences: district and county libraries generally enjoy more stable funding and higher per-capita spending than municipal libraries dependent on city general funds, illustrating how structure shapes fiscal outcomes.

      Library Makerspaces & Fab Labs Network Deep Dive

      A deeper network-level dive into library makerspaces and fab labs, focusing on the equipment domains that define them, the curriculum and STEM integration they enable, the staffing models that sustain them, the documented impact on entrepreneurship and youth engagement, and the national networks -- Fab Foundation, Maker Corps, and Nation of Makers -- that connect them. Figures are best-effort estimates from public surveys and literature, not a precise national census.

      Network Overview

      A library makerspace or fab lab is a dedicated space in a public, academic, or school library offering shared fabrication, computing, and media-production tools for community use, typically free and open-access. It extends the library's mission from providing information to enabling creation. The movement grew from a handful of early-2010s pilots, led by Fayetteville Free Library's 2011 Fabulous Lab, into a mainstream library service. Growth accelerated 2013-2017 with falling equipment costs and IMLS seed grants, then matured into sustained programming through the 2020s. An estimated

      Equipment

      Most library makerspaces start with a single 3D printer and expand to a suite of additive and subtractive fabrication tools plus media-production gear. Vinyl cutters, heat presses, and electronics benches commonly round out the toolkit, with breadth tracking funding and staffing capacity. 3D printers are the gateway and most ubiquitous maker tool, present in roughly 90% of library makerspaces. Fused-filament (FDM) units from MakerBot, Prusa, and Bambu Lab dominate; resin (SLA) printers appear where fine detail is needed but add venting and handling burdens. Laser cutters and engravers -- CO2 m

      Curriculum

      Library makerspaces function as informal learning environments that complement formal schooling through drop-in making, workshops, and camps. Curriculum is typically open-ended and skill-laddered rather than prescriptive, reflecting libraries' self-directed learning ethos. Makerspaces embed STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts, math) into library programming via robotics, coding, electronics, and digital fabrication tied to school standards. Partnerships with schools and the Every Student Succeeds Act's STEAM emphasis have deepened these connections. Project-based learning i

      Staffing

      Staffing is the single greatest determinant of a makerspace's success and sustainability. Models range from dedicated full-time maker librarians to volunteer-mentor collectives, often blended with cross-trained reference and youth-services staff. Maker librarians are dedicated staff who manage equipment, design programs, and train patrons; the role emerged as a specialty in the 2010s and is featured in ALA and Library Journal Movers & Shakers lists. IMLS Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants fund training that prepares librarians for this work. Volunteer and peer mentors sustain ma

      Impact Studies

      Impact research on library makerspaces is growing but still fragmented, drawn from IMLS-funded evaluations, connected-learning studies, and case reports from leading spaces. Most evidence is qualitative and program-level rather than from controlled trials. Makerspaces support local entrepreneurship by giving startups, hobbyists, and side businesses free access to prototyping equipment they could not otherwise afford. Programs like Chattanooga's civic hackathons and Sacramento's prototyping support link making to business creation and local economic development. Youth engagement is th

      National Networks

      Several national networks connect library makerspaces to a broader maker ecosystem, sharing curricula, training, standards, and advocacy. The Fab Foundation, Maker Corps, and Nation of Makers are the most influential, each taking a distinct approach to organizing the field. The Fab Foundation, spun out of MIT's Center for Bits and Atoms, stewards the global Fab Lab network and its shared capability standards. A growing number of U.S. libraries have joined as registered Fab Labs, gaining access to a worldwide curriculum and peer community. Maker Corps, a program of the Maker Education Init

      Key Findings

      • An estimated 400+ library-affiliated makerspaces and fab labs now operate across U.S. public, academic, and school libraries, up from a handful of early-2010s pilots. No authoritative federal census exists, so figures are best-effort estimates triangulated from ALA, IMLS, and network registries.
      • 3D printing is the gateway technology, present in roughly 90% of library makerspaces and almost always the first equipment purchase. Many libraries offer 3D printing without operating a full makerspace, making it the most common single maker service.
      • Laser cutters mark the transition from a printer station to a true fab lab, appearing in about 40-50% of spaces. Ventilation, safety certification, and dedicated space are the main barriers to broader adoption.
      • CNC routers and mills remain the upper bound of library fabrication, present in only 10-15% of makerspaces. Their floor-space, dust, and training requirements confine them to larger, well-funded urban and academic spaces.
      • Curriculum is open-ended and project-based rather than prescriptive, aligning with the connected-learning framework from the MacArthur Foundation's YOUmedia research. STEAM integration is deepened by school partnerships and the Every Student Succeeds Act's emphasis on applied learning.
      • Staffing is the greatest determinant of sustainability, and dedicated maker librarians are the gold standard. IMLS Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants fund the training pipeline that prepares librarians for this specialty.
      • Volunteer and peer mentors sustain many smaller and equity-focused makerspaces, exemplified by the Free Library of Philadelphia's Maker Jawn. The Maker Corps program is a primary national pipeline for seasonal mentor staffing in libraries and museums.
      • Makerspaces support local entrepreneurship by providing free prototyping equipment to startups and side businesses that lack other access. Chattanooga's civic hackathons and Sacramento's prototyping support link making directly to business creation and economic development.
      • Youth engagement is the best-documented impact: makerspaces attract teens who are otherwise hard to reach and build technical identity and self-efficacy. The YOUmedia model demonstrated that interest-driven making can re-engage disengaged youth and has been replicated nationwide.
      • National networks -- the Fab Foundation, Maker Corps, and Nation of Makers -- connect library makerspaces to a broader ecosystem by sharing curricula, training, standards, and advocacy. Joining as a registered Fab Lab gives libraries access to a global peer community and shared capability standards.

      Library Website Design & User Experience Deep Dive

      A structured overview of how U.S. libraries design their websites and deliver a usable, accessible digital experience. It covers accessibility under WCAG 2.1 AA and Section 508, discovery-layer UX in Primo and EBSCO Discovery Service, mobile-first responsive design and library apps, content strategy and plain language, user testing methods, and the platform ecosystem of WordPress, Drupal, and Springshare tools. The goal is to give researchers, librarians, and web teams a single reference for the

      Overview

      Library website design encompasses the architecture, visual layout, content organization, and interactive features of a library's digital presence, including the public-facing site, catalog, discovery layer, and integrated service tools. A well-designed library website is the primary digital front door for patrons, extending access to collections, services, and programs beyond physical branches and reaching users who may never visit in person. Library websites have evolved from static HTML pages listing hours and policies into dynamic, responsive portals that integrate the catalog, event

      Accessibility & WCAG

      Accessibility ensures that library websites are usable by people with disabilities, including visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive impairments, and is both an ethical imperative and a legal requirement for many institutions. WCAG 2.1 AA, the web accessibility standard referenced by most U.S. policies, is organized around four principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and requires text alternatives, keyboard navigation, captions, and sufficient color contrast. Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act, refreshed in 2017, requires federal agencies and federally funded programs to

      Discovery Layer UX

      A discovery layer is the modern search interface that sits atop a library's catalog and databases, aiming to provide a Google-like single-search experience across disparate resources. Primo, from Ex Libris (now part of Clarivate), is a widely adopted discovery layer in academic libraries offering faceted search, bento-style results, and integration with the Alma management system. EBSCO Discovery Service (EDS) provides a unified index of a library's holdings and databases, with relevancy ranking, limiters, and customizable widgets tuned for student research workflows.

      Mobile First

      Mobile-first design prioritizes the smartphone experience, recognizing that a growing share of patrons access library resources on phones and tablets rather than desktop computers. Responsive web design uses flexible grids and media queries so a single codebase adapts layout and navigation to any screen size, the standard approach recommended by library web guidelines. Many public libraries offer branded mobile apps (via vendors such as Communico, Boopsie, and BiblioCommons) for catalog search, account management, event registration, and digital collection access.

      Content Strategy

      Content strategy governs what a library website says, how it says it, and who maintains it, ensuring that information stays accurate, findable, and aligned with patron needs. Plain language writing, using short sentences, common words, and clear structure, helps patrons quickly understand library services and aligns with the federal Plain Writing Act of 2010 for government-funded institutions. Effective visual design uses consistent typography, generous white space, and accessible color palettes to create a welcoming digital environment that reflects the library's brand and reduces cognit

      User Testing

      User testing involves observing real patrons as they attempt tasks on a library website, uncovering pain points that internal staff may not anticipate. Common methods include moderated task-based testing, first-click tests, and remote unmoderated studies using tools like UserTesting or Loop11 to measure success rates and task completion times. Libraries develop personas, archetypal users such as the busy parent, the distance student, or the genealogy hobbyist, to guide design decisions and keep real user needs at the center of prioritization.

      Platform Ecosystem

      Library websites are assembled from a mix of content management systems, discovery tools, and third-party SaaS platforms, creating an ecosystem that must be integrated and consistently branded. WordPress and Drupal are the most common open-source CMS choices for library websites, with Drupal favored by large systems needing granular permissions and WordPress chosen for ease of use and a vast plugin ecosystem. Springshare's suite, LibGuides for research guides, LibCal for booking and events, and LibAnswers for FAQs and chat, is near-ubiquitous in academic libraries, though it requires care

      Key Findings

      • Accessibility is both a legal requirement and a service equity issue; WCAG 2.1 AA is the de facto benchmark for U.S. library websites.
      • Discovery layers like Primo and EDS have reshaped the search experience but introduce vendor lock-in and integration challenges.
      • Mobile-first, responsive design is now essential as the majority of patron web sessions occur on phones and tablets.
      • Plain language content strategy measurably improves task completion and reduces patron support requests.
      • User testing with real patrons consistently surfaces problems that are invisible to library staff and internal reviewers.
      • The Springshare ecosystem is near-ubiquitous in academic libraries, creating both convenience and branding fragmentation risks.
      • Open-source CMS platforms like WordPress and Drupal give libraries control but demand ongoing technical investment and maintenance.
      • Library mobile apps improve engagement but can duplicate effort already spent on responsive websites.
      • Personas and journey mapping help libraries prioritize features that serve real user needs rather than internal org charts.
      • Federally funded libraries must align with Section 508, which since 2017 formally references WCAG 2.0 AA as its technical standard.

      Library Privacy & Surveillance Deep Dive

      An analysis of surveillance technologies, data collection practices, and privacy advocacy in American libraries, covering law enforcement access to patron records, vendor data sharing, the Library Freedom Project's deployment of Tor and encryption tools, and the policy and legal frameworks that protect reader privacy.

      Overview

      Library surveillance refers to the monitoring, collection, and retention of patron reading habits, browsing history, computer use, and circulation records by libraries, vendors, or government agencies. Privacy is foundational to intellectual freedom; patrons must be able to explore controversial or sensitive topics without fear of monitoring, judgment, or reprisal. Libraries balance patron privacy against security needs, funding-mandated data reporting, law enforcement cooperation requirements, and the convenience of digital services that inherently generate data trails.

      Data Collection

      Modern libraries collect extensive data through integrated library systems, digital lending platforms, public computer use logs, and website analytics, much of which persists long after a patron's visit. Circulation and holds records reveal intimate details about a patron's intellectual interests and personal circumstances, making their protection a core ethical obligation under ALA policy. Public access computers and library WiFi networks can log URLs visited, search queries, and session data, creating detailed portraits of patron inquiry if not routinely cleared.

      Law Enforcement Requests

      Law enforcement and intelligence agencies have sought library records to investigate patrons, prompting sustained resistance from librarians and privacy advocates. Section 215 of the USA PATRIOT Act allowed the FBI to obtain 'any tangible thing,' including library and bookstore records, with a FISA court order; the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 narrowed this authority. National Security Letters permitted FBI demands for library records (when libraries functioned as internet service providers) accompanied by indefinite gag orders, famously challenged in Library Connection Inc. v. United Sta

      Library Freedom Project

      Founded by librarian Alison Macrina around 2014, the Library Freedom Project trains librarians in digital privacy tools and advocates for deploying privacy-protective technologies in public libraries. The Project encouraged libraries to host Tor relays and exit nodes, providing anonymous browsing infrastructure; the Kilton Library in Lebanon, NH became the first library exit node in 2015 before facing Department of Homeland Security pressure. Project workshops teach librarians and patrons to use encrypted email, secure messaging, VPNs, disk encryption, and password managers, positioning librar

      Vendor Privacy

      Libraries increasingly rely on third-party vendors for digital lending, discovery layers, and analytics, outsourcing data handling to companies whose privacy practices may not meet library ethical standards. OverDrive and its Libby app collect patron data including reading habits, device information, and location; while governed by contractual data agreements, questions persist about retention, profiling, and law enforcement access. Library websites and catalogs often embed third-party analytics, advertising, and social media trackers that follow patrons across the web, contradicting libraries

      Privacy Policies

      The American Library Association establishes privacy as a core professional value, reinforced by policy interpretations, state laws, and professional ethics codes. The ALA Library Bill of Rights and its interpretations affirm that a person's library use is confidential, and the ALA Code of Ethics obligates librarians to protect patron privacy. Most U.S. states have enacted statutes specifically protecting library circulation records from disclosure, though scope and exceptions vary; some extend protection to digital records while others remain untested.

      Key Findings

      • Library circulation records are legally protected in nearly every U.S. state, but digital lending platforms may transmit patron data outside those protections.
      • Section 215 of the USA PATRIOT Act expanded FBI access to library records, a power the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 partially narrowed.
      • The Library Connection case demonstrated that libraries can successfully challenge National Security Letters and their gag orders in court.
      • The Library Freedom Project reframed libraries as frontline defenders of digital privacy, distributing Tor and encryption tools through trusted community institutions.
      • Tor exit nodes in libraries faced law enforcement resistance, notably when DHS pressured the Kilton Library, but public support often reversed shutdown decisions.
      • Vendor platforms like OverDrive and Libby centralize patron data, raising questions about retention, profiling, and law enforcement access outside library control.
      • Third-party trackers embedded on library websites and catalogs can contradict libraries' privacy commitments unless actively blocked.
      • Public computer and WiFi use generates browsing logs that, if not routinely cleared, create detailed records of patron inquiry.
      • The ALA Code of Ethics obligates librarians to protect patron privacy, but operational reliance on data-generating services complicates compliance.
      • State library privacy laws vary widely in scope, with many untested against modern digital and vendor-mediated data flows.

      Library Security & Safety Deep Dive

      A deep dive into security and safety practices in U.S. public libraries, covering ALA guidelines, staff training, physical security, behavioral response, law enforcement relations, and active shooter preparedness.

      Overview

      Library security and safety refers to the policies, training, and physical measures that protect patrons, staff, collections, and facilities while preserving open access and intellectual freedom. Libraries are among the last free public spaces, attracting diverse populations including vulnerable individuals, which makes balancing safety with equitable access essential. Key challenges include rising behavioral incidents, opioid overdoses, homelessness, privacy concerns, and the need to maintain welcoming environments without over-policing.

      ALA Guidelines

      The ALA provides guidance through interpretations of the Library Bill of Rights, emphasizing that security policies must be viewpoint-neutral and not restrict access based on status or beliefs. The ALA's 'Proper Use of the Library' interpretation holds that behavior policies should address conduct, not status, so that rules apply equally regardless of homelessness or appearance. ALA recommends clearly written, publicly posted behavior policies that define acceptable conduct, outline consequences, and include appeal procedures to ensure due process.

      Staff Training

      Staff training is central to library safety, equipping employees to prevent, recognize, and respond to escalating situations consistently. CPI (Crisis Prevention Institute) verbal de-escalation training teaches staff to read behavior levels, use supportive language, and reduce tension before situations become physical. Crisis prevention training covers recognizing warning signs, safe disengagement, personal safety techniques, and post-incident debriefing to support staff wellbeing.

      Physical Security

      Physical security measures protect library assets and people while remaining unobtrusive enough to preserve a welcoming atmosphere. Many libraries use CCTV cameras in public areas and parking lots, balancing deterrence with patron privacy by avoiding monitoring of reading areas or computer screens. Access control includes secured staff areas, after-hours alarm systems, keycard entry, and controlled entry points during high-risk periods.

      Behavioral Issues

      Behavioral issues range from noise and loitering to substance use and mental health crises, often requiring social rather than punitive responses. An increasing number of libraries respond to homelessness by hiring social workers and peer navigators who connect patrons with housing, benefits, and health services rather than relying on removal. In response to opioid overdoses on library grounds, many libraries train staff in naloxone administration and partner with public health agencies to distribute harm-reduction resources.

      Law Enforcement

      Libraries work with law enforcement for serious incidents but maintain careful boundaries to protect patron privacy and trust. Some libraries partner with police through community-oriented officers or mental health co-response teams that handle crises with minimal escalation. ALA policy and state confidentiality laws generally require a court order before releasing patron records, creating tension when police seek borrowing or computer-use data without warrants.

      Active Shooter Preparedness

      Active shooter preparedness has become a priority for libraries following incidents at public institutions across the country. Preparedness includes lockdown drills, evacuation mapping, staff tabletop exercises, and coordination with local emergency responders. The DHS Run, Hide, Fight protocol advises escaping if possible, hiding and barricading if escape is unsafe, and fighting only as a last resort.

      Key Findings

      • Modern library security increasingly relies on social workers and peer navigators rather than security guards alone, addressing root causes of disruptive behavior.
      • The ALA requires behavior policies to be viewpoint-neutral and based on conduct, not a patron's status such as homelessness.

      • A growing number of libraries equip and train staff to administer naloxone in response to opioid overdoses on site.
      • CCTV and access control systems are common, but libraries limit surveillance to protect patron privacy.
      • State confidentiality laws and ALA policy generally require a court order before patron records are released to law enforcement.
      • Active shooter preparedness typically follows the Run, Hide, Fight model with regular drills and responder coordination.
      • Urban libraries report rising incidents tied to mental health and substance use, straining front-line staff.
      • Co-response models pairing police with mental health professionals reduce escalation during behavioral crises.
      • Balancing safety with open access remains the central tension, as over-policing can deter the vulnerable populations libraries are meant to serve.

      Library Workforce & Staff Demographics Deep Dive

      An evidence-based profile of the U.S. library workforce, covering employment scale, staff demographics, educational credentials, regional salary patterns, union representation, and the diversity initiatives working to broaden the profession.

      Workforce Overview

      The library workforce comprises credentialed librarians (typically MLS/MLIS holders), library technicians, and library assistants across public, academic, school, and special library settings. BLS counts roughly 145,000 librarians and library media specialists, plus an additional 200,000-plus library technicians and assistants, for a total workforce approaching 350,000. Overall librarian employment is projected to grow slowly over the next decade, with flat or modestly declining demand in some traditional roles offset by growth in digital collections, data services, and school media specialist

      Demographics

      Library staff demographics have long been studied by ALA and IMLS, revealing a workforce that is highly gender-skewed and less racially diverse than the general U.S. population, prompting decades of targeted recruitment programs. The profession is approximately 83% female, placing librarianship among the most female-dominated professional occupations in the United States. Men remain a small minority in both public and academic library settings. Roughly 86% of credentialed librarians identify as white, well above the white share of the overall national population. Black, Latino/Hispanic, Asian,

      Education & Credentials

      Professional librarian roles almost always require graduate-level credentials, distinguishing librarians from the technician and assistant roles that typically need less formal education. Most professional librarian positions require a Master of Library Science (MLS) or Master of Library and Information Studies (MLIS) from a program accredited by the American Library Association. School library media specialists additionally face state-level teaching certification or licensure requirements. The ALA Office for Accreditation lists 65 accredited master's programs in library and information s

      Salaries

      Librarian compensation is modest relative to other professions requiring a master's degree, with meaningful variation by region, sector, and union status. BLS reports an average mean wage of about $65,149 and an average median wage of about $64,254 for librarians and media collections specialists, with roughly 133,200 employed in the measured occupation code. Wages are highest on the coasts and in the capital region: the District of Columbia ($94,300), Washington, California, Maryland, and New York lead mean wages, while Southern and Midwestern states such as Alabama, Ohio, and Michigan f

      Unions

      A substantial share of library workers, especially in public library systems, are covered by collective bargaining agreements, which are associated with higher pay and stronger benefits. The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) is the largest union representing public library workers, organizing librarians, clerks, and support staff across many municipal and county systems through its state councils and locals. The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) represents library workers in a number of cities and counties, often as part of broader public-sector b

      Diversity Initiatives

      ALA, IMLS, and individual institutions run scholarships, residencies, and leadership pipelines to recruit and retain librarians of color and other underrepresented groups. Launched in 1997, the ALA Spectrum Scholarship Program provides scholarships and a leadership institute to students of color in ALA-accredited MLS/MLIS programs and has supported more than 1,300 scholars since its founding. Post-MLS diversity residencies at research universities (such as Yale, North Carolina State, Cornell, and the University of Michigan) give early-career librarians from underrepresented backgrounds structu

      Key Findings

      • The library profession is approximately 83% female, making it one of the most gender-skewed professional fields in the United States.
      • Racial diversity remains a persistent challenge, with roughly 86% of credentialed librarians identifying as white despite decades of targeted recruitment efforts.
      • BLS data identify roughly 145,000 librarians and library media specialists employed nationally, supplemented by an additional 200,000-plus library technicians and assistants.
      • A Master's degree from an ALA-accredited program is required for most professional librarian positions; there are 65 such programs, 56 of them in the United States.
      • The median annual wage for librarians is about $64,254, with mean wages ranging from about $49,200 in the lowest-paying states to about $94,300 in the District of Columbia.
      • Regional salary disparities are pronounced: Northeast and West Coast states (District of Columbia, Washington, California, Maryland, New York) pay the highest, while Southern and Midwestern states pay the least.
      • The library workforce is aging, with a large cohort of senior librarians nearing retirement age and too few younger professionals entering to replace them.
      • A significant share of public library workers are unionized, primarily through AFSCME and SEIU, which correlates with better wages, benefits, and job protections.
      • Right-to-work laws in roughly 27 states suppress union density and are associated with lower library worker wages and weaker collective bargaining power.
      • The ALA Spectrum Scholarship Program, established in 1997, has awarded more than 1,300 scholarships to library school students of color, and university residency programs help diversify early-career librarianship.

      Libraries & Civic Data Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how U.S. libraries serve as civic-data and open-government infrastructure. It covers the 2020 Census and Complete Count Committees, voter registration drives and National Voter Registration Day, libraries as polling places, open data access and Data.gov, the Federal Depository Library Program and government-information collections, civic technology partnerships with Code for America brigades and hackathons at libraries, notable programs, and key findings.

      Civic Overview

      Civic data is the body of information generated by and about government -- demographic counts, election records, legislation, budgets, and public-service metrics -- that citizens need to understand, scrutinize, and participate in their government. Open government is the principle and practice of publishing such data in machine-readable forms so the public can freely access and reuse it. Access to civic data underpins accountable governance: it lets residents verify how tax dollars are spent, track election outcomes and representation, apply for benefits, and hold officials to their records. Wh

      Census Partnership

      The U.S. Census Bureau relies on a national network of trusted local partners to encourage participation in the decennial census, because an accurate count determines congressional apportionment and the annual distribution of hundreds of billions of federal dollars. Libraries are core partners in this effort. The 2020 census was the first U.S. census to offer a full internet response option and was conducted amid the COVID-19 pandemic with Census Day on April 1, 2020. Because millions of households lacked home broadband, library computers and WiFi -- much of it supported by the federal E-Rate

      Voter Registration

      Libraries are legally recognized voter-registration sites. The National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (the Motor Voter Act) requires states to offer voter registration at designated public agencies, including public libraries, so residents can register while visiting a familiar, nonpartisan institution. Libraries also support online registration by providing the public computers and internet that unconnected patrons need. National Voter Registration Day, first held on September 25, 2012, is a nonpartisan civic holiday observed on a Tuesday in September. It was launched by roughly 2,000 civic

      Open Data Access

      Open data is information published in machine-readable formats for free public reuse, and it is the foundation of civic technology. Libraries both consume open government data for reference and programs and increasingly publish their own operational data -- circulation, visits, and program attendance -- as open datasets. Data.gov is the U.S. government open-data portal, launched in late May 2009 by federal Chief Information Officer Vivek Kundra to improve public access to high-value, machine-readable datasets from the executive branch and from state, local, and tribal governments. Libraries ar

      Government Information

      Government information is the published output of federal, state, and local agencies -- statutes, regulations, congressional records, statistical reports, and agency publications. Libraries have distributed government information to the public at no cost for more than two centuries through the Federal Depository Library Program. The Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP), rooted in an 1813 Congressional Joint Resolution and codified in its modern form by the Depository Library Act of 1962, makes U.S. federal publications available to the public at no cost through designated depository libra

      Civic Tech

      Civic technology uses software, data, and design to improve the relationship between people and government, including service delivery, decision-making, and political participation. Libraries participate as civic-tech access points and community partners, providing the connectivity and meeting space that civic-tech projects rely on. Code for America is a 501(c)(3) civic-tech nonprofit founded in 2009 by Jennifer Pahlka to promote civic hacking and bring modern technology to government. Its volunteer brigades build open-source tools for local governments, and the organization partners with agen

      Key Findings

      • The 2020 census made libraries indispensable to the decennial count, because it was the first census to allow online self-response and libraries provided the computers, WiFi, and staff that unconnected households needed to be counted.
      • Libraries are legally designated voter-registration sites under the National Voter Registration Act of 1993, which requires states to offer registration at public libraries alongside motor-vehicle offices and other public agencies.
      • National Voter Registration Day, first held September 25, 2012, and endorsed by the National Association of Secretaries of State and the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, has become a signature annual library civic-engagement event.
      • Libraries are among the most common public buildings used as polling places and ballot drop-off locations, prized for ADA accessibility, central locations, public ownership, and nonpartisan trust.
      • Data.gov, launched in May 2009, is the federal open-data portal, and the IMLS Public Libraries Survey is published there as open datasets, making nationwide library data freely reusable by the public.
      • Many cities publish library usage, circulation, and computer-session data on local open-data portals, modeling how libraries both consume and contribute to open government.
      • The Federal Depository Library Program, rooted in an 1813 resolution and modernized by the 1962 Depository Library Act, distributes federal publications at no cost through roughly 1,082 depository libraries, including 167 public libraries.
      • GPO's GovInfo provides online access to more than 2,200 databases of federal publications, extending depository access beyond physical collections to any resident with internet.
      • Code for America, founded in 2009 by Jennifer Pahlka, operates volunteer brigades that partner with local governments to build civic-tech tools, and libraries serve as the meeting venues that connect technologists with residents.
      • Libraries bridge the digital divide that would otherwise lock millions of Americans out of online civic participation, providing the computers, broadband, and digital navigation that make census, voter, and open-government services reachable.

      Library Philanthropy & Foundations Deep Dive

      A focused overview of the national and institutional philanthropic forces behind American libraries: the nationwide Friends of the Library movement and its ALA division United for Libraries, the major philanthropic foundations and federal funders that have shaped library development (Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Carnegie Corporation of New York, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services), and the fundraising vehicles of capital campaigns, planned giving, endowments, and corporate

      Philanthropy Overview

      Library philanthropy is the giving of private wealth, corporate resources, and planned gifts to build, sustain, and expand library services, distinct from the public tax revenues that fund day-to-day operations. It spans individual major gifts and bequests, family and corporate foundations, federally administered grant programs, Friends-group grassroots fundraising, and Library Foundation capital and endowment campaigns at systems of every size. Recent decades show a shift from brick-and-mortar building philanthropy toward technology access, digital inclusion, early literacy, and equity-focuse

      United for Libraries

      United for Libraries is the American Library Association (ALA) division that serves as the national umbrella for library trustees, advocates, Friends of the Library groups, and library foundations across the United States. It was formed in 2009 by the merger of Friends of Libraries U.S.A. (FOLUSA) and the American Library Trustees Association (ALTA); originally named the Association of Library Trustees, Advocates, Friends and Foundations (ALTAFF), it was renamed United for Libraries in 2012. It provides trustee and Friends training, advocacy toolkits, an annual conference track, awards and lit

      Major Foundations

      A small number of large foundations and federal funders have disproportionately shaped American library development, complementing thousands of local library foundations with transformational, system-wide investments. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation's U.S. Library Program, launched in 1997, invested roughly $250 million to install computers, internet access, and training in public libraries across all 50 states, later expanding into the Global Libraries initiative, which the foundation announced it would wind down in 2018.       Capital Campaigns

      Capital campaigns are multi-year, goal-driven fundraising efforts, typically run by Library Foundations, to finance new central libraries, branch renovations, and major capital improvements that exceed ordinary public budgets. Notable 21st-century campaigns funded landmark buildings such as the Seattle Central Library (2004) and the Salt Lake City Main Library (2003), often pairing a public bond with tens of millions in private contributions for furnishings, technology, and programming. Campaigns offer naming rights for buildings, reading rooms, children's areas, and collections as incent

      Planned Giving

      Planned giving channels future gifts through estate plans, allowing donors to support libraries at a scale far beyond annual giving while realizing tax and income benefits. Bequests -- gifts made through a will or living trust -- are frequently the largest single contributions a library foundation ever receives, sometimes funding entire branches, collections, or scholarship endowments. Endowments are restricted funds whose principal is preserved in perpetuity while investment income supports designated purposes, providing libraries a stable revenue stream that insulates programs from fluctuati

      Corporate Giving

      Corporate giving to libraries takes the form of cash grants, in-kind technology donations, employee volunteer programs, and cause-marketing sponsorships tied to literacy and community engagement. Target Corporation, through its long-running 'Ready. Sit. Read!' early-literacy initiative and historic pledge to give 5% of its profits to communities, donated books, funded library reading programs, and sponsored library makeovers across the country.       Library Bookmobiles & Mobile Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of bookmobiles, mobile outreach services, pop-up libraries, and mobile hotspot lending programs across U.S. public libraries.

      Mobile Overview

      A bookmobile or mobile library is a vehicle designed for use as a library that expands the reach of traditional libraries by transporting books and services to readers in underserved locations. U.S. mobile library service now also includes pop-up libraries, book bikes, mobile Wi-Fi hotspot lending, and outreach vans equipped with computers and connectivity. The American bookmobile tradition dates to the 1839 American School Library and the 1905 book wagon of librarian Mary Lemist Titcomb in Washington County, Maryland, who distributed 1,008 volumes in the wagon's first six months. Motoriz

      Bookmobile Fleet

      Bookmobiles remain a core outreach tool for public libraries, especially in rural states where a single vehicle can replace the cost of building and staffing a new branch. They are tracked as a distinct field in the IMLS Public Libraries Survey. The IMLS Public Libraries Survey FY2024 state-level aggregation reports approximately 767 bookmobiles across 49 states and territories, down from the historically cited figure of roughly 900-1,000 in earlier survey years. Kentucky leads with 74 bookmobiles, followed by Ohio (68), California (65), South Carolina (35), and Washington (33). Bookmobiles se

      Pop-Up Libraries

      Pop-up libraries are temporary, lightweight library setups that appear at parks, transit hubs, farmers' markets, festivals, and other public spaces to reach people where they already gather. They lower the barrier to library use by offering instant card sign-ups, giveaways, and quick programming without a permanent facility. Seattle Public Library's Books on Bikes (2013) and Volusia County's Library Cruiser (2015) put library services on custom bicycle trailers, while the Free Black Women's Library in Brooklyn (2015) pops up with books by Black women. Miami's Booklegge

      Mobile Hotspots

      Mobile hotspot lending lets patrons check out cellular Wi-Fi hotspots for home use, directly addressing the digital divide for households without affordable internet. ALA characterizes the service as a mature, decade-old offering as of 2023. Early and large adopters include the New York Public Library and Chicago Public Library, with many urban and suburban systems following suit. Patrons typically borrow a hotspot and charger for one to several weeks, often paired with digital-literacy support. Hotspot lending helps students complete homework, job seekers apply for work, and families access t

      Rural Mobile Services

      In rural and low-density areas, mobile services are often the most cost-effective way to deliver library access, since a fixed branch may not be sustainable for a small, spread-out population. Bookmobiles and outreach vans therefore play an outsized role in rural library service. Rural mobile services face high fuel and maintenance costs, long driving distances, limited staffing, and aging vehicle fleets that are expensive to replace. The national decline in bookmobile counts from roughly 900-1,000 to about 767 reflects these persistent budget pressures. State library agencies and federal Libr

      Key Findings

      • The IMLS Public Libraries Survey FY2024 reports approximately 767 bookmobiles across 49 states and territories, a decline from the historically cited range of roughly 900-1,000 in earlier survey years. Kentucky (74), Ohio (68), and California (65) report the most bookmobiles.
      • The American bookmobile tradition began in 1905 when librarian Mary Lemist Titcomb launched the first U.S. book wagon in Washington County, Maryland, distributing 1,008 volumes in its first six months. The WPA Pack Horse Library Project later carried books on horseback through Appalachian Kentucky from 1935 to 1943.
      • In 2021 the ALA, the Association of Bookmobile and Outreach Services (ABOS), and the Association for Rural and Small Libraries (ARSL) rebranded National Bookmobile Day as National Library Outreach Day to recognize the full range of outreach work beyond bookmobiles.
      • Libraries are diversifying mobile service beyond traditional vans, adding book bikes (Seattle, Volusia County), bicycle-powered carts for people experiencing homelessness (Street Books in Portland), and pop-up library stands at community events.
      • Bookmobiles are a cost-effective alternative to building new branches in low-density rural areas, where the population cannot sustain a fixed facility but still needs regular library access. States with large rural populations like Kentucky and Ohio maintain the largest fleets.
      • Mobile hotspot lending grew rapidly from about 2013 to 2023, with early adopters including the New York Public Library and Chicago Public Library, to address the digital divide for patrons without home internet.
      • The FCC's 2023 Learn Without Limits initiative and 2024 rule allowed E-rate funds to support off-premises Wi-Fi hotspot lending, but the FCC voted in October 2025 to end that support, prompting ALA-led opposition.
      • During the COVID-19 pandemic many libraries extended Wi-Fi to parking lots and expanded hotspot lending so students and patrons could access the internet even when buildings were closed.
      • Mobile services reach populations that fixed branches cannot, including homebound seniors, residents of care facilities, immigrant communities, people experiencing homelessness, and children in daycare and rural schools.
      • Some bookmobile manufacturers now offer solar/battery, hybrid, and all-electric chassis to reduce the carbon footprint of mobile outreach, while 'm-libraries' deliver content electronically to mobile devices as a digital complement to physical vehicles.

      Library Entrepreneurship & Small Business Support Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how U.S. public libraries support entrepreneurs, small businesses, inventors, and startups through resource centers, coworking, maker labs, and partnerships.

      Entrepreneurship Overview

      Library entrepreneurship support refers to the programs, spaces, databases, and partnerships through which public libraries help individuals start, sustain, and grow businesses and inventions. Libraries function as low-barrier business incubators, offering free market research tools, meeting rooms, makerspaces, patent search assistance, and referrals to expert mentors. ALA and IMLS reporting show entrepreneurship programming expanding rapidly since the 2010s, driven by post-recession startup growth and the gig economy, with maker labs and business centers now common in mid- and large-sized sys

      Business Resource Centers

      Business resource centers are dedicated library units that curate business databases, market research tools, and reference staff trained to serve entrepreneurs and job seekers. Typical services include access to ReferenceUSA/Gale Business, industry and demographic data, business plan templates, one-on-one research consultations, and notary or printing support for filings. Centers frequently co-locate with SCORE mentors, Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), and local chambers of commerce to deliver workshops and confidential business advising on site.

      Patent & Trademark Resource Centers

      The Patent and Trademark Resource Center (PTRC) program, administered by the USPTO and tracing its roots to 1871, designates libraries to provide patent and trademark information services to the public. There are roughly 80-plus designated PTRCs spread across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico, including the Library of Congress, New York Public Library, and Los Angeles Public Library. PTRC staff are trained by USPTO to help inventors search prior art, navigate PatFT, AppFT, and TESS databases, and understand the application process, often through free inventor workshops.

      Coworking Spaces

      Many public libraries now function as informal coworking spaces, supplying free Wi-Fi, power, study rooms, and quiet workspace that freelancers and early-stage founders use in lieu of paid offices. Systems such as Chicago Public Library and Hartford Public Library have formalized coworking with reservable studios, while others repurpose meeting rooms for drop-in coworking hours. ALA surveys consistently show that meeting-room use by community and business groups is among the fastest-growing library services, with many systems offering free or low-cost reservations online.

      SCORE Partnerships

      SCORE, the SBA's volunteer mentoring partner founded in 1964, operates more than 250 chapters with roughly 10,000 volunteers who deliver free mentoring to hundreds of thousands of clients yearly. SCORE chapters commonly station mentors at public libraries for free, confidential one-on-one business counseling, often on weekly or monthly walk-in schedules. Libraries host SCORE-led workshops on business planning, marketing, financing, and ecommerce, pairing SCORE's curriculum with the library's research tools and space.

      • Libraries increasingly act as free coworking spaces, supplying Wi-Fi, meeting rooms, and reservable studios that reduce overhead for early-stage founders and freelancers.
      • Maker labs such as Chicago Public Library's 2013 Maker Lab give entrepreneurs access to 3D printers, laser cutters, and CNC tools for low-cost product prototyping.
      • Dedicated business resource centers at Brooklyn Public Library and the Free Library of Philadelphia's BRIC bundle market research databases with advising to serve entrepreneurs directly.
      • ALA and IMLS reporting show business and entrepreneurship programming among the fastest-growing service categories at mid-sized and large public library systems since the 2010s.
      • Public libraries often co-locate with Small Business Development Centers and chambers of commerce, creating a single free access point for research, advising, and workshops.
      • Meeting-room use by business and community groups is one of the most rapidly expanding library services, reflecting demand for affordable gathering and presentation space.
      • Rural and small libraries join the PTRC and SCORE networks through regional partners, extending patent mentoring and business advising beyond major metro areas.
      • The library-as-incubator model reframes the institution as economic infrastructure, particularly for under-resourced founders who lack paid coworking or professional advising budgets.

      Library Closures & Defunding Crisis Deep Dive

      A deep summary of library closures, defunding battles, budget cuts, and community responses across the United States.

      Closures Overview

      A library closure is the permanent shuttering of a branch or system building, while defunding refers to significant reductions in operating appropriations that force service cuts without necessarily closing doors. Both are symptoms of the locally dominated, tax-base-dependent US funding model. Across the roughly 16,800 public library buildings tracked by IMLS, closures and severe cuts have hit urban systems (New York, Detroit, Boston, Los Angeles), small-city and rural systems (Salinas, Oak Hill), and state library agencies alike, with the worst episodes clustering around recessions and munici

      Major Closures

      A handful of widely publicized closure crises have come to define the public understanding of library defunding. They share a pattern: a municipal or state budget shortfall targets libraries as discretionary, the threat mobilizes community and national advocacy, and outcomes range from full reversal to permanent branch loss. In late 2004, Salinas, California -- birthplace of John Steinbeck -- announced it would close all three of its public libraries by mid-2005 because of a roughly $3 million structural deficit, which would have made it the largest US city with no public library. A national &

      Budget Cuts

      Budget cuts are the most common form of library defunding, taking the shape of reduced municipal appropriations, slashed state aid, or threatened elimination of federal grant agencies. Cuts rarely close a whole system but erode hours, materials, staff, and programming over time. State library aid has repeatedly been cut during downturns: Oregon's State Library faced major budget reductions and restructuring proposals that threatened services, and Connecticut sustained years of cuts to its state library and aid programs. In 2025, the federal IMLS itself was targeted by an executive order (

      Hours Reductions

      Reduced hours are the most frequent and visible consequence of library defunding, often the first response before any branch closes. Libraries cut evening, weekend, and summer hours to save staffing costs, disproportionately affecting working patrons and students. Hours reductions curtail access to homework help, job searching, computer use, and English-language programming, and they fell hardest on the FY2019-to-FY2020 COVID period when visits dropped 41.6% nationwide. Even as income held steady, many systems kept reduced schedules for years after reopening. By FY2024, IMLS data showed visits

      Community Responses

      Communities respond to closure and defunding threats through ballot measures, advocacy campaigns, lawsuits, and direct fundraising. These responses have repeatedly reversed cuts, reflecting broad public support for libraries. From 2013 through 2026, EveryLibrary tracked 176 library funding ballot measures (bonds, levies, millages) totaling over $757 million requested, with 123 passing -- a 69.9% pass rate. Voter-approved dedicated property taxes have become a primary shield against annual general-fund cuts. National groups including the ALA, EveryLibrary, and the EveryLibrary Institute run bal

      Recovery Efforts

      Recovery from closures and cuts depends on restoring appropriations, passing dedicated levies, and rebuilding patron demand. Systems that win voter-approved dedicated funding recover faster and more durably than those reliant on annual general-fund appropriations. Federal relief has repeatedly stabilized libraries in crisis: New Deal WPA labor in the 1930s, ARRA broadband support in 2009, and roughly $228 million in IMLS CARES/ARP pandemic aid in 2020-2021 plus the $10 billion Emergency Connectivity Fund for devices and connectivity. Usage recovery lags budget recovery: by FY2024 income had gr
