      Key Findings

      • The Library of Congress NLS network of 101 cooperating libraries (55 regional, 32 subregional, 14 advisory/outreach centers) served 219,589 active readers and circulated more than 22.2 million braille, audio, and large-print items in FY2024, yet remains substantially under-enrolled relative to the eligible population.
      • BARD, NLS's web download service launched online in 2010 with BARD Mobile following in 2013, lets eligible patrons download thousands of audio and electronic-braille titles free, and in FY2024 NLS circulated 447,288 ebraille items alongside 155,519 hard-copy braille items.
      • NLS completed the nationwide rollout of approximately 8,500 refreshable braille eReader devices in FY2024, loaned free to eligible patrons -- a major braille-access expansion, though commercial refreshable displays remain expensive and the deployed units cover only a fraction of eligible readers.
      • Per the WebAIM Screen Reader Survey #9 (2023), NVDA (NonVisual Desktop Access), a free open-source Windows reader from NV Access, is the most-used screen reader, overtaking the long-dominant commercial JAWS (Vispero) that remains widely installed on library accessible workstations.
      • Built-in, no-cost screen readers -- Apple VoiceOver, Google TalkBack, and Microsoft Narrator -- make screen-reader access possible even at low-budget libraries, though staff and patrons are often unaware these tools exist.
      • Induction hearing loops transmit audio directly to telecoil-equipped hearing aids and cochlear implants, and the HLAA-led 'loop America' movement has driven loop installations in renovated library auditoriums and service counters; the 2010 ADA Standards mandate assistive listening systems in assembly areas with 50+ seats or amplification.
      • Approximately 15% of U.S. adults (about 25 million people) report some degree of hearing trouble (NIDCD), making captioning, CART, ASL interpretation, and assistive listening core rather than niche library services; NLS also supplies a high-volume talking-book player amplified to 120 dB for hard-of-hearing readers.
      • Under ADA Title II, public libraries must provide effective communication through auxiliary aids and services, and the DOJ's April 2024 final rule requires state and local government web and mobile app content (including library sites and catalogs) to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA.
      • Commercial assistive technology such as JAWS, ZoomText, and Kurzweil carries per-seat licensing costs that strain small-library budgets, and IT staff at small and rural libraries often lack the expertise to deploy and maintain AT software, making LSTA and IMLS grant funding a critical equalizer.
      • Library makerspaces are a growing source of community-produced assistive technology, fabricating 3D-printed tactile graphics, braille signage, and switch-adapted devices, often in partnership with the National Federation of the Blind and university tactile-book initiatives such as the University of Colorado Boulder Tactile Picture Books Project.

      Library Translation Services & Language Access Deep Dive

      A deep summary of translation services, interpreter access, multilingual signage, indigenous language preservation, and translation technology at U.S. public libraries.

      Translation Overview

      Library translation and language access is the set of services, collections, signage, and technologies by which public libraries serve patrons with limited English proficiency (LEP), including translated materials, in-person and telephonic interpretation, multilingual wayfinding, world-language collections, and language-learning resources. The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey finds that roughly 68 million Americans aged 5 and over speak a language other than English at home (about 21.6% of that age group), and that more than 25 million report speaking English less than '

      Interpreter Services

      Interpreter access lets a patron who does not speak English fluently communicate with library staff in real time for help with a library card, a program registration, a benefits referral, or a computer session, and is delivered through telephonic/on-demand interpreting, in-person interpreters, and bilingual staff. Many public libraries contract with on-demand telephonic interpretation vendors such as Language Line Solutions, which connects staff to a live interpreter in 240 or more languages within seconds via a dedicated phone line or app, giving even small branches instant access to rarely s

      Multilingual Signage

      Multilingual signage and wayfinding make a library usable on first entry for patrons who do not read English, covering directional signs, department labels, restroom and computer-lab markers, and program notices, and is a low-cost, high-impact form of language access that requires no staff time per encounter. Systems serving large Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, Arabic, or Haitian Creole communities commonly post directional signage in those languages alongside English (for example, Spanish/English in Los Angeles and Miami, Chinese/English in San Francisco and New York), following ALA guidance t

      Indigenous Languages

      Indigenous language preservation is a distinct strand of library language access focused on Native American, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and other indigenous languages, many of which are endangered; UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger and tribal language surveys document the urgency, and libraries serve both as preservation archives and as active revitalization sites. IMLS Native American Library Services and Native Hawaiian Library Services grants fund tribal libraries and cultural institutions to record, digitize, teach, and circulate indigenous-language materials

      Translation Technology

      Translation technology spans patron-facing tools (website translation widgets, multilingual catalogs, language-learning platforms) and staff-facing tools (machine translation of forms and notices, terminology glossaries), letting libraries extend language access far beyond what bilingual staffing alone could provide. Libraries commonly provide online language-learning platforms such as Mango Languages, Rosetta Stone, and Transparent Language Online (often licensed statewide), multilingual e-book and audiobook collections through Libby/OverDrive and Kanopy, and Google Translate-style widgets on

      Key Findings

      • The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey finds that roughly 68 million Americans aged 5 and over speak a language other than English at home (about 21.6% of that group), with Spanish (about 42 million speakers) dwarfing every other non-English language.
      • After Spanish, the most-spoken non-English languages at home in the U.S. are Chinese (about 3.5 million), Tagalog (about 1.7 million), Vietnamese (about 1.5 million), Arabic (about 1.4 million), French and French Creole (about 1.2 million), Korean (about 1.1 million), German (about 900,000), Russian (about 870,000), and Hindi (about 875,000), driving demand for translation and interpretation across many language groups, not just Spanish.
      • More than 25 million Americans report speaking English less than 'very well,' a population whose access to libraries, benefits, healthcare, and civic services depends heavily on interpretation and translated materials that libraries help provide.
      • On-demand telephonic interpretation vendors such as Language Line Solutions, which connect staff to live interpreters in 240 or more languages within seconds, let even small and rural branches serve patrons in rare languages without maintaining bilingual staff for each one.
      • Major urban systems including New York Public Library and Queens Public Library operate World Languages collections and New Americans programs covering dozens of languages, while REFORMA (an ALA affiliate founded in 1971) advocates nationally for Spanish-language and Latino library services.
      • Multilingual signage and wayfinding are among the most cost-effective forms of library language access, and systems in Los Angeles, Miami-Dade, San Francisco, and New York routinely post directional and departmental signage in Spanish, Chinese, Haitian Creole, and other locally prominent languages.
      • Language access increasingly extends to digital interfaces, with library websites offering translation widgets, online catalogs displaying in multiple languages, and self-check kiosks configured for the local language mix, so that the patron's first language barrier is often digital rather than at a service desk.
      • IMLS Native American Library Services and Native Hawaiian Library Services grants fund tribal and Native Hawaiian libraries to preserve and teach indigenous languages such as Navajo (Diné), Cherokee, Lakota, and ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, positioning libraries as both archives and active revitalization sites for endangered languages.
      • Translation technology such as Mango Languages, Rosetta Stone, Transparent Language Online, and multilingual Libby/OverDrive collections lets libraries extend language-learning and reading access far beyond what bilingual staffing alone could support, often licensed statewide for all member libraries.
      • Neural and generative AI translation tools let libraries draft multilingual flyers and forms quickly, but libraries apply human review for high-stakes legal, medical, benefits, and immigration content where a machine-translation error could seriously mislead a patron with limited English proficiency.

      Library Government Documents & Civic Literacy Deep Dive

      A deep summary of government document collections, civic literacy programs, government information literacy, and democracy tools at U.S. public libraries. It covers the Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP) network, GPO's GovInfo digital access, civic literacy and civic education programming, the ALA Government Documents Round Table (GODORT), government transparency resources including FOIA support and open-government data, notable programs, and key findings.

      GovDocs Overview

      Government documents (or government information) are the published informational output of federal, state, and local agencies -- statutes, regulations, congressional records, statistical reports, agency publications, and court opinions -- produced at government expense or as required by law. Title 44 of the U.S. Code defines a government publication as informational matter published as an individual document at government expense, and it governs how these works are distributed to the public. The Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP), rooted in an 1813 Congressional Joint Resolution and mod

      GovInfo Access

      GovInfo (govinfo.gov) is the official website of the U.S. government that houses federal government information, operated by the Government Publishing Office. It replaced the Federal Digital System (FDsys), which in turn replaced GPO Access, with a modern information management system that authenticates, preserves, and provides permanent public access to federal government documents from all three branches. Its goal is a complete historical record of federal government documents from the founding of the United States to the present. GovInfo provides online access to more than 2,200 databases a

      Civic Literacy

      Civic literacy is the knowledge and skills citizens need to understand and participate in government -- knowing how government is structured, how laws are made, how to engage with elected officials, and how to evaluate information about public affairs. It builds on civics, the study of the rights and obligations of citizens, and intersects with information literacy, which the Association of College and Research Libraries defines as the abilities to discover, evaluate, and use information in creating new knowledge and participating ethically in communities. Public libraries run civic education

      GODORT Role

      The Government Documents Round Table (GODORT) is a round table of the American Library Association dedicated to government information and its effective use. It serves as the professional home for government documents librarians, providing training, resources, and a national voice for the government-information community across all types of libraries. As an ALA round table, GODORT organizes librarians around government-information practice through committees, task forces, and interest groups that address cataloging of government documents, depository management, digitization, access to interna

      Transparency Resources

      Government transparency is the principle, codified in the open-government doctrine, that citizens have the right to access the documents and proceedings of government to allow effective public oversight. Libraries advance transparency by housing government documents, guiding patrons to public records and open data, and hosting civic events that teach residents how to hold government accountable. The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. section 552, is the federal law that requires full or partial disclosure of previously unreleased information and documents controlled by the U.S. govern

      Key Findings

      • The Federal Depository Library Program, rooted in an 1813 Congressional resolution and modernized by the 1962 Depository Library Act, distributes federal publications at no cost through roughly 1,082 depository libraries, including 46 regional and about 1,036 selective depositories, with 167 public libraries participating.
      • GovInfo, the GPO's online service that replaced FDsys, provides permanent public access to more than 2,200 databases of federal publications, extending depository access beyond physical collections to any resident with internet.
      • The Congressional Record, Federal Register, Code of Federal Regulations, and Statutes at Large -- the core legal record of the federal government -- are all published by GPO and made accessible to the public through the FDLP network and GovInfo.
      • GODORT, the Government Documents Round Table of ALA, is the professional home for government documents librarians, advocating for free and permanent public access to government information and selecting the annual ALA Notable Government Documents list.
      • Civic literacy at libraries combines civics -- the rights and obligations of citizens -- with information literacy, helping residents understand government structure, engage elected officials, and evaluate information about public affairs.
      • Public libraries deliver civic education through Constitution Day programs, citizenship preparation classes, naturalization-test study sessions, and civics tutoring, operationalizing the PLA service response 'Be an Informed Citizen.'
      • Libraries provide the practical tools of democracy -- voter registration under the 1993 National Voter Registration Act, polling places, passport acceptance, and public computers for e-government -- making them everyday civic infrastructure.
      • The Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. section 552) requires disclosure of government records on request, and libraries support FOIA use by housing public records, guiding patrons to agencies, and participating in Sunshine Week each March.
      • Open government increasingly means machine-readable open data, and libraries both consume government data for reference and publish their own operational data; the IMLS Public Libraries Survey is distributed as open datasets on Data.gov.
      • Regional depositories retain permanent comprehensive collections while selective depositories tailor holdings, ensuring that historical government records remain accessible even as access shifts digital, and that public libraries extend federal information into neighborhoods without a nearby academic or law library.

      Library Food Programs & Nutrition Support Deep Dive

      A deep summary of food programs, summer meals, food pantries, SNAP/EBT access, and nutrition support at U.S. public libraries.

      Food Overview

      Library food programs encompass any nutrition or food-access service delivered through a public library, including USDA-sponsored summer meals for children, on-site food pantries or Little Free Pantry boxes, SNAP/EBT enrollment assistance, farmers market partnerships that accept nutrition benefits, and community or seed libraries that support home food production. Feeding America reports that tens of millions of people in the United States are food insecure in a given year, including millions of children. Food insecurity is concentrated in rural counties, Southern states, and low-income urban

      Summer Meals

      The USDA Summer Food Service Program (SFSP) reimburses sponsors for free meals served to children and teens in low-income areas when school is out. Nationally, SFSP operates thousands of meal sites each summer across all 50 states and serves tens of millions of meals, though the program still reaches only a fraction of children who qualify for free or reduced-price school meals. Public libraries have become a meaningful and growing category of SFSP site because they are already open in the summer, are child-friendly, and serve neighborhoods where kids congregate. The American Library Associati

      Food Pantries

      Food pantries distribute free groceries to households in need and are typically operated by food banks in the Feeding America network, which comprises more than 200 member food banks and tens of thousands of partner pantry and meal-program sites nationwide. Recognizing that pantries can be stigmatizing or hard to reach, a growing number of public libraries host pantry service, either through weekly on-site distributions with a food-bank partner or through always-open, self-serve models like the Little Free Pantry. Library-based pantry models vary. Some libraries host scheduled food-bank distri

      SNAP & EBT

      The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), delivered via Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards, is the largest U.S. anti-hunger program and serves tens of millions of people each month. Libraries increasingly function as SNAP access points by providing application assistance, public computers for online enrollment, and referral to state SNAP agencies, lowering the barrier for households who may not visit a social-services office. Many public libraries assist patrons with SNAP enrollment by offering computers and internet access, trained staff or social workers who help navigate ap

      Community Gardens

      Community gardens provide space for residents to grow their own food, increase access to fresh produce, and build food skills. Public libraries have increasingly embraced gardening as an extension of community service, installing gardens on library grounds, offering gardening programs, and hosting seed libraries that let patrons borrow and return seeds for free. Library gardens range from small raised-bed plots to larger demonstration and teaching gardens. They are used for hands-on STEM and nutrition education for children, as sources of fresh produce for adjacent pantry or meal programs, and

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries serve as USDA Summer Food Service Program meal sites in communities nationwide, with hundreds of branches participating and collectively serving hundreds of thousands of meals to children each summer, helping close the seasonal hunger gap created when schools close.
      • The American Library Association's Libraries & Summer Food initiative formalizes the ALA-USDA partnership, providing libraries with toolkits, guidance, and peer models to become SFSP sites and pair federally reimbursed meals with summer reading and enrichment programming.
      • Summer meal service at libraries is concentrated in urban systems such as Hartford, DC, Philadelphia, San Antonio, Los Angeles, and Columbus, but also extends to small-town and rural libraries, demonstrating the model's scalability.
      • On-site food pantries at libraries are a growing practice, with systems like Hartford Public Library and DC Public Library hosting scheduled food-bank distributions and pairing pantry service with benefits referrals and social-work support.
      • The Little Free Pantry movement, launched in 2016 by Jessica McClard in Fayetteville, Arkansas, has expanded to hundreds of locations, including many public libraries that install always-open outdoor pantry boxes to extend food access beyond library hours.
      • Libraries increasingly serve as SNAP/EBT access points by providing public computers, application assistance, multilingual materials, and benefits screening; systems with embedded social workers, such as San Francisco and DC, routinely fold SNAP enrollment into patron case management.
      • Farmers market partnerships at libraries, exemplified by Oak Park Public Library in Illinois, connect SNAP-eligible patrons with produce-incentive programs like Double Up Food Bucks, stretching benefits on fresh fruits and vegetables and linking libraries to local food systems.
      • Community and demonstration gardens at libraries - such as those at Pikes Peak Library District (CO) and Greensboro Public Library (NC) - support hands-on nutrition and STEM education and can supply fresh produce for adjacent meal or pantry programs.
      • The seed library movement, popularized by Richmond Grows Seed Lending Library at Richmond Public Library in California and adopted by hundreds of libraries including Pima County (AZ), lets patrons borrow, grow, and return seeds, advancing food self-sufficiency and seed sovereignty.
      • Despite growth, library food programs reach only a fraction of the children who qualify for free or reduced-price school meals, and food insecurity remains high nationally; libraries are valuable low-stigma access points but depend on sustained partnerships with USDA sponsors, Feeding America food banks, and local funders to scale.

      Library Crisis Response & Emergency Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of libraries as emergency shelters, opioid overdose response sites, crisis support hubs, disaster relief centers, and pandemic response.

      Crisis Overview

      Library crisis response is the body of emergency, public-health, and social-safety-net services that U.S. public libraries provide during and after crises -- including opioid overdoses, mental-health crises, natural disasters (hurricanes, wildfires, floods, tornadoes), extreme heat and cold, and public-health emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Because libraries are free, centrally located, staffed, wired for power and internet, and open without appointment or eligibility requirements, they recur as ad hoc crisis-response sites in nearly every major U.S. emergency. Libraries' crisi

      Opioid Response

      The U.S. opioid epidemic -- driven increasingly by synthetic opioids such as fentanyl -- has produced tens of thousands of overdose deaths per year. Public libraries, as open and low-barrier public spaces, have encountered overdoses among patrons and sometimes staff, prompting the field to adopt naloxone (commonly by the brand name Narcan) as a life-saving tool. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses an opioid overdose by displacing opioids from receptors; it is administered as a nasal spray or injection. All 50 states and the District of Columbia have laws expanding naloxone a

      Disaster Relief

      Libraries are repeat players in U.S. disaster response. After landfall or destruction, libraries that retain or regain power become lifelines: they offer device charging, free Wi-Fi for FEMA registration and insurance claims, air-conditioned refuge, and trusted recovery information. Recovery funding combines FEMA Public Assistance (typically a 75% federal / 25% non-federal cost share, raised to 90%+ federal in catastrophic events), property insurance, state library agency LSTA funds, IMLS grants, and private donations. The Heritage Emergency National Task Force (HENTF), co-sponsored by FEMA an

      Warming & Cooling Centers

      Libraries are formally designated cooling and warming centers in many U.S. cities and counties during extreme-weather emergencies. Because libraries are publicly owned, staffed, climate-controlled, and free to enter, they are natural refuges during heat domes, polar vortex events, and the post-storm heat that often follows summer hurricanes. This function is increasingly recognized in local emergency-response plans and in public-health guidance on protecting vulnerable populations during extreme temperatures. Libraries also serve as clean-air refuges during wildfire smoke events, when HVAC fil

      Pandemic Response

      COVID-19 produced the largest simultaneous disruption in U.S. library history. Following CDC guidance and ALA recommendations, nearly all U.S. public libraries closed by mid-March 2020, then innovated through curbside pickup, virtual programming, and expanded digital lending before phased reopening. The pandemic caused the sharpest one-year drop in U.S. public library usage on record: visits fell 41.6% and circulation fell 25.0% from FY2019 to FY2020 (IMLS Public Libraries Survey). Federal relief channeled historic sums to libraries through IMLS: $50 million via the CARES Act (2020, of which $

      Key Findings

      • A growing number of U.S. public libraries stock intranasal naloxone (Narcan) and train staff to recognize and reverse opioid overdoses, supported by naloxone-access laws and Good Samaritan protections in all 50 states and D.C., and by partnerships with local health departments; the FDA approved the first over-the-counter naloxone nasal spray in March 2023.
      • San Francisco Public Library pioneered the full-time library social worker around 2009 (Leah Esguerra, with peer 'health and safety associates'), launching a model now adopted by dozens of urban and suburban systems that embed social workers and peer navigators to connect patrons to mental-health, housing, and substance-use services.
      • Hurricanes consistently show libraries staying open through the response: Houston Public Library's Central Library stayed open during Harvey (2017), New Orleans branches served through Katrina (2005) and Ida (2021), and Lee and Collier County libraries reopened as recovery hubs after Ian (2022).
      • Wildfires make libraries dual-purpose institutions: clean-air refuges during smoke events (HVAC filtration reducing PM2.5) and charging hubs during utility Public Safety Power Shutoffs, while branches in burn zones -- Paradise (2018), Lahaina (2023), Pacific Palisades (2025) -- are destroyed and must be rebuilt as anchors of recovery.
      • Libraries are formally designated cooling and warming centers in many U.S. cities; during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, Oregon and Washington libraries operated as cooling sites, and libraries routinely serve as daytime warming centers during polar vortex events and winter power outages.
      • COVID-19 was the largest simultaneous disruption in U.S. library history, with visits falling 41.6% and circulation 25.0% in FY2020; libraries responded with parking-lot Wi-Fi, contactless curbside pickup, and virtual programming, and later became COVID-19 vaccination and testing sites.
      • Federal relief was historic and decisive: the CARES Act (2020) gave IMLS $50 million (with $30M for digital inclusion), and the American Rescue Plan Act (2021) gave IMLS $200 million (about $178M to states via LSTA) -- the agency's largest single infusion -- funding hotspots, device lending, and digital access for underserved communities.
      • Recovery funding after disasters combines FEMA Public Assistance (typically 75% federal, rising to 90%+ in catastrophic events), property insurance, LSTA and state funds, IMLS grants, and private donations, but underinsurance of special collections is a recurring gap between insurance proceeds and actual rebuild cost.
      • The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, launched July 16, 2022, and administered by SAMHSA, gave libraries a single, memorable crisis number to promote alongside the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-HELP), positioning libraries as safe, knowledgeable points of connection to behavioral-health crisis care.
      • Libraries' value as connectivity infrastructure is most visible when telecom fails: Hurricane Helene (2024) turned western North Carolina libraries into 'internet oases' essential for FEMA registration and family contact when cell service was down for weeks.

      Library Notary Services & Legal Aid Deep Dive

      A deep summary of free notary services, legal aid clinics, expungement programs, tenant rights workshops, and legal navigation at U.S. public libraries.

      Notary Overview

      A notary public is a public officer constituted by law to serve the public in non-contentious matters -- chiefly validating signatures, administering oaths and affirmations, taking affidavits and statutory declarations, and acknowledging deeds and other conveyances. In the United States, most notaries are lay persons (not attorneys) whose commissions are issued by a state authority; Louisiana, Puerto Rico, and parts of Quebec are civil-law exceptions. There are an estimated 4.5 million notaries public in the United States, far more per capita than other common-law countries. Public libraries h

      Free Notary Services

      A growing number of U.S. public library systems offer notary services free of charge, though policies vary widely: some libraries provide free notarization as a core service, others charge a nominal per-stamp fee (often $1-$5) capped by state law, and others offer the service free only for a limited number of stamps per patron per visit. Where state statute sets a maximum notary fee, libraries that charge typically charge at or below that ceiling. Typical library notary programs commission one or more staff members as notaries public through their state's secretary of state or equivalent

      Legal Clinics

      Public libraries increasingly host free civil legal clinics in partnership with local legal aid societies, bar association pro bono committees, and law school clinics. The Legal Services Corporation -- the largest single funder of civil legal aid in the United States -- explicitly identifies public libraries as trusted community access points through its Public Library Initiative, and partners with OCLC and WebJunction to train library staff to recognize civil legal issues and refer patrons to help. LSC funds 129 independent nonprofit legal aid organizations operating 900+ offices across all 5

      Immigration Legal Services

      Public libraries are a frontline access point for immigration legal information, particularly for patrons who are low-income, limited-English-proficient, or geographically far from a Board-of-Immigration-Appeals-accredited representative. While libraries themselves cannot provide legal advice, they host citizenship classes, naturalization application assistance events, and 'know your rights' presentations in partnership with DOJ-recognized organizations and immigration legal aid providers. Citizenship corners -- dedicated spaces or service desks offering naturalization study material

      Law Librarians

      The American Association of Law Libraries (AALL), founded in 1906, is a nonprofit educational organization of approximately 5,000 members across the United States, comprising law librarians and legal information professionals in courthouses, law schools, law firms, state governments, and public law libraries. AALL's mission is to promote the value of law libraries, foster the law librarianship profession, and advocate for fair and equitable access to authentic current and historic legal information.       • The United States has an estimated 4.5 million notaries public, and a growing share of U.S. public library systems now commission staff to offer free or low-cost notarization, treating it as a core community convenience service.
      • The Legal Services Corporation -- the largest single funder of civil legal aid in the U.S. -- funds 129 independent nonprofit legal aid organizations operating 900+ offices across all 50 states, serving more than 6.4 million people annually, with 30+ million individuals using grantees' online self-help resources.
      • LSC's landmark 'justice gap' research found that all legal aid offices nationwide, LSC-funded or not, together met only about 20 percent of the estimated civil legal needs of low-income Americans, underscoring why libraries have become important referral points.
      • Through its Public Library Initiative, LSC formally identifies public libraries as trusted community access points for civil legal information and partners with OCLC/WebJunction to train library staff to recognize legal issues and refer patrons to help.
      • The Minnesota Legal Kiosk Project deployed more than 270 legal kiosks across the state -- many in public libraries -- and in 2022 received a $299,866 LSC grant to enhance the software and create step-by-step legal plans for low-income Minnesotans.
      • In 2025, LSC's Technology Initiative Grant program funded Nevada Legal Services to enhance a statewide network of legal kiosks in 28 libraries with an AI-powered, multilingual search assistant improving access for rural and underserved patrons.
      • Expungement and record-sealing clinics hosted at libraries in cities such as Charlotte, Detroit, St. Louis, and San Francisco help eligible residents clear qualifying records, unlocking employment, housing, and professional licensing opportunities.
      • Tenant rights and eviction-defense workshops have expanded sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic; LSC partnered with OCLC to build WebJunction's 'Eviction and Housing Resources' training so library staff can respond to housing questions with confidence.
      • Major urban library systems -- including New York Public Library, Brooklyn Public Library, Los Angeles Public Library, San Francisco Public Library, and Chicago Public Library -- operate citizenship corners and naturalization services in partnership with USCIS and DOJ-recognized immigration legal providers.
      • The American Association of Law Libraries, founded in 1906 with about 5,000 members, advances access to authentic legal information and trains law librarians who serve pro se litigants, complementing public library legal-navigation efforts.

      Library Energy Assistance & Utility Help Deep Dive

      A deep summary of energy assistance enrollment, utility bill help, EV charging, solar installations, and energy efficiency at U.S. public libraries.

      Energy Overview

      Library energy assistance and utility help refers to the cluster of services and infrastructure through which public libraries help households afford and access energy: assisting patrons with enrollment in the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) and state/utility bill assistance and shutoff-prevention programs; hosting utility-company community outreach and energy-fair events; providing device and medical-equipment charging and cooling/warming refuge during power outages and extreme weather; and deploying clean-energy infrastructure on library property such as rooftop so

      LIHEAP Enrollment

      LIHEAP is a federally funded block grant administered by HHS/ACF and distributed to states, territories, and tribes, which in turn set their own eligibility (commonly up to 150% of the federal poverty level or 60% of state median income) and application procedures. Because many states take applications online or through community partner agencies, libraries serve as informal enrollment sites: staff and volunteers help patrons find their state's LIHEAP portal, gather required documents, scan and upload paperwork, and complete the online application on public-access computers. ACF reports t

      Utility Help

      Beyond LIHEAP, libraries connect patrons to a wide range of utility-bill and shutoff-prevention help: utility-company bill-assistance and discount programs (for example the Percentage of Income Payment Plan in several states, and ratepayer-funded fuel funds); state moratoria on winter shutoffs and medical-certificate protections; arrearage management programs; and emergency assistance from nonprofit fuel funds operated by groups such as the Salvation Army, Catholic Charities, and 211 referral lines. Library staff and public computers are the front door for many low-income households who lack h

      EV Charging

      Public libraries have become a recognizable site category for public EV charging. The DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center tracks thousands of public charging stations nationwide, and library parking lots are an increasingly common location type because they are publicly owned, centrally located, open long hours, and already visited by the public for reasons unrelated to charging. Chargers at libraries are typically Level 2 units suited to the multi-hour dwell time of a library visit, though some library sites host DC fast chargers. Documented examples of library-hosted EV charging span many stat

      Solar & Efficiency

      Rooftop solar and energy-efficiency retrofits at libraries serve a dual purpose: they cut municipal operating costs and greenhouse-gas emissions, and they function as highly visible public demonstrations of clean-energy technology in neighborhoods that might otherwise never see it. DOE's Solar Power in Your Community guidebook has highlighted municipal and community buildings, including libraries, as prime candidates for distributed solar, and EPA's Energy Star program provides benchmarking tools that libraries use to measure and reduce building energy use. Multiple U.S. libraries ha

      Key Findings

      • LIHEAP, the main federal home-energy safety net, typically serves about 5 to 6 million U.S. households per year with a regular appropriation of roughly $3.7 billion, yet ACF reports it reaches only about one-fifth of income-eligible households, making trusted community enrollment sites like libraries essential to closing the access gap.
      • Public libraries act as informal LIHEAP enrollment sites by providing the computers, scanners, internet, and staff navigation help that patrons need to complete online applications, particularly in states that take applications electronically through their LIHEAP grantee or community action agency network.
      • Beyond LIHEAP, libraries connect patrons to utility bill-assistance programs, low-income discount rates, Percentage of Income Payment Plans, fuel funds, and shutoff-prevention protections such as winter moratoria and medical-emergency certificates, with legal-aid partners often co-located for clinics.
      • Roughly 9,200 public library main and branch buildings across the United States give the library network a large geographic footprint for energy outreach, and ALA has formally adopted sustainability as a core value, encouraging libraries to model environmental stewardship.
      • Rooftop solar is documented at multiple U.S. libraries, including Fayetteville Public Library (Arkansas), whose LEED-registered Blair Library generates about 6% of its energy use from rooftop panels, plus Athens-Clarke County Library (Georgia, LEED Gold), Reading Public Library (Pennsylvania), and Montgomery County's Silver Spring Library (Maryland, LEED Gold).
      • EV charging stations are an increasingly common library amenity, with publicly accessible chargers documented at libraries including Westport (Connecticut), Canton and Ann Arbor (Michigan), Reading (Pennsylvania), Skokie and Arlington Heights (Illinois), Fayetteville (Arkansas), and Sno-Isle (Washington), often funded by state, utility, or Clean Cities coalition programs.
      • Libraries are attractive EV-charging partners because they control their own parking, are open long hours, and generate dwell-time demand suited to Level 2 charging; the federal NEVI program and state energy offices have increasingly named libraries among priority public sites for charger deployment.
      • Energy-efficiency retrofits are even more widespread than solar at libraries, supported by utility rebates, state energy-office grants, and DOE Energy Efficiency and Conservation Block Grant funding; typical measures include LED lighting, high-efficiency or geothermal HVAC, envelope upgrades, and building-management controls.
      • As extreme-weather events increase, libraries increasingly serve as resilience hubs -- designated cooling centers during heat waves and warming centers during cold snaps -- where patrons charge phones and medical equipment and access conditioned shelter, a role encouraged by EPA heat-island guidance and ALA disaster-response resources.
      • The Sustainable Libraries Initiative certifies libraries that commit to measurable energy, water, and waste reductions, giving the field a common framework for tracking progress and spreading proven practices across the roughly 9,200-building public library system.

      Library Citizenship & Naturalization Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries support immigrants seeking citizenship and naturalization, covering USCIS partnerships, Citizenship Corners, citizenship classes, immigration legal aid, and civics test preparation, with notable programs across multiple states.

      Citizenship Overview

      Citizenship and naturalization refer to the legal process by which a foreign national becomes a U.S. citizen, typically after meeting residency, good moral character, and English and civics requirements and filing Form N-400 with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). Naturalization is a complex, paperwork-intensive process that many immigrants navigate without legal representation; libraries serve as trusted, free, and community-accessible hubs where applicants can find reliable information, study materials, classes, and referrals at no cost. Public libraries function as neutral,

      Naturalization Corners

      Citizenship Corners (also called New Americans Corners) are dedicated spaces within libraries stocked with official USCIS naturalization study materials, civics and English test flash cards, Naturalization Information Center resources, and guidance on the N-400 application process. Beginning around 2013, USCIS formalized partnerships with public library systems across the country to establish Citizenship Corners, signing agreements to supply libraries with free official study publications and training library staff to direct patrons to legitimate information rather than immigration scams. Mate

      Citizenship Classes

      Many library systems host or co-sponsor free citizenship preparation classes—often taught by volunteers, adult-education partners, or community organizations—that walk applicants through the naturalization application and interview process in a supportive group setting. Classes focus on the two components of the naturalization test: the civics test (covering U.S. history and government) and the English test (reading, writing, and speaking), with instructors drilling the 100 civics questions and modeling the N-400 interview questions applicants will hear from a USCIS officer. Because many appli

      Legal Aid

      Libraries frequently partner with nonprofit legal service providers to host immigration legal clinics, naturalization application workshops, and 'know your rights' presentations, often offering free or low-cost assistance with N-400 filings and fee waivers. Licensed immigration attorneys and Accredited Representatives from partner organizations provide direct assistance, document review, and case consultations during library-hosted clinics, helping applicants avoid unauthorized practitioners ('notarios') who exploit immigrants with fraudulent services. Many partner organiza

      Civic Test Resources

      The civics component of the naturalization test requires applicants to demonstrate knowledge of U.S. history, government, and civic principles; libraries curate and circulate the official USCIS study tools and supplement them with multimedia, flash cards, and practice sessions. USCIS publishes a standardized list of 100 civics questions and answers; during the naturalization interview the applicant is asked up to 10 of these and must answer at least 6 correctly to pass under the long-standing 2008 test version, which remains the standard after the 2020 test version was paused and ultimately re

      • Many library citizenship classes are offered in multiple languages and pair civics content with English as a Second Language instruction.
      • Libraries frequently partner with BIA-accredited representatives and immigration attorneys to host free or low-cost naturalization legal clinics.
      • Mock naturalization interviews at libraries help applicants practice the N-400 interview and reduce test anxiety.

      Library 3D Printing & Additive Manufacturing Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries provide 3D printing and additive manufacturing services through makerspaces, covering equipment, patron access models, education programs, and the equity role libraries play in democratizing manufacturing tools.

      Printing Overview

      Additive manufacturing, commonly called 3D printing, builds three-dimensional objects layer by layer from a digital model, most often through fused deposition modeling (FDM) that extrudes heated thermoplastic filament. Public libraries offer this technology as a free or low-cost service within makerspaces, frequently alongside 3D scanning, laser cutting, and computer-aided design (CAD) workstations. As additive manufacturing becomes central to prototyping, STEM education, and small-batch production, patrons including students, hobbyists, and entrepreneurs need access to equipment and design sk

      Maker Equipment

      Library makerspaces typically center on desktop FDM 3D printers supplemented by 3D scanners, laser cutters, vinyl cutters, electronics benches, and CAD workstations, forming an integrated digital fabrication environment. Equipment is selected to balance reliability, safety, and ease of use in a public, multi-user setting. The most common printer brands are MakerBot (Replicator and Replicator+ series, widely deployed in early library makerspaces), Prusa (i3 MK3 and MK4, valued for reliability, print quality, and open-source design), and Ultimaker (Ultimaker 2, 3, and S series, favored for dual-

      Patron Access

      Access models range from staff-mediated printing, in which patrons submit a file for staff to print and collect later, to fully self-service booking where certified patrons operate the machines directly. The staff-mediated model is common at smaller or newly launched programs, while mature makerspaces often move toward self-service after an orientation or certification step. Libraries use online booking calendars, often integrated with their integrated library system or tools such as Springshare's LibCal, to reserve printer time in slots typically ranging from one to three hours. Many pro

      Education Programs

      Libraries run structured workshops, drop-in clinics, and one-on-one appointments covering the full pipeline from digital design to physical printing, often led by maker librarians, resident artists, or teen-services specialists. Programming frequently targets youth, teens, and adult learners in separate tracks. Common CAD and design training covers Tinkercad (browser-based and beginner-friendly), Autodesk Fusion 360, Blender, and Onshape, with curricula spanning basic shape modeling to mechanical part design and parametric modeling. Many programs integrate 3D-scanning and file-preparation (sli

      Equity & Access

      Library 3D printing is a notable equity intervention, bringing advanced manufacturing tools to communities and individuals who lack the capital to access them commercially. By situating fabrication equipment in free, trusted public spaces, libraries extend maker opportunities to low-income, rural, and underrepresented patrons. By removing both cost and knowledge barriers, libraries democratize additive manufacturing, enabling low-income patrons, students, and rural communities to prototype, learn, and create physical goods on roughly equal footing with well-resourced makers.       • 3D printing is a core service in hundreds of US public library makerspaces, typically offered free or at per-gram cost-recovery rates.
      • MakerBot, Prusa, and Ultimaker are the dominant desktop 3D printer brands deployed in library makerspaces, with Bambu Lab machines growing in adoption.
      • PLA is the default filament in nearly all library programs due to safety and ease of use, while PETG and ABS are offered where equipment and ventilation permit.
      • Patron access ranges from staff-mediated file submission to certified self-service booking via tools such as Springshare LibCal.
      • Most libraries recover material costs through per-gram pricing of roughly $0.05 to $0.50 per gram, though many subsidize printing entirely as a free public service.
      • CAD training most commonly uses Tinkercad for beginners, with Fusion 360, Blender, and Onshape for intermediate and advanced patrons.
      • Early leaders such as Fayetteville Free Library, Westport Library, and Chicago Public Library established the public library makerspace model beginning around 2011 to 2013.
      • Library 3D printing democratizes access to additive manufacturing for low-income, rural, and underrepresented communities that lack commercial access.
      • Entrepreneurs use library 3D printers for low-cost prototyping, frequently paired with business research, patent assistance, and small-business development partnerships.

      Library Passport Acceptance Services Deep Dive

      An overview of how public libraries across the United States serve as passport acceptance facilities under a partnership with the U.S. Department of State, processing first-time passport applications, providing passport photos, and retaining a per-application execution fee as library revenue.

      Passport Overview

      A passport acceptance facility is a location designated by the U.S. Department of State to receive and review in-person passport applications on the government's behalf. Acceptance agents verify the applicant's identity, confirm that required documents and photos are present, administer the required oath, witness the applicant's signature, and seal the application into an envelope that is mailed to a passport processing agency. Acceptance facilities include U.S. post offices, clerks of court, other government offices, and increasingly public libraries. First-time adult applicant

      Acceptance Process

      At a library acceptance facility, the applicant brings a completed Form DS-11, proof of U.S. citizenship (such as a certified birth certificate or naturalization certificate), government-issued photo identification, one compliant passport photo, and payment. The trained library acceptance agent reviews the documents for completeness and obvious errors, confirms identity against the photo ID, asks the applicant to raise their right hand and take an oath attesting to the truthfulness of the application, watches the applicant sign the form, and then places the sealed application and supporting do

      Photo Services

      Because a compliant passport photo is a mandatory part of any application, many library acceptance facilities also offer on-site passport photo service as a convenience and an additional revenue stream. Offering photos in the same visit eliminates a common point of failure in the application process, since photos taken at unrelated retail locations are frequently rejected by the State Department for being the wrong size, poorly lit, retouched, or non-compliant in other ways. By pairing photo capture with application execution, libraries ensure the photo matches State Department specifications

      Rural Access

      In rural and small-town America, post offices have been consolidating and reducing hours for years, clerks of court may serve multiple counties from a distant county seat, and dedicated passport agencies exist only in a handful of major metropolitan areas. For a rural resident, the nearest facility able to execute a passport application can be a long drive away. Public libraries, by contrast, exist in thousands of small communities as the most persistent piece of public infrastructure, making them natural sites to host passport acceptance and bring a federal service within reach of populations

      Revenue Model

      The passport acceptance program is structured so that non-federal acceptance facilities, including public libraries, retain a per-application execution fee as compensation for the staff time, supplies, training, and overhead involved in executing applications. This converts a federal service duty into a modest but reliable revenue stream for the library, which is one of the main reasons libraries elect to participate. The model aligns incentives: the library is paid for each application it executes, so busier passport desks generate more revenue, and libraries can layer on a separate photo fee

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries are designated by the U.S. Department of State as passport acceptance facilities, alongside post offices, clerks of court, and other government offices.
      • Acceptance facilities execute in-person applications for first-time applicants, most minors, and applicants ineligible for mail-in renewal, verifying identity, administering the oath, and sealing the application for mailing.
      • Libraries retain the $35 per-application execution fee as revenue, creating a modest but reliable income stream that is unrestricted and can support library operations.
      • The execution fee is collected separately from the passport application fee payable to the Department of State, which must be paid by check or money order.
      • Many library acceptance facilities also offer on-site passport photo services, capturing compliant photos in the same visit and earning an additional fee per applicant.
      • Libraries fill rural and small-town service gaps where post offices have closed or no longer accept passport applications, sparing residents long drives to distant facilities.
      • Most library passport desks operate by appointment, using online or phone booking to manage staff time and interview space while balancing passport duties against core library work.
      • Library staff help patrons select the correct form, assemble required citizenship and identity documents, and navigate family applications for children, which require additional consent documentation.
      • Passport demand surges driven by the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative, REAL ID, and post-pandemic travel have made library acceptance facilities an important pressure-relief valve for federal processing.
      • Hosting passport services increases library foot traffic, introduces non-traditional users to library resources, and strengthens the library's role as a civic-services hub during budget deliberations.

      Library Tax Preparation & IRS Assistance Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries serve as trusted, no-cost access points for tax preparation, IRS-assistance programs (VITA and TCE/AARP Tax-Aide), IRS Free File use on library computers, multilingual tax help, EITC outreach, and refund-claim support for unbanked taxpayers.

      Tax Overview

      Tax preparation and IRS assistance services at public libraries refer to free, in-person or computer-based help that libraries provide during the January-April filing season so that low- and moderate-income, senior, and limited-English-proficient taxpayers can file accurate federal and state returns without paying commercial preparer fees. The two backbone IRS programs are Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA), for households generally earning about $67,000 or less, persons with disabilities, and limited-English speakers, and Tax Counseling for the Elderly (TCE), focused on taxpayers age 60 a

      VITA Sites

      VITA sites are free tax-preparation clinics staffed by IRS-certified volunteers who prepare and electronically file federal and state returns for eligible taxpayers, generally those earning about $67,000 or less, persons with disabilities, and limited-English speakers. Public libraries are one of the most common VITA venue types, alongside community centers, churches, schools, and credit unions. Each site uses IRS-provided TaxWise software, follows intake and quality-review procedures, and issues the taxpayer a copy of the completed return. Many library VITA sites run by appointment only from

      Free File

      IRS Free File is a public-private partnership that lets taxpayers with adjusted gross income at or below a threshold (historically around $84,000) use brand-name commercial tax software to prepare and e-file federal returns at no cost, with many states offering free state filing through the same providers. Taxpayers above the income cap can use Free File Fillable Forms, the electronic version of paper forms. Libraries are a primary on-ramp because they supply the computer, broadband, and privacy that home-internet-limited patrons need to use the IRS Free File provider lookup and complete a ret

      Multilingual Help

      Limited-English-proficient taxpayers face elevated risk of errors, missed credits, and exposure to notario fraud, so multilingual tax assistance is a core library service in immigrant-rich communities. VITA grant requirements emphasize language access, and IRS publications, the Form 1040, and many schedules are issued in Spanish, with key publications available in Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean, Russian, and Haitian Creole. Libraries compound this access by pairing bilingual volunteers, translated signage, and multilingual collection materials with the trusted-community reputation that immigrant

      Refund Claims

      Refund-claim assistance helps eligible taxpayers actually receive the federal and state refunds they are owed, particularly the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, which can be worth thousands of dollars per family. Libraries and their VITA partners focus on outreach to non-filers, prior-year back-filing (up to three years of refunds), and steering filers away from refund-anticipation loans and checks that erode refund value. Free preparation paired with direct deposit lets the full refund reach the household, making library tax help a measurable anti-poverty intervention. EITC Awar

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries are among the most common VITA and TCE/AARP Tax-Aide venue types in the United States, providing free space, computers, printing, and broadband that IRS-certified volunteers need to prepare and e-file returns.
      • VITA serves households generally earning about $67,000 or less, persons with disabilities, and limited-English speakers, while TCE (largely through AARP Tax-Aide) focuses on taxpayers 60 and older; libraries host both programs under the same roof.
      • IRS Free File lets eligible taxpayers use commercial software for free, and libraries are the primary on-ramp for filers without home internet, a printer, or a private device.
      • Library staff do not give tax advice; instead they enable IRS-certified volunteers and partner nonprofits such as United Way, AARP Foundation, and CASH coalitions to deliver preparation under IRS quality-review standards.
      • EITC Awareness Day in late January anchors library outreach campaigns targeting the roughly one in five eligible workers who fail to claim the Earned Income Tax Credit.
      • Multilingual library VITA sites in Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, Arabic, and Haitian Creole reduce errors, missed credits, and exposure to notario fraud among limited-English-proficient taxpayers.
      • Libraries pair tax preparation with ITIN-renewal assistance and immigration-legal-aid clinics, helping mixed-status families claim refunds and child benefits they would otherwise lose.
      • Unbanked filers are steered away from refund-anticipation checks and check-cashing fees toward direct deposit, prepaid cards, and Bank-On credit-union accounts opened at or near the library.
      • Back-filing outreach at library sites helps eligible non-filers recover up to three years of prior-year refunds, frequently worth thousands of dollars per household.
      • Program hours, branch participation, and appointment systems change each filing season, so current-season details must be confirmed directly with each library system or the IRS VITA and TCE locator tools.

      Library Voter Registration & Election Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries provide voter registration and election services -- from NVRA agency designation and National Voter Registration Day participation to serving as polling places, ballot drop sites, and nonpartisan civic information hubs. The summary captures both the policy mechanisms and the specific library-system programs that put them into practice across many states.

      Voter Overview

      Library voter services are the nonpartisan election-related services that public libraries offer to their communities. They include voter registration assistance, distribution of ballots and voter guides, hosting of candidate forums, and serving as polling or ballot drop-off locations. The framing treats the library as an entry point to democratic participation rather than only as a reading room, while still respecting the legal limits on partisan electioneering at publicly funded sites. Tens of millions of eligible Americans are not registered to vote, and the registration gap is widest among

      Registration Drives

      Voter registration drives are among the most common election services libraries run. Staff and trained volunteers set up registration tables, post QR codes and links to online registration portals, and help patrons navigate paper forms. Many systems integrate registration prompts into existing patron touchpoints such as new library card sign-ups, computer bookings, and citizenship or English-language classes, so that registration becomes a routine byproduct of a normal library visit. National Voter Registration Day, held on the fourth Tuesday of September since 2012, is a single-day nonpartisa

      Polling Sites

      Because library branches are ADA-accessible, centrally located, and already open to the public, election offices frequently use them as physical voting locations. The same qualities that make libraries good registration sites -- visibility, accessibility, neutrality -- make them attractive to election administrators seeking well-known, easy-to-find venues that voters already know how to reach. On Election Day, many libraries serve as neighborhood precinct polling places, with voting machines or booths set up in meeting rooms, lobbies, or community spaces. Election offices value libraries for t

      Civic Information

      Beyond logistics, libraries function as nonpartisan election information hubs. They curate and display authoritative materials -- registration deadlines, ID requirements, polling hours, and sample ballots -- and direct patrons to official election offices and trusted resources such as Vote.org, Ballotpedia, and the League of Women Voters. Librarians' reference skills make them well suited to pointing patrons to accurate, jurisdiction-specific answers rather than partisan commentary. Libraries routinely stock and display sample ballots, state voter pamphlets, and nonpartisan ballot-measure

      Get Out the Vote

      Get-out-the-vote (GOTV) work at libraries extends beyond registration to reminding and motivating already-registered patrons to actually cast ballots. Libraries use their communication channels -- websites, newsletters, social media, in-branch signage, and bookmarks -- to share election dates, deadlines, and voting locations without endorsing candidates or ballot positions, keeping the effort legally nonpartisan. Libraries partner with national nonprofits such as Vote.org, TurboVote (Democracy Works), When We All Vote, and Rock the Vote, which supply free toolkits, embeddable registration widg

      • Public libraries operate in more than 17,000 locations across the US, making them among the most widespread civic institutions available for voter engagement.
      • National Voter Registration Day, held the fourth Tuesday of September, consistently lists public libraries as top community partners, with hundreds of branches hosting registration events each year.
      • Under Section 7 of the NVRA, states may designate public libraries as official voter registration agencies, and several states and counties have done so, making registration a routine library service.
      • Libraries' trusted, nonpartisan reputation makes them especially effective at registering voters who are skeptical of partisan or government-only outreach.
      • In all-mail states such as Oregon, Washington, and Colorado, libraries commonly serve as official ballot drop-off sites, increasing secure return options.
      • Many library systems serve as Election Day precinct polling places or early-voting and vote centers because branches are ADA-accessible and centrally located.
      • Partnerships with Vote.org, TurboVote, When We All Vote, and the League of Women Voters give libraries free toolkits to run registration drives and send election reminders.
      • The American Library Association issues guidance and 'Libraries = Voter Registration' resources encouraging every public library to offer nonpartisan election services.
      • Libraries increasingly provide sample ballots, voter pamphlets, and Ballotpedia and League of Women Voters guides, filling information gaps for new and infrequent voters.

      Library Housing Assistance & Eviction Prevention Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries address housing insecurity through embedded social workers, eviction-prevention legal aid referrals, renter rights education, Section 8 and Housing Choice Voucher information, mail and address services for unhoused patrons, and wraparound supports such as hygiene facilities and navigation centers.

      Housing Overview

      Library housing assistance encompasses the constellation of services public libraries provide to patrons experiencing housing insecurity, imminent eviction, or homelessness, including embedded social workers, referrals to emergency shelter and permanent housing, legal aid navigation, renter rights education, Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) information, and basic-needs services such as mail reception and hygiene access. Libraries function as low-barrier, drop-in access points rather than housing providers themselves. Housing insecurity affects tens of millions of US households, with cost-bur

      Eviction Prevention

      Eviction prevention in libraries combines information provision, legal-aid referrals, and direct assistance such as help completing rental assistance applications and accessing emergency rental funds. Libraries curate tenant-rights booklets, host know-your-rights workshops with legal aid partners, and offer public computers and scanners so patrons can file court responses, upload documents, and attend virtual hearings. Many library systems formalize partnerships with Legal Aid Societies, LSC-funded programs, and law school clinics to deliver free tenant defense. Models range from scheduled in-

      Homeless Services

      Homeless services in libraries have grown from informal staff response into structured programs featuring professional social workers, peer staff with lived experience, and formal partnerships with homeless continuums of care. Libraries offer daytime safe space, information referral, mental-health de-escalation, and connection to outreach teams, recognizing that patrons experiencing homelessness use libraries heavily for shelter, connectivity, and dignity. Beginning with San Francisco Public Library's 2009 hire of Leah Esguerra as the nation's first full-time library social worker, d

      Housing Resources

      Housing resources at libraries span curated information, application assistance, and direct referrals across the housing continuum, from emergency shelter to permanent supportive housing. Libraries maintain community resource databases, distribute HUD and local housing-authority publications, and increasingly staff community resource specialists who maintain up-to-date knowledge of waitlist openings, eligibility rules, and application deadlines. Libraries are a primary public-access point for Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) information, providing the computers, internet, and printing patron

      Wraparound Support

      Beyond housing-specific help, libraries provide wraparound supports that stabilize the broader conditions of housing-insecure patrons: daytime respite from weather, restrooms and hygiene facilities, charging and connectivity, health and behavioral-health navigation, and benefit-application assistance. These supports reduce the friction that prevents people from pursuing and keeping housing. A small but growing set of libraries offer or host hygiene services such as showers, laundry, and restroom-access programs, often through partnerships with mobile shower nonprofits, public health department

      • Public libraries function as universal, low-barrier front doors to the housing-safety net because they are free, walk-in, trusted, and present in nearly every US community.
      • San Francisco Public Library's 2009 hire of Leah Esguerra is widely credited as the first full-time social worker embedded in a US public library and seeded a national Social Workers in Libraries movement.
      • Dozens of library systems now employ MSW-credentialed social workers or community resource specialists, including DC, Dallas, Denver, Philadelphia, Queens, Salt Lake City, Hartford, and Long Beach.
      • Eviction prevention in libraries combines tenant-rights collections, know-your-rights workshops, and formal partnerships with Legal Aid Societies and LSC-funded tenant-defense programs.
      • Libraries supply the computers, internet, printing, scanning, and notary services that patrons need to apply for Housing Choice Vouchers, respond to eviction filings, and attend virtual court hearings.
      • Mail and address services are a foundational housing-stability intervention, with several libraries allowing unhoused patrons to use the library as a general-delivery address or to hold mail for pickup.
      • Shelter directories and community resource databases are maintained by library social workers and resource desks, often in cooperation with local continuums of care and updated for seasonal capacity.
      • Peer staffing using individuals with lived homeless experience, such as SFPL's Health and Safety Associates, improves engagement and reduces the crisis-response burden on librarians.
      • Wraparound supports such as restrooms, charging, daytime respite, and in some cases showers and laundry reduce the friction that prevents housing-insecure patrons from pursuing and keeping housing.
      • The library 'navigation center' model uses co-located social workers and scheduled partner-agency visits to triage shelter intake, benefits, ID replacement, and legal aid at a single trusted site.

      Library Oral History & Storytelling Projects Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries collect, record, and preserve oral histories and community stories through partnerships with organizations such as StoryCorps and tribal nations. It covers recording technology, community storytelling initiatives, Indigenous oral tradition preservation, and the access and preservation strategies that sustain these collections.

      Oral History Overview

      Oral history is the systematic collection and preservation of personal spoken recollections, memories, and life stories through recorded interviews. In a library context it spans structured life-history interviews, topical community documentary projects, and informal storytelling events, and the resulting recordings are described, archived, and made accessible alongside the library's other local history holdings. Oral history captures voices and lived experiences that written records routinely omit, including the perspectives of marginalized communities, recent immigrants, elders, and wit

      Recording Technology

      Modern library oral history work relies on accessible digital recording technology, typically combining portable digital audio recorders such as the Zoom H series and Tascam DR series, broadcast-quality condenser microphones, and pop-filter-equipped interview setups. Video is captured with multi-camera rigs or single fixed cameras where budgets allow, and raw files are transferred to library workstations for editing, description, and ingest into a preservation system. A growing number of public libraries have built dedicated recording studios and media labs equipped with sound-treated booths,

      Community Stories

      Community storytelling initiatives document the everyday experiences of neighborhoods through recorded interviews, listening events, and public programs that elevate voices often absent from the historical record. These projects tend to be place-based and participatory, training community members as interviewers so that the resulting archive reflects local priorities rather than an outside researcher's frame. StoryCorps, the national oral history nonprofit, has partnered extensively with libraries through initiatives such as the IMLS-funded StoryCorps @ your library program developed with

      Indigenous Oral Traditions

      Indigenous oral traditions encompass the spoken transmission of knowledge, history, ceremony, language, and law across generations, carrying cultural meaning that differs fundamentally from a Western interview-based oral history. Public and tribal libraries engaged in this work must recognize that oral traditions may be sacred, governed by protocol, and intended for specific audiences rather than broad public release. Public and tribal libraries increasingly collaborate with Native nations to support oral tradition preservation, with tribal libraries such as the Navajo Nation Library and progr

      Access & Preservation

      Ensuring long-term access to oral histories requires active preservation planning, including file format migration, redundant storage, and clear rights and consent documentation. Libraries balance the goal of broad public access against privacy concerns, cultural sensitivities, and the consent terms under which interviews were originally recorded. Digital repositories such as the Digital Public Library of America, the Internet Archive, and library-hosted Omeka and Islandora sites aggregate and share oral histories with searchable metadata. Many libraries also contribute to regional and nationa
