      Key Findings

      • Public libraries increasingly serve as accessible recording hubs and long-term stewards of community oral history across the United States.
      • StoryCorps partnerships, including the IMLS-funded StoryCorps @ your library program, helped seed oral history recording in public libraries nationwide.
      • New York City's three public library systems host some of the country's most active programs, including the Queens Memory Project and Brooklyn's Our Streets, Our Stories.
      • The DC Oral History Collaborative demonstrates a successful multi-institution model pairing a public library with a history center and a humanities council.
      • Civil rights oral history collections at libraries in Birmingham, Nashville, Greensboro, and Atlanta document movement veterans and community witnesses.
      • Dedicated recording studios and media labs lower barriers for community members to record and digitize personal stories with professional equipment.
      • Digital repository platforms such as Omeka, Islandora, the Internet Archive, and the Digital Public Library of America enable online preservation and discovery of oral histories.
      • Transcription projects combining automated speech-to-text with volunteer review make oral history audio searchable and accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
      • Indigenous oral tradition preservation depends on tribal sovereignty, informed consent, and community control over what may be recorded, stored, and accessed.
      • Sustainability through stable funding, trained staffing, and long-term digital preservation remains the central challenge for library oral history initiatives.

      Library Dementia & Alzheimer's Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries serve people living with dementia and Alzheimer's and their caregivers through memory cafes, music-based and tactile reminiscence programs, staff training, and dementia-friendly environmental design.

      Dementia Overview

      Dementia is an umbrella term for a decline in cognitive function severe enough to interfere with daily life; Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause. It progressively affects memory, thinking, orientation, comprehension, language, and judgment, and it is not a normal part of aging. More than six million Americans are living with Alzheimer's disease, with millions more affected by other dementias or serving as unpaid caregivers. As the population ages, libraries serve growing numbers of patrons experiencing cognitive change and families who need inclusive, low-barrier community s

      Memory Cafes

      A memory cafe (also called an Alzheimer's cafe or memory gathering) is a welcoming, stigma-free social gathering for people living with dementia and their care partners, typically held monthly in a public venue. Libraries increasingly host these in meeting rooms at no cost to attendees. Unlike clinical day programs, memory cafes follow a social model: there are no assessments, no therapy goals, and no attendance requirements. They offer conversation, music, art, refreshments, and themed activities that honor each person's remaining strengths and life story. Memory cafes give caregive

      Sensory Programs

      Libraries develop sensory and reminiscence-based programming that engages multiple senses (sound, touch, sight) to stimulate memory, spark conversation, and reach people whose verbal communication has changed. These rest on evidence that sensory cues can temporarily improve mood and recall. The Music & Memory program, run by a nonprofit of the same name, equips libraries and care partners to loan iPods or mp3 players loaded with personalized playlists drawn from a patron's life soundtrack. Familiar music can trigger memories and reduce anxiety, and Westerville Public Library in Ohio h

      Staff Training

      Frontline library staff regularly encounter patrons in cognitive decline and their families, yet few receive preparation for these interactions. Dementia-friendly training equips staff to respond with understanding rather than distress and to adapt services accordingly. Training programs, often delivered through partnerships with the Alzheimer's Association, its state chapters, or Dementia Friendly America communities, cover the basics of dementia, common behaviors, environmental triggers, and practical strategies. Many culminate in staff becoming 'Dementia Friends' who pledge s

      Dementia-Friendly Design

      Dementia-friendly library design addresses how the physical environment affects people with cognitive impairment. Confusion, overstimulation, and poor signage can make a building inaccessible even when its collections and programs are welcoming. Clear, high-contrast, plainly worded signage with both text and universal symbols, consistent color-coding, and uncluttered sightlines help patrons navigate independently. Some libraries add large-print directional cues and remove visual clutter that competes for attention. Modifications include lowering ambient noise through carpeting, acoustic panels

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries are increasingly recognized as dementia-friendly community hubs because they are free, trusted, and physically accessible spaces that can reduce the isolation facing people with dementia and their caregivers.
      • Memory cafes are the most widely adopted library dementia program, following a social rather than clinical model and typically meeting monthly with music, conversation, and themed activities.
      • The Music & Memory program brings personalized iPod playlists into libraries and care settings, and Westerville Public Library in Ohio is a frequently cited early public-library adopter of the model.
      • Reminiscence and tactile lending collections, themed kits of objects, photos, and prompts, circulate like books and support both individual reminiscence and group programs.
      • Dementia Friendly America, building on Minnesota's ACT on Alzheimer's work, designates communities and recognizes libraries as a key sector for dementia-inclusive change.
      • The Alzheimer's Association is the most common training partner for library staff, alongside state and local dementia-friendly coalitions that turn staff into Dementia Friends.
      • Effective staff communication relies on patience, short sentences, one question at a time, extra wait time, validation rather than correction, and attention to nonverbal cues.
      • Environmental design matters as much as programming: clear wayfinding signage, reduced noise, glare-free lighting, and color contrast help patrons with dementia navigate and stay calm.
      • Caregiver support is a core co-benefit of library dementia programs, giving families respite, peer connection, and access to information and referrals alongside the person living with dementia.
      • Most library dementia services are funded through grants, Friends of the Library groups, and partnerships rather than core operating budgets, which makes sustained, well-publicized programs uneven across the country.

      Library Robotics & Automation Education Deep Dive

      A summary of how US public libraries deliver robotics, coding, and automation education through makerspaces, kits, clubs, and competitions, serving learners from early childhood through adulthood.

      Robotics Overview

      Robotics education in libraries combines building, electronics, and programming to teach learners how autonomous and remote-controlled machines sense, decide, and act. Programs range from dragging visual blocks to control a rolling robot, to wiring microcontrollers and writing code that drives custom-built machines. Workforce demand for automation, mechatronics, and programming skills is rising across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, and agriculture, yet many communities lack school-based engineering pathways. Libraries fill the gap by offering free, low-barrier access to hardware and men

      Youth Robotics

      Youth robotics introduces children and teens to computational thinking through age-appropriate platforms that emphasize play, teamwork, and iterative problem-solving. Library youth programs typically run as weekly clubs, summer camps, or one-day workshops led by librarians, teen volunteers, or visiting mentors. FIRST Lego League (FLL), run by FIRST and the LEGO Group, challenges teams of children ages 4-16 to build and program LEGO Mindstorms or SPIKE Prime robots to complete missions on a themed mat, while also researching a real-world innovation project. Libraries host FLL teams, provide pra

      Robot Kits

      Off-the-shelf robot kits lower the barrier to entry by packaging sensors, motors, and a friendly programming environment into a single durable product. Libraries circulate kits for in-house use and checkout, and structure progressive lessons that move learners from block coding toward text-based languages. The Sphero BOLT is a durable, translucent sphere packed with an 8x8 LED matrix, light and compass sensors, infrared for robot-to-robot communication, and a rechargeable battery. Libraries use the free Sphero Edu app to teach block-based, JavaScript, and drawing-based programming, running act

      Adult Maker

      Adult maker programming targets hobbyists, career changers, and entrepreneurs who want hands-on electronics and coding experience beyond introductory toys. Libraries provide open lab hours, structured workshops, and access to soldering stations, oscilloscopes, and component libraries that individuals could not justify buying themselves. Arduino is an open-source microcontroller platform that libraries use to teach circuit prototyping and embedded C/C++ programming through projects like weather stations, motorized plant-watering systems, and LED displays. Library Arduino workshops typically cov

      Competitions

      Competitive and showcase events turn individual skill-building into communal celebrations that draw families and media attention. Libraries stage these events as entry points for newcomers and as capstones for club members to demonstrate what they built over a season. Robot battle and sumo events invite participants to build or code robots that push each other out of a ring or navigate combat-style challenges, combining engineering, strategy, and showmanship. Libraries run these events using Sphero, LEGO, or custom Arduino bots and often tie them to summer reading themes, drawing large interge

      • Public libraries have become primary free providers of robotics and automation education, especially in communities without school-based STEM pathways.

      • Arduino and Raspberry Pi workshops target adult hobbyists and career changers, building embedded systems and IoT skills relevant to automation careers.
      • Robot battle and sumo events are popular summer-reading tie-ins that draw large intergenerational crowds new to the library.
      • Makerspaces in libraries lower financial barriers by lending expensive hardware, from microcontrollers to 3D printers, that individuals could not justify buying.

      Library Immigration & New American Services Deep Dive

      A comprehensive summary of how American public libraries serve immigrants and new Americans through citizenship resources, English language instruction, multilingual collections, and community integration programming. It synthesizes the frameworks, partnerships, and notable library-system programs that anchor immigrant services across the United States.

      Immigration Overview

      Immigration services in the public library context describe the constellation of resources, programs, and referrals that libraries provide to foreign-born residents, including recent immigrants, refugees, asylees, long-term lawful residents, and individuals pursuing naturalized U.S. citizenship. This population is highly diverse across legal status, country of origin, home language, education, and length of U.S. residence, and the term 'new Americans' is increasingly used to frame these patrons as aspiring or future citizens rather than outsiders. Immigrant patrons arrive with inter

      New Americans Initiative

      The 'New Americans' framing is a contemporary, asset-based approach to immigrant services that emphasizes civic integration, contributions, and belonging rather than deficit or illegality. Many library systems have formalized 'New Americans' programs under this banner, bundling citizenship preparation, English instruction, cultural programming, and navigation assistance into a single welcoming service line. The terminology aligns with national welcoming-city work and with funders that prioritize immigrant integration. Welcoming America is a nonprofit organization that devel

      Language Access

      Language access is foundational to serving new Americans because the ability to obtain information in one's own language shapes every other service interaction. Libraries address language access through multilingual collections and signage, bilingual staff and volunteers, translated program materials, interpretation at events, and digital resources in multiple languages, ensuring that limited-English-proficient patrons can use the library independently. Free English as a Second Language (ESL or ESOL) instruction is among the most common immigration-related services libraries offer. Format

      Citizenship Pathway

      Naturalization is the legal process by which a lawful permanent resident becomes a U.S. citizen, and it requires meeting eligibility criteria, filing an application, passing English and civics tests, and completing an interview and oath ceremony. Libraries support this pathway not by providing legal advice but by offering accurate information, study materials, preparatory classes, and referrals to qualified immigration legal service providers, reducing informational and cost barriers for applicants. Through the USCIS Citizenship Corner partnership, launched around 2013, libraries display dedic

      Community Integration

      Beyond legal status and language, immigrant integration involves social, civic, economic, and cultural participation in the receiving community. Libraries foster this broader integration by convening people across cultures, hosting programming that celebrates heritage while building shared belonging, and connecting new Americans to jobs, health, education, and civic-life resources, positioning the library as a community living room where cross-cultural relationships form. Cultural programming includes heritage-month celebrations, cultural festivals, author talks, music and dance performances,

      Key Findings

      • Public libraries are among the most trusted and accessible public institutions for immigrants because they serve everyone free of charge without regard to legal status.
      • The USCIS Citizenship Corner partnership, launched around 2013, has placed official naturalization study materials in hundreds of public libraries nationwide.
      • Queens Public Library's New Americans Program, founded in 1977, is one of the oldest and most comprehensive library immigrant-services models in the United States.
      • ALA formally supports library services to immigrants of all statuses and opposes policies that would require libraries to collect or share patron immigration status.
      • The Welcoming America framework certifies welcoming communities through the Welcoming Standard, with libraries serving as anchor institutions that operationalize integration at the neighborhood level.
      • Free ESL and ESOL instruction is among the most common immigration-related library service, delivered through conversation groups, one-on-one tutoring, and formal classes.
      • Major urban library systems maintain multilingual collections spanning dozens of languages, with Queens Public Library offering materials in more than 50 languages.
      • Libraries function as naturalization support hubs by providing civics and English test preparation, mock interviews, and naturalization information sessions led by USCIS officers.
      • Programs such as Hartford's The American Place and Denver's Plazas demonstrate how libraries can serve as one-stop integration centers pairing legal referrals with education and cultural programming.
      • Effective immigrant services combine partnerships with USCIS, adult-education providers, Board-of-Immigration-Appeals-recognized legal organizations, and community-based groups to wrap services around immigrant needs.

      Library Genealogy & DNA Research Deep Dive

      This deep summary examines how US public libraries support genetic genealogy and digital family-history research, moving beyond traditional record-based genealogy to address consumer DNA testing education, autosomal and haplogroup analysis, ethnicity-estimate interpretation, Ancestry Library Edition and HeritageQuest Online database access, African American genealogy centered on enslaved-ancestor recovery and the Freedmen's Bureau, and the digitization equipment libraries provide for patron

      DNA Overview

      Genetic genealogy is the use of DNA testing to research ancestry, confirm or refute documentary lineages, identify biological relatives, and infer population origins. Three test types dominate the consumer market. Autosomal DNA tests, offered by AncestryDNA, 23andMe, MyHeritage, and FamilyTreeDNA, survey across all family lines and report cousin matches out to roughly the sixth-cousin range. Y-DNA tests, sold chiefly by FamilyTreeDNA, trace the direct paternal line through the Y chromosome inherited father-to-son and power surname projects. Mitochondrial DNA tests trace the direct maternal lin

      Genetic Genealogy

      Genetic genealogy education in libraries spans a continuum from introductory 'what is DNA testing' sessions to advanced workshops on chromosome mapping, triangulation, and the WATO (What Are the Odds?) probability trees used to evaluate hypothetical relationships among match groups. The field's rapid evolution means programming is frequently updated and often co-led by volunteer experts from genealogical societies and DNA special-interest groups. The largest systems employ dedicated genealogy librarians who maintain current knowledge of autosomal matching, haplogroup migration,

      Database Access

      Subscription genealogy databases are the single most valuable electronic resource libraries provide for family researchers, because the consumer subscriptions cost hundreds of dollars per year while the library editions are free to patrons on site or, in some cases, remotely with a library card. The standard library genealogy suite bundles Ancestry Library Edition for depth of U.S. records on site, HeritageQuest Online for remote access and the Periodical Source Index (PERSI), and increasingly MyHeritage Library Edition for international coverage. During the COVID-19 pandemic many vendors temp

      African American Research

      African American genealogy presents distinctive challenges because the standard documentary trail -- vital records, census schedules, and inherited surnames -- is interrupted or absent for ancestors held in slavery, where families were legally treated as property and records were kept in account books, bills of sale, and plantation ledgers rather than vital registers. Libraries have responded by building dedicated African American genealogy collections, partnering with the Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society and the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Cult

      Preservation Tools

      As family-history research draws patrons into their own family archives -- boxes of photographs, letters, reel-to-reel tapes, VHS cassettes, and fragile documents -- libraries have expanded from providing microfilm readers to offering digitization stations and 'memory labs' where patrons can scan, capture, and preserve personal materials. This equipment-intensive service extends the library's genealogy mission from helping patrons find ancestors to helping them save the evidence the next generation will need, and it aligns with the broader digitization work libraries undertake f

      Key Findings

      • Genetic genealogy -- the use of autosomal, Y-DNA, and mitochondrial DNA testing to confirm lineages, find relatives, and infer origins -- has become a core public-library genealogy service, with libraries teaching interpretation of match lists, shared centimorgans, and ethnicity estimates even though they do not administer tests.
      • AncestryDNA-focused workshops are the most common DNA offering because AncestryDNA is the largest consumer database and the test most patrons bring to the library; librarians teach reading the match list and shared matches while explaining the absence of a chromosome browser and the value of transferring raw data to GEDmatch, FamilyTreeDNA, MyHeritage, and DNA Painter.
      • Ancestry Library Edition, deployed in more than 10,000 libraries, gives patrons free in-building access to the census, vital, immigration, and military records that corroborate the family lines a DNA match suggests, positioning it as the documentary engine that powers library DNA research.
      • HeritageQuest Online remains the principal remote-access genealogy database, licensed for home use with a library card, and its inclusion of the Freedman's Bank records, Revolutionary War pensions, and PERSI makes it especially valuable for African American and early-American research after library hours.
      • Library programming now explicitly addresses the limits of ethnicity estimates for Indigenous, African, and other underrepresented populations, where reference-panel gaps make results imprecise, and frames estimates as directional clues to be tested against documentary and match-list evidence rather than as definitive statements of origin.
      • African American genealogy depends on records outside the standard vital-register system -- enslaver-family wills, bills of sale, plantation ledgers, and the Freedmen's Bureau records of 1865-1872 -- and libraries teach researchers to work backward from the 1870 census through these sources.
      • The Freedmen's Bureau records were digitized through a partnership of the National Archives, FamilySearch, the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture, and the Afro-American Historical and Genealogical Society, and libraries anchor post-emancipation African American research around this freely searchable archive.
      • The 10 Million Names project led by American Ancestors and Villanova University's Last Seen: Finding Family After Slavery project represent a new generation of reconnection initiatives that libraries promote and support, aiming to recover the names of enslaved people and reunite descendants with family separated by sale and forced migration.
      • A growing number of public libraries operate digitization stations and memory labs -- modeled on the District of Columbia Public Library Memory Lab -- equipped with photo, slide, microfilm, and analog-video capture hardware that lets patrons preserve family archives alongside their genealogy research.
      • Libraries play a trusted-advisor role on the privacy and ethics of DNA testing, leading community conversations on consent, unexpected discoveries such as misattributed parentage and unknown siblings, law-enforcement use of consumer databases, and the data-sovereignty concerns of Indigenous and underrepresented communities.

      Library Reentry & Justice-Involved Support Deep Dive

      A structured summary of how US public libraries serve formerly incarcerated people through reentry support, including expungement and record-sealing clinics, job-seeking assistance, technology and device access, and family reconnection resources, drawn from documented programs across many states.

      Reentry Overview

      Reentry, in the library context, refers to the bundle of services public libraries provide to people returning to the community after incarceration in a jail, prison, or detention facility. It is distinct from prison library service (collections and reference inside correctional facilities) and instead centers the public library as a front-door community resource for the roughly 600,000 people released from state and federal prisons and the millions cycling through local jails each year. Services span identification and benefits enrollment, legal record relief, employment, digital access, hous

      Expungement Services

      Expungement and record-relief clinics are among the most concrete reentry services libraries offer. A criminal record, even for an old or dismissed charge, shows up on the background checks that gate employment, housing, licensing, and volunteering. Library-hosted clinics bring volunteer attorneys, public-defender staff, law students, or legal-aid paralegals into the library to screen patrons for eligibility, pull rap sheets, complete petitions, and file them with the court, often at no cost. Because eligibility rules differ by state, charge type, and time elapsed, the clinic model pairs legal

      Job Seeking

      Employment is the single most requested reentry service at most public libraries, and libraries respond with a combination of one-on-one career coaching, resume and interview workshops, employer hiring events, occupational licensing guidance, and connections to American Job Center / workforce-development partners. Librarians help patrons frame gaps in work history, translate skills gained inside (such as culinary, warehousing, or trades work) into civilian resume language, and access online learning platforms and certifications (Northstar, LinkedIn Learning, Google Career Certificates) that re

      Technology Access

      Technology access is foundational to reentry because nearly every reentry task--applying for benefits, scheduling a probation meeting, job searching, telehealth, court e-filing, keeping in touch with family--now assumes a smartphone, an email address, and basic digital literacy. People released after long sentences may never have used a smartphone, app store, or two-factor authentication. Public libraries address this with public computers, free Wi-Fi, printing and scanning, hotspot and device lending, one-on-one tech help, and structured digital-literacy curricula, frequently offered alongsid

      Family Reconnection

      Incarceration severs and strains family relationships, and rebuilding those bonds is both a reentry goal in its own right and a predictor of successful community reintegration. Public libraries support family reconnection by offering a neutral, child-friendly, free meeting space; parenting and co-parenting resources; children's books and early-literacy programming that a returning parent can join; and help with the communications technology that keeps families in contact across distance and confinement. Libraries increasingly treat family reconnection as a distinct reentry service tier al

      Key Findings

      • Public library reentry service treats the library as a free, non-stigmatizing front door for the ~600,000 people released from prison each year, distinct from prison library service inside facilities.
      • Expungement and record-sealing clinics are the most common legal service libraries host, relying on partnerships with legal aid, public defenders, law-school clinics, and Clean Slate / Code for America initiatives.
      • Employment help is the most requested reentry service and is delivered through resume workshops, interview prep, fair-chance employer lists, and connections to American Job Center workforce partners.
      • Libraries actively support Ban the Box both by educating patrons on local fair-chance hiring ordinances and by removing the conviction checkbox from their own municipal hiring as fair-chance employers.
      • Digital literacy for reentry covers basics general classes assume -- email, smartphones, two-factor auth, benefit portals, telehealth -- and is often delivered alongside legal and employment clinics.
      • Device access has moved beyond public computers to lending hotspots, Chromebooks, and tablets, with some libraries partnering with refurbishers to give returning citizens laptops they can keep.
      • Family reconnection is an emerging service tier: libraries offer child-friendly meeting space, parenting classes, storytime, and video-visitation booths that avoid commercial per-minute prison-call fees.
      • Pioneer systems including San Francisco Public Library, Brooklyn Public Library, and DC Public Library helped establish the field after ALA formally prioritized justice-involved service around 2015.
      • Mid-size and rural systems (Gwinnett County GA, Central Arkansas, Grand Rapids MI, Loudoun County VA) demonstrate that reentry clinics scale beyond big cities when legal-aid and reentry-council partners are engaged.
      • Trauma-informed staff training and dedicated reentry staffing, rather than ad-hoc referral, distinguish mature programs and reduce the shame and disclosure barriers that keep returning citizens from seeking help.

      Library Automated Lockers & Kiosks Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries deploy automated material pickup lockers, self-checkout kiosks, and RFID-based self-service technology to extend access beyond physical buildings, serve underserved communities, and reallocate staff labor toward higher-value public service.

      Lockers Overview

      Automated library lockers are secure, often climate-controlled self-service cabinets installed at library branches or off-site partner locations that let patrons retrieve held materials outside staffed hours using a library card, PIN, or app-generated access code. They function analogously to parcel-delivery lockers but are integrated with the library catalog and holds queue so that an item requested online is delivered to a compartment and checked out automatically to the patron upon retrieval. Demand for lockers is driven by several converging needs: patrons who cannot visit during staffed h

      Automated Lockers

      Automated pickup lockers integrate directly with a library's integrated library system (ILS) and holds queue. Staff load requested items into individual compartmented bins, the system notifies the patron by email or text with a one-time access code, and the patron opens the assigned compartment with a card, PIN, or code to retrieve the item, which is checked out automatically or upon retrieval. Many units also accept returns, checking items in and routing them back to the collection or a sorter. The most common configuration is a dedicated holds-pickup locker, but vendors also offer retur

      Self-Checkout

      Self-checkout kiosks let patrons borrow and return items themselves through barcode or RFID scanning, receipt or email confirmation, and security-tag desensitization, reducing checkout queues and freeing staff to focus on assistance and programming. Kiosks are the operational backbone of unattended hours and extended-access service models, and they are typically paired with automated return and sorting equipment for end-to-end self-service. RFID (radio-frequency identification) tags replace or supplement barcodes and electromagnetic security strips; a stack of tagged items placed on the kiosk

      Rural Access

      Lockers and self-service technology are especially valuable for rural and underserved areas where constructing and staffing a full-service branch is not financially viable. A single automated locker placed at a trusted partner site such as a post office, grocery store, school, or community center can deliver library service to a remote town that would otherwise have none, turning a small footprint into a full-service access point. Off-site lockers extend the library's reach into towns and neighborhoods without a branch; patrons browse and request online, staff deliver materials to the loc

      Cost & Benefit

      Self-service technology requires meaningful upfront capital expenditure for RFID collection conversion, kiosks, lockers, and automated material handling, but it yields recurring savings and service-quality gains: faster checkout, shorter queues, the ability to reallocate staff to patron assistance and programming, and expanded hours and locations without proportional increases in staffing cost. For many systems the return on investment is measured both in labor efficiency and in expanded equitable access. By automating routine transactions such as checkout, returns, sorting, and holds pickup,

      • Automated library lockers let patrons retrieve holds 24/7 from secure, card-activated cabinets at branches or off-site community locations, extending service beyond building walls and staffed hours.
      • Bibliotheca smartlockers, EnvisionWare, Tech Logic, and D-Tech International are the leading vendors supplying lockers, self-checkout kiosks, RFID, and automated material handling to US public libraries.
      • RFID self-checkout kiosks read a stack of tagged items simultaneously in a single step, dramatically speeding transactions and enabling automated sorting and security compared with older barcode and electromagnetic systems.
      • Toledo Lucas County Public Library's Library Lockers is a widely cited early US program placing automated pickup lockers at community partner sites for off-hours retrieval.
      • Automated material handling sorters paired with RFID, as at Mid-Continent Public Library's Library Services Center, dramatically increase returns processing throughput for high-volume systems.
      • Self-service models such as Anythink Libraries' retail-style design, which rely on RFID self-check kiosks and reposition staff as roaming guides, demonstrate how kiosks reshape library service design and staffing.
      • Off-site and 24/7 lockers are a key equity strategy for rural and underserved communities, giving branchless neighborhoods local pickup without the cost of building and staffing a new branch.
      • Converting a collection from barcode and EM security to RFID is the foundational capital investment that unlocks self-checkout, automated sorting, and locker integration, but it requires tagging every item.
      • Self-service technology reallocates staff labor from routine transactions to higher-value assistance, reader's advisory, programming, and outreach, improving service quality while controlling labor cost.
      • Platforms such as bibliotheca's open+ extend unattended self-service hours, letting libraries open branches to authorized cardholders during closed hours using access control, kiosks, and surveillance.

      Library Board Games & Tabletop Gaming Deep Dive

      A focused deep dive into board game and tabletop role-playing game services at U.S. public libraries, covering circulating board game collections, Dungeons & Dragons and tabletop RPG programming, family and adult strategy game nights, and the American Library Association's International Games Day initiative. It profiles fifteen notable library board game and tabletop RPG programs across many states and ten key findings about tabletop gaming as a community-building and literacy tool.

      Board Games Overview

      Board games and tabletop gaming in libraries encompass circulating board game collections (modern hobby board games alongside family classics), in-library tabletop events, and structured tabletop role-playing game programs such as Dungeons & Dragons. Together they treat tabletop play as a legitimate, collectible library format and program type distinct from video game lending and esports. Tabletop gaming fills a documented community need for screen-free, face-to-face social activity, offering intergenerational play, low-cost entertainment, and skills development in strategy, negotiation, r

      Game Lending

      Board game lending treats board games as a circulating format analogous to DVDs and video games: patrons check out a boxed game for a fixed loan period, take it home, and return it. Lending collections range from a few dozen family titles at small branches to many hundreds of cataloged hobby games at larger systems, with modern eurogames like Catan, Ticket to Ride, Carcassonne, Azul, and Wingspan among the most common titles alongside party games such as Codenames and Ticket to Ride. Circulating board game collections are typically loaned for one to two weeks, often non-renewable and limited t

      Tabletop RPGs

      Tabletop role-playing game programs bring Dungeons & Dragons and similar RPGs into the library as facilitated, recurring programming. Unlike lending collections, RPG programs emphasize in-person, multi-session play led by a staff Dungeon Master or volunteer Game Master, building ongoing relationships with teen and adult patrons and developing narrative, math, and social skills through collaborative storytelling. Dungeons & Dragons programming surged in U.S. libraries after the launch of D&D fifth edition in 2014 and the mainstream popularity of Stranger Things and Critical Role. Li

      Game Nights

      Library board game nights are recurring, drop-in tabletop events where patrons learn and play games together with library-owned copies and often a staff or volunteer game teacher. They are among the cheapest programs a library can run, requiring only tables, a circulating collection, and a facilitator, and they consistently attract a mix of regulars and first-time visitors across age groups. Family board game nights target children and caregivers with accessible, quick-to-teach titles and emphasize intergenerational play, early literacy, and take-home social-emotional learning. Common selectio

      International Games Day

      International Games Day @ your library is an ALA-coordinated annual event in which participating libraries worldwide open their doors for a single day (later a week) of gaming programming, showcasing board games, tabletop RPGs, video games, and tournaments as legitimate library services. It is the flagship national visibility moment for library tabletop gaming and drives donations of board games from publishers to participating libraries. The event began as National Gaming Day @ your library, first held on November 15, 2008, and was organized by the American Library Association to promote gami

      Key Findings

      • Board game lending is one of the lowest-cost, highest-return services a public library can offer, with modern tabletop collections circulating briskly and drawing patrons who do not otherwise use the library.
      • Dungeons & Dragons is among the most-requested teen programs in U.S. public libraries, with demand surging after D&D fifth edition (2014) and mainstream popularity driven by Stranger Things and Critical Role, often producing waiting lists that force libraries to add tables.
      • National Gaming Day @ your library (2008) became International Games Day (2012) and then International Games Week, reaching more than 1,800 participating libraries across all 50 states and dozens of countries by 2013.
      • The ALA formally recognizes games, including board games and tabletop RPGs, as a legitimate library format through its Games and Gaming Round Table (GamERT, est. 2011), which supplies toolkits and best practices for tabletop programming.
      • Circulating board game collections favor gateway and award-winning hobby titles such as Catan, Ticket to Ride, Azul, Carcassonne, Wingspan, and Codenames, with Spiel des Jahres winners a common selection guide.
      • Tabletop RPG programs build not only social connection but concrete literacy and numeracy skills through rule comprehension, character-sheet math, and collaborative storytelling, aligning with library education missions.
      • Family board game nights and adult strategy game clubs serve distinct audiences and are among the cheapest recurring programs to run, requiring only tables, a lending collection, and a facilitator.
      • Publisher donation drives coordinated through ALA's International Games Day have seeded and expanded board game collections at hundreds of libraries, lowering the barrier to launching tabletop lending.
      • Board game lending requires deliberate cataloging and component-tracking practices, with libraries commonly barcoding whole boxes, limiting loans to one or two games per card, and inventorying pieces to manage loss.
      • No authoritative national census of library board game lending or tabletop RPG programming exists; figures are best-effort estimates drawn from ALA, GamERT, IMLS, and trade press rather than a single federal dataset.

      Library Telehealth & Virtual Health Services Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries deliver telehealth and virtual health services through private kiosks, VA access points, virtual mental-health therapy, and digital-navigator support for health insurance enrollment and health literacy.

      Telehealth Overview

      Telehealth is the delivery of clinical and behavioral health care via real-time, two-way audio-video technology, store-and-forward imaging, and remote patient monitoring. In a library setting it typically means a patron enters a private, sound-isolated space equipped with a monitor, camera, and vital-signs peripherals and connects to a licensed clinician at a distant clinic or health system for a scheduled or walk-in visit. Rural counties, low-income urban neighborhoods, and veteran populations often lack nearby primary care, mental-health providers, or specialists. Patients who cannot travel

      Telehealth Kiosks

      Telehealth kiosks are dedicated, semi-permanent installations inside a library that combine a private enclosure with clinical-grade audio-video and biometric equipment so a patron can complete a full primary-care or behavioral-health visit onsite. The model grew out of rural broadband projects and the COVID-19 surge in virtual care, and is now used in systems across Texas, Tennessee, South Carolina, and several Gulf Coast states. Kiosks are housed in sound-attenuating booths or converted study rooms to satisfy HIPAA privacy requirements, with doors that lock from the inside, occupancy indicato

      Mental Health Telehealth

      Mental-health telehealth at libraries brings licensed therapists and psychiatric providers to patrons who face long waitlists, transportation barriers, cost, or stigma. Because the visit occurs in a private library room rather than a clinic, the model lowers the threshold for people who would not otherwise seek counseling. Virtual therapy sessions are delivered through HIPAA-compliant video platforms, usually by community mental-health centers or nonprofit counseling partners that contract with the library. Sessions are scheduled in advance through library staff or a self-service portal, and t

      VA Telehealth

      The Department of Veterans Affairs operates one of the largest telehealth programs in the country through the Office of Connected Care. Its ATLAS (Accessing Telehealth through Local Access Sites) initiative places VA-equipped telehealth rooms in non-VA community locations, and public libraries are a flagship ATLAS venue type alongside American Legion and VFW posts and Walmart Supercenters. Under ATLAS the VA supplies the room build-out, medical peripherals, and encrypted video infrastructure, while the host library contributes private space, power, broadband, and staff who help veterans log in

      Digital Navigators & Health

      Digital navigators are trained library staff or volunteers who provide one-on-one help with devices, broadband, and online forms. Because so much of the U.S. health system is now online--patient portals, appointment booking, prescription renewal, insurance marketplaces--navigators have become a frontline health-access workforce embedded in the library. During annual and special Affordable Care Act Marketplace open enrollment periods, navigators help patrons create HealthCare.gov accounts, compare plans, upload income and immigration documents, and complete subsidy applications. Many libraries

      • Telehealth kiosks in libraries combine a private HIPAA-compliant booth with a monitor, camera, and biometric peripherals so patrons can complete full clinical visits onsite.
      • The VA's ATLAS initiative is the most formal federal partnership placing VA-equipped telehealth rooms in public libraries, especially in rural states such as North Dakota, Montana, and Alaska.
      • Rural libraries such as Pottsboro (TX) pioneered the library telehealth kiosk model, drawing national recognition from Library Journal and IMLS for rural innovation.
      • Virtual mental-health therapy at libraries lowers stigma and access barriers by offering confidential rooms and staff scheduling rather than requiring a clinic visit.
      • Library crisis support increasingly uses tablets or stations that connect patrons directly to 988 Lifeline counselors and local mobile crisis teams.
      • Digital navigators have become a frontline health-access workforce, helping patrons with patient portals, prescription renewal, telehealth device setup, and reliable health information.
      • During ACA Marketplace open enrollment, many libraries host certified application counselors who provide free one-on-one HealthCare.gov enrollment help.
      • Telehealth visits typically run over encrypted platforms such as Teladoc, Amwell, Doxy.me, or the VA Video Connect application, depending on the clinical partner.
      • Library telehealth partnerships usually split responsibility: the health system supplies clinicians and software while the library supplies the private room, broadband, devices, and scheduling support.
      • Privacy, accessibility, and trust are the defining advantages of the library as a telehealth venue, especially for veterans, older adults, and patrons without home broadband or private space.

      Library Community Gardens & Urban Agriculture Deep Dive

      A deep dive into U.S. public library community gardens, rooftop gardens, urban farming education, composting, and harvest-sharing programs -- how libraries are turning their grounds and rooftops into hands-on sites for food production, agricultural literacy, and neighborhood food sovereignty.

      Gardens Overview

      A library community garden is a cultivated growing space -- raised beds, in-ground plots, containers, or a rooftop installation -- maintained on library property or under library auspices and used for hands-on food production, environmental education, and neighborhood gathering. Unlike a park landscape, a library garden is a working agricultural site paired with the library's educational mission: it is both a place that grows food and a programming platform where planting, composting, seed saving, cooking, and ecology are taught. Many library neighborhoods, especially low-income urban blo

      Library Gardens

      On-site library gardens have proliferated since the early 2010s as libraries reimagined their grounds as active community assets. They range from a few raised beds outside a branch building to full demonstration gardens with hoop houses, pollinator plantings, and outdoor classroom seating. Most are built and maintained through partnerships with master gardener programs, Cooperative Extension, local nonprofits, Friends groups, and volunteer gardeners, because libraries rarely have horticultural staff in-house. Typical on-site gardens use raised beds or containers so they can be installed on law

      Seed Libraries

      Seed libraries housed in public libraries are the connective tissue of library urban agriculture: a free cabinet of packets that patrons borrow at planting time, grow, and replenish with saved seed at season's end. Popularized by Richmond Grows Seed Lending Library at Richmond Public Library (California) in 2010, the model has spread to an estimated 500+ libraries and is almost always paired with the growing education this deep dive centers. A seed library without gardening instruction is just a cabinet; paired with workshops, demonstration gardens, and master-gardener partnerships, it be

      Urban Farming

      Beyond single garden beds, a number of libraries have moved into fuller urban-farming education -- teaching the skills needed to produce meaningful amounts of food in cities and tight spaces, including intensive raised-bed growing, container and vertical gardening, season extension with hoop houses and row covers, and small-space techniques suited to apartment dwellers. This work positions the library as a neighborhood hub for urban-agriculture training, often in cities like Detroit, Cleveland, and Oakland where a broader urban-farming movement is already active and the library extends it with

      Food Education

      Library food education converts garden produce and growing skills into nutrition, cooking, and sharing outcomes. It is the layer that ensures a library garden does more than grow food -- it teaches patrons how to eat well from what they grow and how to distribute surplus to neighbors. This ties urban agriculture back to the library's food-security mission documented in the broader library food programs work, but here the education is rooted in the garden itself rather than in meal service or pantry distribution.       Key Findings

      • Library community gardens pair free public land with the library's educational mission, making them programmed gardens rather than passive landscapes: planting, composting, seed saving, cooking, and ecology are taught in the beds alongside story times and STEM lessons.
      • On-site library gardens overwhelmingly use raised beds and containers so they can be installed on lawns, patios, or paved lots without major earthwork, and are typically built and maintained through partnerships with Cooperative Extension Master Gardeners, Friends groups, and volunteers because libraries rarely have horticultural staff.
      • Rooftop gardens on library buildings, such as the Salt Lake City Public Library Main Library and the Fort Vancouver Regional Library central branch, demonstrate urban greening and stormwater management while serving as elevated agricultural classrooms, though they require structural engineering and irrigation that make them more capital-intensive than ground-level beds.
      • Seed libraries are the connective tissue of library urban agriculture: popularized by Richmond Grows at Richmond Public Library in 2010 and now estimated at 500+ sites, they are most powerful when paired with growing and seed-saving workshops that turn a seed cabinet into a food-self-sufficiency engine.
      • The 2014 Pennsylvania seed-law concern and the subsequent AASCO resolution clarified that noncommercial community seed sharing should be accommodated, giving library seed libraries and the gardens they feed a secure legal footing to expand.
      • Urban-farming education at libraries emphasizes intensive raised-bed growing, container and vertical gardening, and season extension, and is concentrated in cities like Detroit, Cleveland, and Oakland where a broader urban-agriculture movement already exists and the library extends it with free, open-access training.
      • Composting programs -- including worm bins and compost workshops -- close the food-waste loop at the library and tie garden work to sustainability and climate goals, with libraries like Fayetteville Public Library demonstrating the soil-to-food-to-soil cycle that patrons can replicate at home.
      • Nutrition and cooking classes rooted in library gardens, exemplified by the Free Library of Philadelphia's Culinary Literacy Center, convert garden produce into practical healthy-eating skills and often partner with SNAP-Ed and Extension nutrition educators to reach low-income families.
      • Harvest sharing routes garden output back to the community through donations to on-site food pantries and Little Free Pantry boxes, produce giveaways at children's programs, harvest festivals, and give-and-take tables, turning library gardens into neighborhood food resources.
      • No single authoritative registry counts library community gardens or urban-agriculture programs; figures such as the estimated 500+ seed libraries are widely cited community estimates, and program attributions should be verified against current library publications before publication or advocacy use.

      Library Creative Writing & Author Support Deep Dive

      A consolidated reference on how US public libraries support creative writers through workshops, NaNoWriMo write-ins, poetry slams, poet laureate partnerships, memoir classes, and self-publishing services. It documents the library role as an accessible, low-cost incubator for aspiring and emerging authors across diverse communities.

      Writing Overview

      Creative writing and author support programs are library-hosted services that help individuals develop, refine, and publish original literary work. They range from single-session craft workshops and ongoing critique groups to mentorship series, writing contests, author talks, and access to publishing tools such as book printers and design software. Aspiring writers often lack access to affordable instruction, peer feedback, and publishing infrastructure. MFA programs and private writing conferences can be costly and geographically out of reach, so public libraries fill a critical gap by offeri

      Writing Workshops

      Creative writing workshops are among the most common author-support programs offered by US public libraries. Typically led by a published author, a librarian, or a community writing instructor, these sessions cover craft fundamentals such as character development, plot structure, dialogue, setting, revision, and submission strategies. Formats vary from drop-in generative writing sessions to multi-week series that culminate in a public reading. Ongoing creative writing groups meet weekly or monthly at libraries to share works-in-progress and offer peer critique. Many libraries host open writing

      NaNoWriMo

      National Novel Writing Month (NaNoWriMo) is an annual internet-based creative writing challenge that runs each November, challenging participants to draft a 50,000-word novel manuscript in thirty days. Public libraries have become one of the most important physical anchors for the challenge, hosting organized events that give writers accountability, quiet space, and community. Through NaNoWriMo's free Come Write In program, libraries register as official writing locations and receive resources such as promotional kits, signage, and facilitator guides. In November, participating libraries

      Poetry Programs

      Poetry programming at public libraries spans readings, craft workshops, open mics, and youth engagement. Because poetry demands little in the way of materials, it is an accessible entry point for new writers, and libraries frequently use it to celebrate National Poetry Month each April with themed events, displays, and contests. Poetry slams are competitive spoken-word events judged by audience members, and many libraries host them as a youth and young-adult engagement strategy. Library slams are often run in partnership with local poetry slam organizations or with Brave New Voices-affiliated

      Self-Publishing Support

      As the self-publishing industry has matured, public libraries have moved from merely collecting indie titles to actively helping authors produce them. Self-publishing support now includes workshops on ebook formatting, cover design, ISBNs, and metadata; access to production equipment; and platforms that let patrons create and distribute their own books. Libraries support indie authors through digital platforms such as Pressbooks Public, which lets patrons design and export professional-quality ebooks and print-ready files inside the library's online catalog. Many systems also curate self-

      • NaNoWriMo's Come Write In program formalizes the library-as-writing-space role, with hundreds of US library systems registering as official November write-in locations each year.
      • Self-publishing support has expanded well beyond collection development to include Pressbooks, the Indie Author Project, SELF-e, and on-demand book printing equipment.
      • The Sacramento Public Library's I Street Press, built around an Espresso Book Machine, is a landmark example of a library functioning as a micro-publisher for local authors.
      • Poet laureate partnerships are frequently anchored at the public library, which provides venue, programming staff, and archival support for the laureate's community work.
      • Library poetry slams, especially teen-focused events, are a high-engagement pathway that connects youth spoken-word artists with regional and national slam circuits.
      • Memoir and life-story writing classes serve strong demand among older adults and increasingly link to local history and oral history archives hosted by the library.
      • Library makerspaces increasingly include zine and chapbook production tools such as risographs, letterpresses, and bookbinding equipment, lowering barriers to physical publication.
      • Partnerships with nonprofits such as Write Around Portland and national bodies such as the Academy of American Poets let libraries extend writing programming they could not sustain alone.

      Library Podcast Studios & Media Production Deep Dive

      A deep summary of the physical podcast recording studios, audio booths, video production studios, and media production equipment that U.S. public libraries provide for patron use. Complementing the library_podcasts_deep summary (which covers library-produced audio content), this file focuses on the studios, gear, software, and access policies that let community members record their own podcasts and media.

      Studios Overview

      A library podcast or media-production studio is a dedicated, library-operated space -- ranging from a sound-treated audio booth to a full video studio with green screen and lighting -- where patrons can record, edit, and finish podcasts, videos, music, and other media using library-provided equipment and software. These facilities are typically part of a library's makerspace, digital media lab, or teen center, and they give community members access to professional-grade production tools that would be costly to obtain individually. Podcasting and video creation have become mainstream chann

      Recording Studios

      Library media facilities range widely in scope. At the simplest end, a library may offer a single sound-treated podcast booth with a USB microphone and a computer. At the most elaborate, major systems operate multi-room digital media labs with isolated audio booths, video studios with green-screen walls and three-point lighting, and post-production editing suites. Studios grew out of the makerspace movement of the late 2000s and the YOUmedia teen-learning initiative seeded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, which pushed large urban systems to build media-production spaces fo

      Equipment

      Library studios are typically outfitted with a mix of prosumer and professional equipment chosen for durability and ease of use. Gear is curated so that a beginner can operate it after a short orientation while still producing broadcast- credible audio and video. Libraries invest in the same categories of equipment that independent podcasters and small studios use -- microphones, headphones, audio interfaces or mixing consoles, computers, cameras, lighting, and acoustic treatment -- and frequently publish their equipment lists so patrons can learn what they are booking. Condenser and dynamic m

      Software Access

      Library media labs provide the editing software that turns raw recordings into finished podcasts and videos. A deliberate tiered approach is common: free, open-source, or bundled software for beginners, and professional creative-suite software for advanced projects. Because licensing commercial software for public use is costly, libraries often mix free tools with a limited number of paid seats, and some subscribe to Adobe Creative Cloud for in-lab use only. Audacity is the most widely deployed podcast editing software in public libraries: it is free, open-source, cross-platform, and sufficien

      Patron Access

      Access to library studios is governed by booking systems and training requirements designed to protect expensive equipment while keeping the resource equitable. Most systems require a valid library card, a completed orientation or certification, and a reservation; walk-in use is rare. Studios are typically free to use but are time-limited so that many patrons can access them. Policies often restrict use to in-library work only (no off-site equipment checkout for high-end gear), though some libraries loan simpler podcast kits and USB microphones for home use through the circulating collection.

      • Library podcast and media studios grew out of the makerspace movement and the MacArthur Foundation's YOUmedia initiative, which seeded teen media-production spaces in major urban library systems before spreading to all-ages patrons.
      • Audio booths with professional microphones and mixing consoles are the most common library media-production facility, while full video studios with green screens and lighting remain concentrated in larger and better-funded systems.
      • DC Public Library's Studio Lab and Memory Lab at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library are flagship examples, offering recording booths, podcasting gear, and personal archiving equipment after the central library's 2020-2021 modernization.
      • Skokie Public Library's Digital Media Lab, opened in 2009, is a frequently cited early adopter that established the model of a library-run recording booth with certification-based patron access.
      • Nearly all library studios require a valid library card, a completed orientation or certification, and a reservation, making training a built-in digital-literacy benefit rather than a barrier.
      • Audacity is the dominant free, open-source podcast editing software in public libraries because it can be installed on every lab computer without licensing cost and lets patrons continue work at home.
      • Professional creative software such as Adobe Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Adobe Audition is offered on dedicated editing stations in labs that subscribe to Adobe Creative Cloud or maintain Mac-based suites, often alongside the free DaVinci Resolve.
      • Common studio hardware includes Shure SM7B and Audio-Technica microphones, Zoom PodTrak or Rode RodeCaster Pro podcast consoles, Focusrite Scarlett interfaces, Sony MDR-7506 headphones, and green-screen video setups.
      • Some libraries loan simpler podcast kits and USB microphones through the circulating collection for home use, extending access beyond the building while reserving high-end gear for in-lab use only.
      • Booking is typically managed through the library's online reservation system in one- to two-hour blocks, with staff oversight and no-show policies that protect equitable access to scarce studio time.

      Library Coding Classes & Computer Science Deep Dive

      A deep summary of how US public libraries provide coding instruction and computer science education through youth programming, adult reskilling pathways, gender-equity initiatives, and open-source contribution support, serving as free, trusted entry points to computing skills for patrons of all ages and backgrounds.

      Coding Overview

      Computer science education in the public library context encompasses structured and drop-in instruction in computational thinking and programming, spanning visual block-based languages for children (Scratch, Blockly), introductory text-based languages (Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS), and applied topics such as robotics, web development, data science, and game design. Libraries deliver this through staff-led classes, volunteer-led clubs, online curriculum platforms, and self-paced learning circles rather than formal accredited coursework. As computing skills become foundational to modern employm

      Youth Programs

      Youth coding is the most developed strand of library CS education, offered through after-school clubs, summer camps, robotics sessions, and drop-in tinkering times that target children and teens roughly ages 5 to 18. Libraries frequently partner with national curriculum providers and run age-banded sequences that move learners from drag-and-drop blocks toward text-based programming, often tied to creative projects such as animations, games, and story apps. Scratch, developed by the MIT Media Lab and now stewarded by the Scratch Foundation, is the most widely used visual programming environment

      Adult Reskilling

      Adult coding and reskilling programs address workers seeking to change careers, re-enter the workforce, or strengthen digital skills, and grew sharply as libraries responded to economic disruption and employer demand for tech talent. Offerings range from single-session introductions to HTML, Python, or Excel to multi-week structured courses modeled on bootcamp curricula, delivered by library staff, partner nonprofits, or vendor-provided online learning platforms. Libraries partner with coding bootcamps and workforce organizations such as Per Scholas, NPower, Year Up, and LaunchCode to provide

      Girls in Tech

      Gender-equity coding programs respond to the persistent underrepresentation of women and girls in computing, which despite modest gains still sees women earning roughly a fifth to a quarter of US computer science degrees. Public libraries host girls-focused coding clubs and summer programs designed to build confidence and belonging before stereotype threat and peer pressure intensify in the middle-school years, offering safe, mentored spaces often staffed by women instructors and near-peer mentors. Girls Who Code is a national nonprofit that operates free after-school Clubs for students in gra

      Open Source Contribution

      Open-source contribution support helps patrons move from consuming software to producing it publicly, teaching version control, collaboration etiquette, and project communication alongside coding itself. Libraries frame open source as both a technical skill and a civic participation opportunity, aligning with their broader mission of public access and community contribution. Library GitHub workshops typically introduce Git concepts (repositories, commits, branches, pull requests), the GitHub interface, and platform features such as Issues, Projects, and GitHub Pages for free website hosting.       Key Findings

      • US public libraries function as free, trusted on-ramps to computer science education for patrons of all ages, especially where schools lack certified CS teachers.
      • ALA's Libraries Ready to Code initiative, launched with Google support, formally established libraries as CS education providers and seeded hundreds of coding programs nationwide.
      • Scratch and Blockly-based block coding are the dominant entry points for youth programming, frequently paired with Makey Makey, micro:bit, and LEGO robotics kits for physical computing.
      • Hour of Code, organized by Code.org each December, is among the most widely hosted coding events in public libraries, often serving as a gateway to recurring clubs.
      • Google CS First provides free, theme-based video curricula that libraries use to run multi-session clubs for grades 4 to 8 without requiring instructor expertise.
      • Girls Who Code Clubs, hosted at many libraries, move students from Scratch in grades 3 to 5 toward Python and JavaScript and culminate in a community impact project.
      • Adult reskilling programs partner libraries with bootcamps and nonprofits such as Per Scholas, NPower, Year Up, and LaunchCode and with platforms like Udemy and LinkedIn Learning.
      • GitHub workshops and Hacktoberfest events help patrons make first open-source contributions, teaching version control alongside collaboration and documentation skills.
      • Career-transition coding tracks pair technical instruction with resume coaching, mock interviews, and portfolio building to support displaced workers and re-entry populations.
      • Leading systems including Chicago, New York, Queens, Orange County, King County, and Free Library of Philadelphia demonstrate scalable models spanning youth, adult, and equity-focused coding education.

      Library Art Exhibits & Gallery Programs Deep Dive

      A deep summary of gallery spaces, rotating art exhibits, artist-in-residence programs, permanent public art installations, and community and youth art shows at U.S. public libraries.

      Art Overview

      Library art exhibits and gallery spaces are the dedicated walls, vitrines, galleries, and integrated architectural features through which U.S. public libraries display visual art - including paintings, prints, photography, sculpture, textiles, and digital media - for public viewing free of charge. Public libraries are among the most accessible civic spaces in the country, open to all without admission fees, making them uniquely positioned to give every community member - regardless of income or geography - direct contact with original artwork and the artists who make it, addressing a real gap

      Gallery Spaces

      Dedicated gallery spaces in public libraries range from formal named galleries with professional lighting and hanging systems to informal corridor and lobby walls used for monthly rotations, and nearly every medium and large system operates at least one such space at its central library while many branches maintain their own exhibit walls. Exhibition areas typically include a central library gallery with track lighting and museum-grade hanging hardware, branch meeting-room and corridor display walls, glass-fronted display cases for three-dimensional work, and outdoor sculpture gardens or plaza

      Artist Residencies

      Library artist-in-residence programs embed practicing artists in a branch or system for a defined term, giving them studio space, a stipend, and public engagement obligations so that patrons can watch art being made and participate in workshops alongside the resident. Notable residencies include Madison Public Library's Bubbler program, which hosts local artists-in-residence who run workshops and create work in library spaces; the Free Library of Philadelphia's artist residencies tied to neighborhood branches; and Phoenix Public Library's artist-in-residence initiative, all stru

      Public Art

      Permanent public art integrated into library buildings makes the architecture itself a cultural destination, with murals, sculptures, stained glass, and site-specific installations commissioned through percent-for-art programs, capital campaigns, and partnerships with city public-art offices. Iconic permanent installations include the New York Public Library's murals in the Rose Main Reading Room and the sculpted lions Patience and Fortitude flanking the entrance; the Boston Public Library's Edwin Austin Abbey murals and John Singer Sargent murals in the McKim Building; the Minneapol

      Community Art

      Community art programming positions the library as the default neighborhood venue for non-professional and emerging artists, with juried community shows, themed group exhibitions, and dedicated display walls reserved for local creators who lack gallery representation. Many libraries run juried annual community art shows open to any resident, often coordinated with city arts commissions; the Pratt Library in Baltimore, Multnomah County Library in Portland, and Pikes Peak Library District in Colorado all host recurring local-artist exhibition cycles that pair display opportunities with sales sup

      • Public libraries are among the few free, no-admission venues where Americans can encounter original visual art in their everyday routines, making gallery and exhibit programming a core equity strategy for arts access.
      • Dedicated gallery spaces now exist in libraries of widely varying scale, from named galleries at large central libraries like Hartford's ArtWalk and San Francisco's Art and Music Center to corridor walls at small branches.
      • Rotating exhibit calendars - typically four to eight weeks per show - let medium and large systems give dozens of regional artists per year a public venue, often without the commission structure of commercial galleries.
      • Artist-in-residence programs such as Madison Public Library's Bubbler and Phoenix Public Library's residency embed practicing artists in branches who lead workshops and make their creative process visible to patrons.
      • Permanent public art integrated into landmark library buildings - NYPL's Rose Main Reading Room murals, Boston's Abbey and Sargent murals, and Seattle's commissioned installations - makes the architecture itself a cultural destination.
      • Municipal percent-for-art ordinances have channeled capital construction budgets into library public art, as seen at Denver's Central Library and San Antonio's Legorreta-designed Central Library.
      • Community and juried art shows at libraries like Pratt, Multnomah County, and Pikes Peak lower barriers for emerging and non-professional artists to exhibit work and connect with audiences.
      • Youth art displays tied to Youth Art Month and school partnerships give children and teens public exhibition experience and signal to families that libraries value young creative work as genuinely as literacy.
      • ALA, IMLS, and NEA initiatives - including NEA Big Read and IMLS grant programs - have funded arts programming and exhibitions at hundreds of libraries, reinforcing libraries as anchors of local arts ecosystems.
      • Smaller and rural libraries extend gallery access beyond major cities, with branch exhibit walls and community shows giving underserved regions free contact with local artists that museums rarely reach.

      Library Language Learning & World Languages Deep Dive

      A deep dive into how American public libraries support world-language learning and multilingual literacy through digital subscriptions, conversation groups, multilingual collections, foreign film access, and citizenship-language preparation, focused on foreign-language acquisition and heritage-language literacy rather than ESL instruction.

      Language Overview

      World language learning at public libraries refers to services that help patrons acquire and improve proficiency in foreign languages (languages other than English) alongside broader multilingual literacy that lets communities read, speak, and engage with materials in multiple languages. Unlike dedicated ESL instruction, this scope centers on foreign-language acquisition, such as Spanish, Mandarin, French, Arabic, or Korean, and on maintaining literacy in heritage languages. Demand comes from several groups: students meeting academic language requirements, travelers and professionals needing w

      Digital Tools

      The backbone of library world-language learning is a set of vendor-built online platforms that libraries license and patrons unlock free with a library card, in-branch or from home. Mango Languages, Rosetta Stone Library Edition, Pronunciator, and Transparent Language Online are the most common. They differ in pedagogy, conversational, immersive, or drill-based, but all extend equitable, app-based learning to anyone with borrowing privileges. Mango Languages, founded in 2007 and headquartered in Farmington Hills, Michigan, is the most widely adopted library language platform in the United Stat

      Conversation Groups

      Beyond software, libraries sustain human-centered language practice through in-person and virtual groups. These gatherings turn passive study into active speaking, lower the affective barrier of making mistakes, and build cross-cultural community. They range from lightly facilitated drop-in sessions to structured language-exchange pairings, and they complement digital tools by giving learners a live audience for what they study online. Language-exchange programs pair speakers who want to learn each other's languages, for example a native Spanish speaker learning English paired with an Eng

      World Language Collections

      Physical and digital collections in non-English languages are a core, often under-recognized pillar of multilingual literacy. Large urban systems maintain dedicated world-language collections so that heritage speakers, immigrant families, and language learners can read for pleasure and study in their target language. These collections also support children's bilingual literacy, a documented factor in long-term academic outcomes. Major systems hold books, magazines, newspapers, and audiobooks in dozens of languages. NYPL, Chicago Public Library, and Los Angeles Public Library curate collec

      Citizenship Language

      Citizenship language preparation is the crossover where civics content meets English-language readiness for the U.S. naturalization process. Although adjacent to ESL, it is a distinct library service focused on the specific vocabulary, history, and government knowledge the naturalization exam requires. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) formally partners with public libraries to host Citizenship Corners and related programming, making libraries a frontline venue for naturalization readiness. Civics English instruction targets the language and content of the naturalization test:
